## 2026-08-11 - the rule that lets screen readers type is now a tested rule (T222)

Injected text - a screen reader, an on-screen keyboard, `SendInput` with
`KEYEVENTF_UNICODE` - arrives as `VK_PACKET`, and only `TranslateMessage` turns
that packet into the `WM_CHAR` carrying its character. Ghoztty deliberately
SKIPS `TranslateMessage` for keys aimed at a terminal surface (handleKeyEvent
calls ToUnicode itself, and translating a second time races the per-queue
dead-key state - that is what broke ABNT2 composition). So the packet needs an
exemption, and the key handler needs a matching one on its own side: drop the
synthetic key, and clear the produced-text flag first or the injected character
is eaten as a duplicate.

Both halves were bare `if`s - one buried in the message loop, one a third of
the way down a 200-line key handler - and NEITHER had a test, because the thing
that reaches them cannot be delivered to an automated run. A real
`SendInput(KEYEVENTF_UNICODE)` is refused off the input desktop (T207), and the
obvious workaround was measured and does not work: a POSTED `WM_KEYDOWN`
carrying `VK_PACKET` is never translated, since a real packet carries its 16-bit
character out of band and a posted lParam has only the 8-bit scan-code field to
put it in. Delete either `if` and the whole floor stays green; the first person
to notice is someone using a screen reader.

The policy now lives in `src/apprt/win32/translate_policy.zig` - pure, no OS
import - as `isKeyMessage` / `skipTranslate` / `keyDisposition`, with the
reasons written where the rules are. `App.run` and `Surface.handleKeyEvent` both
read it, and `App.zig` carries the drift guard that pins each literal to the
real `w32.*` constant, the same shape `viewer_accel.zig` uses. The loop keeps
its `GetClassLongW` behind `isKeyMessage` so no class-atom syscall lands on a
mouse move or a timer tick, and a unit test sweeps `0..0x1000` requiring
`skipTranslate` to answer false for every message that gate rejects - so the
cheap gate and the real policy cannot drift apart either.

What makes this coverage rather than a refactor is the negative control, run on
the box: dropping the `VK_PACKET` arm of `skipTranslate` exits the win32 lane 1
naming both packet assertions, and restoring it goes green. The interactive
`kb-actions.ps1 -Interactive` still drives the true `SendInput` round trip by
hand; that stays a fallback, not coverage, exactly as T222 required.

Filed T733: running that same broken tree under `-Dtest-filter="T64"` exited 0
with no output, twice, while the unfiltered lane failed immediately. A narrow
re-run is the shortcut `go.md` step 3 points at (`floor-lane.ps1 -Filter`), and
a filter that matches nothing must not be indistinguishable from a filter whose
tests all passed - the same vacuous-green shape as T216/T217/T219, hiding inside
the tool those are run with.

Floor: all three lanes PASS via `floor-lane.ps1 -Lane all` (none 286s, win32
344s, agent 340s); P1-P3 ALL PASS; `kb-actions.ps1` ALL PASS (42 assertions).

## 2026-08-11 - the divider's resize arrow now has to point the right way (T228)

Point at the line between two split panes and the cursor becomes a double
arrow, which is how you know the line can be dragged. Which arrow was decided
by a bare conditional inside a 7000-line window procedure and checked by
nothing: `WM_SETCURSOR` carries no coordinates, so the handler reads
`GetCursorPos`, which answers `-1,-1` on a background desktop and takes the
whole path through to `DefWindowProcW`. T218 measured that when it moved
`split-divider.ps1` off the input desktop and dropped four cursor assertions;
a build that showed a left-right arrow on a line you drag up and down would
have shipped with every lane and every acceptance script green.

The recovery is off the box rather than a weaker probe on it.
`split_geometry.dividerCursor` names the rule - a `horizontal` split puts its
children side by side, so its divider is a VERTICAL line dragged east-west -
and carries the `IDC_*` numbers rather than importing `win32.zig`, which is
what keeps its tests running in every lane, the Mac seat's `none` included.
`Window.zig` calls it for both the split and the hero/carousel divider, and
holds the staple: a win32-lane test asserting those numbers still equal
`w32.IDC_SIZEWE` / `w32.IDC_SIZENS`. Without that second half the pure module
could drift from the constants the handler actually loads and nothing would go
red. Both halves were teeth-checked by breaking them (`67 passed; 1 failed`
standalone, `4466/4536 passed, 1 failed` in the lane) - which is also how the
win32-lane test was proven to be COMPILED into that lane, since T733 makes a
`-Dtest-filter` re-run indistinguishable from a filter that matched nothing.

T228's other half was the cross-pane stale-line scan, and its filed direction -
"fold into T214" - turned out to be closed: T214 finished by deciding routes
1-4 and deliberately NOT building route 0, the app-side GL readback, which is
T275. Re-measuring also narrowed what is worth wanting. The 13 divider-colored
runs a `PrintWindow` capture shows are not a defect any build could fix: the
parent never erases and only repaints the band region, so a healthy product
genuinely leaves old lines in its backing store under the panes, and scoring
them needs a composite the parent is not part of. So the pixel-perfect version
is re-pointed at T275 (filed T734 as its consumer) and the expressible margin
was put back instead, as two assertions per axis that the old wide scan never
made either: the band is solid at THREE points along its length rather than at
its midpoint alone, and the panes tile the split across the other axis, so the
gap is the only parent-visible strip there is. That second one is
`split_geometry`'s tiling invariant - the reason an under-pane stale line is
unreachable on screen - measured on the live layout instead of assumed. Both
come out of one capture, so neither adds a SKIP site; inverting the two
predicates fails exactly the six new assertions and moves nothing else.

Floor: all three lanes PASS via `floor-lane.ps1 -Lane all` (none 135s, win32
334s, agent 367s); P1-P3 ALL PASS; `split-divider.ps1` ALL PASS (57 assertions,
up from 51) three times, with `-NegativeControl` still failing.

## 2026-08-11 - the app now tells tests where its tabs are (T231)

`+list --json` reports each window's tab-strip hit regions - the content band,
every tab, the "+" and the "=" - as a `chrome` object in client coordinates.
They are not a fresh layout pass: `Window.stripRegions` hands back the very
rects `paintTabBar` published and the hit tests read, moved into client space
by `tab_strip_layout.clientRect`. So what a caller is told and what a click
reaches cannot disagree, which a second implementation of the layout can never
promise.

That second implementation is what this deletes. The win32 harness kept one and
it rotted twice against a completely healthy product: a fixed "46px left of the
right edge" written when a single tab still stretched to fill the strip, which
at 125% DPI landed inside the menu button (five failing menu-bar assertions);
then a modelled tab width that stopped matching the moment T235 sized tabs to
their titles (~250px modelled against a real ~344px tab, so the "+" click
landed inside tab 1). T257's answer - measure the run off a capture - fixed the
width but still kept a private copy of the "+"'s own travel rule.

The rule the report hangs on is that an EMPTY rect goes on the wire as `null`:
the "=" on a window whose caption hosts the menu, a tab that did not fit, every
region of a strip that has not painted. Offsetting a zero rect into client
space instead would publish `{0, 40, 0, 72}` - still unhittable, no longer
recognizable as absent - and a consumer taking its center clicks x = 0, which
is tab 1. `tab_strip: null` (no strip on this window) stays distinct from the
whole `chrome` key being absent (a server that cannot say), and the harness
throws on the latter rather than reading it as "no tabs".

Harness side, `ChromeGeometry.ps1`'s header now names THREE sources of truth
where it named two: PUBLISHED (ask the product - for any click target),
DERIVED (a DIP constant restated exactly), MEASURED (a capture - the only one
that can prove something was PAINTED, and now used only for that). `menu-bar`'s
`Strip-Geometry` models nothing at all any more, and `Strip-Top` - a datum that
moved three times in three tasks - is gone, since every point is client-space
to begin with. `tab-strip.ps1` keeps its chiclet scan, because "an inactive tab
is visible against the strip" is a claim only pixels can settle, and now checks
that scan against the published rects; that turned a heuristic into a measured
one on the first run (the scan is 1px generous at each end, chiclet
antialiasing).

Deciding to publish in `+list --json` rather than behind a debug-only verb is
D66 - a debug-gated surface would mean the acceptance suite exercising a path
that does not exist in a shipped build, which is T350's mistake in a new place.
The Mac server half is T735.

Floor: all three lanes PASS via `floor-lane.ps1 -Lane all` (none 130s, win32
178s, agent 335s); P1-P3 ALL PASS. `menu-bar.ps1` (78), `tab-strip.ps1` (58, 1
pre-existing SKIP) and `tab-color.ps1` (17) each ALL PASS three times, with
`menu-bar -NegativeControl` still failing. The three harness sweeps
(exit-code, skip-visibility, verdict-exit) stay at zero.

## 2026-08-11 - a wrong-drive zig cache is now an error sentence, not a panic (T243)

`zig build` from a shell that had not exported `ZIG_GLOBAL_CACHE_DIR` did not
fail here, it PANICKED: `reached unreachable code` out of
`std/Build/Step/Run.zig`, with no `error:` line naming anything in this repo.
The cause is environmental and has nothing to do with whatever was being built -
zig 0.15.2's `Run.convertPathArg` makes an argument relative to the child's cwd
with `std.fs.path.relative`, and across two Windows drives there is no relative
path, so `relative` hands back an absolute one and the assert on the next line
fires. The repo is on `D:`, the default global cache is under `C:\Users\...`,
and a dependency that sets a cwd (uucode's `setCwd(b.path(""))`) is enough to
reach it.

The expensive part was never the failure, it was the misattribution. A panic
with no repo-relative error reads as a transient, so it earns a verbatim retry -
which is exactly what happened in the T225 turn, where the first `zig build` of
the turn panicked, was re-run unchanged on the assumption of a flake, and
panicked identically. Four separate turns paid this (T242, T257/T262, T225), and
two of them searched, failed to find each other's task, and filed a duplicate.
Documentation that has to be *found* kept failing; a diagnostic that fires at
the moment of the panic cannot be missed.

So `build()`'s first statement is now `checkGlobalCacheDrive(b)`, ahead of
anything that could reach the assert. It compares the build root's drive letter
against the resolved global cache's and refuses with one `std.log.err` naming
both drives, the `$env:` and `set` lines to paste, and
`error.GlobalCacheOnDifferentDrive`. It never *sets* the variable: a build
script that silently relocates a user's global cache is its own surprise, and
removing surprises is the whole point.

The decision is pure (`src/build/drive_check.zig`) and **"cannot tell" is always
answered as "no mismatch"** - a POSIX path, a UNC share, a relative path or a
null `Cache.Directory.path` all mean silence. That is what makes this inherently
a no-op on the Mac seat and on any single-drive checkout, rather than something
gated off by OS that could rot. `absoluteRootPath` falls back to the open
handle's `realpathAlloc` when `Cache.Directory.path` is null or relative,
because otherwise the guard would no-op in exactly the shell it exists for; the
`\?\` prefix that comes back from there is understood, `\?\UNC\` is not.

Wiring the tests turned up a second hole worth naming: the main test binary
roots at `src/main.zig` and reaches **no** build logic at all, so a `test` block
written next to a build helper runs in no step. `src/build/build_test.zig` is
the aggregator that fixes that, wired into `test_step` outside the
`emit_lib_vt` guard since it depends on nothing.
`wasm_patch_growable_table.zig`'s blocks are still orphaned and are filed as
**T736** (with a note that a sweep would be better than remembering).

Measured both directions at this HEAD, only the variable changing: unset ->
exit 1 with the diagnostic and no `panic:` in the output; `D:\zig-global-cache`
-> unchanged. Floor: `floor-lane.ps1 -Lane all` PASS (none 141s, win32 339s,
agent 372s), P1-P3 ALL PASS, and `--summary all` shows `run test
ghoztty-build-helpers-test 9 passed`. Docs in CLAUDE.md's Windows build bullet
and in go.md beside the `Select-Object -First N` rule - same trap shape, same
place a turn is already reading when a build fails oddly.

## 2026-08-11 - the tab strip stops dancing when a shell retitles itself (T249)

T235 made a tab's width its title's width, which is what the user asked for and
is right. T249 was filed to go and LOOK at the consequence nobody had checked: a
tab's width is now a function of a string the shell rewrites constantly.

It jumps, and nothing has to be configured for it to. Measured with the app's
own published tab rects (T231's `chrome.tab_strip` in `+list --json` - the rects
its hit tests read, so no second model to rot), 3 tabs, 1400x800, 125% DPI,
default `cmd.exe`, no synthetic titles anywhere: one ordinary
`ping -n 6 127.0.0.1` moved tab 2 and the "+" **+186 px when it started and
-186 px when it finished**, because stock `cmd.exe` retitles itself
`<cmd.exe path> - <command>` for the duration of every command. Mid-command, the
point that had been tab 2's centre was **inside tab 1** - a click there selects
the wrong tab. Over a sweep of six realistic shell titles the per-command deltas
were +152, -363, +46, +365, -423 px, up to 30% of the window width; two of the
five transitions put tab 2's old centre inside tab 1 and two more put it on
empty strip, where a click does nothing at all. Repaint COUNT was never the
issue and is unchanged: `onPaneTitleChanged` dirtied the whole strip band before
T235 too, and only the layout inside it now varies.

The fix is a grow-only ratchet (`tab_strip_layout.applySticky`, pure, asserted
at 1.0/1.25/1.5/2.0). A tab widens the instant its title needs the room; it
narrows only at a structural relayout - a tab opened, closed or reordered, the
window resized, the DPI changed, or the user explicitly renaming the tab. The
split is by who caused the motion: the grow happens as you press Enter, the
shrink fires minutes later attributable to nothing, and an unattributable move
is what walks a click target out from under a stationary hand. The marks are
**released rather than allowed to truncate** - once they no longer fit, every
tab drops back to what its own title needs, so grow-only can never be the reason
a title ellipsizes or the strip goes under pressure. That is the whole reason
the obvious "grow-only forever" shape was not shipped: a tab that once ran
`zig build test -Dapp-runtime=win32` would have kept 546 px for a string nobody
can see.

Same fixture afterwards: 186 px out, **0 px back**; the six-title sweep went
from 1349 px of total strip motion to 200, with the wrong-tab hit gone from
every transition. `test/win32/tab-strip.ps1` grew a section 8 that asserts the
no-motion rule and the re-fit, with two GROW controls beside them so the arm
cannot pass against a frozen strip - and it was shown to fail: `T249_NEUTERED =
true` makes `applySticky` a pass-through, and that build failed exactly the
three no-motion assertions plus the re-fit one (the tab went 526 -> 70 px, the
"+" walked 456) while both grow controls stayed green.

Alternatives are in **D67** (freeze entirely / quantise / debounce - each gives
back something T235 bought, or delays the jump instead of removing it). The
residual is **T737**: a first-ever-longer title still moves the strip once, so
the wrong-tab hit is rare rather than impossible; the candidate is freezing
widths while the pointer is inside the strip, to be measured before it is built.
Design-system §6b gained the rule as its point 5, since it applies to any run of
content-bearing chrome, not just tabs.

One self-inflicted lesson worth the line: a `Get-Content -Raw | Set-Content
-Encoding utf8` round-trip on `tab_strip_layout.zig` mojibaked every em dash and
added a BOM (the known PS5.1 trap), and the repair script then hit a SECOND
PS5.1 trap - comma binds tighter than `+`, so `@('find', 'a' + $x + 'b')` is a
four-element array and `$p[1]` was only `'a'`, truncating 13 lines. Both were
caught and reversed before anything was committed, by a guard in the repair
script and by requiring `git diff` to show a pure-addition diff. Use the Edit
tool on repo text files; PowerShell is for running things, not rewriting them.

## 2026-08-11 - a terminal that comes back twice keeps its history both times (T666)

Quit or crash Ghoztty and your panes came back with their scrollback. Do it a
second time and the scrollback was gone: the pane came back holding only what
was on screen when it died, with no warning and no way to get the rest back.
`test/win32/session-persistence.ps1` had been red on exactly that for days
(B2.7, B3.7), and the shape of the failure - "the pane is 144 bytes" - was in
the task from the start.

**Neither side was dropping it.** The app delivers the history and the agent
delivers the history; a repaint then paints over it. A re-attaching pane paints
the app's own persisted VT snapshot of the screen it had when it was last saved
(WP-D3), and a repaint has no line feeds in it, so every row lands on the
VISIBLE screen and nothing scrolls. The very next thing on the wire is a
full-viewport repaint that homes to row 1: the agent's own `grid_snapshot`,
which opens `ESC[H ESC[2J`, and behind it ConPTY's post-attach fresh paint
(`ESC[?25l ESC[H` + per-line `ESC[K`). Both overwrite exactly the rows the
restore had just drawn. Only what had already reached SCROLLBACK survived - and
in a freshly restored pane, nothing has. That is why the first restore looked
fine (its whole history still fitted in the viewport) and every one after it
came back holding one screen.

This was read off the wire rather than deduced: `drainRing` was temporarily
instrumented to dump each post-attach chunk, and the first chunk of the second
restore is the eraser, in full. Suppressing the agent's `grid_snapshot`
capability (`GHOSTTY_AGENT_SUPPRESS_CAPS=grid_snapshot`, the T469 seam) removed
that chunk and lost the history anyway - which is how ConPTY's own repaint was
identified as the second, independent eraser. A fix aimed at either one alone
would have looked right and changed nothing.

**The fix is the invariant T106 already named for the other attach path**: on
Windows, content survives an attach only if it is in scrollback before the
repaint lands. The pane now PARKS its restored screen - puts the cursor on the
last row and emits one line feed per occupied row, the one operation that moves
a row into scrollback - at the agent's snapshot head, the exact offset where the
replay that continues that screen ends and the repaint of the current one
begins. The repaint then gets a blank viewport, and the history sits above it.
The rule is `src/termio/restore_park.zig` (pure, six none-lane tests), and it is
gated on the peer advertising `grid_snapshot`: a peer that promises no repaint
never has its viewport blanked with nothing coming to fill it.

Parking then exposed a second thing the eraser had been hiding. T106's
replay-geometry reflow was gated to the full-ring attach path, so on the
snapshot path the gap-fill - the same raw, geometry-bound ConPTY bytes, only
shorter - was parsed at whatever width the pane happened to have mid-restore,
and its in-place redraws overwrote the wrong columns. The result was legible
only as shredded text (`...>SPMKal or external command,MK...C1' is not`), and
for as long as the repaint erased it a frame later nobody could see it. Keeping
the history means replaying it correctly, so that reflow now covers both paths;
both boundaries fire at the same offset and share one split of a straddling
chunk (`finishAttachBoundary`, reflow back first so the park scrolls at the
geometry the user is actually looking at).

`session-persistence.ps1` is ALL PASS, including section D's
no-runaway-duplication arm - one screenful may legitimately appear twice now
(the restored tail, then the repaint of it), which is the duplication that
section has always allowed. `session-snapshot-reattach.ps1` (28) and
`session-reattach.ps1` (44) stay ALL PASS.

The fix lives in shared core, so macOS gets it too and has not been watched
doing it (**T741**). Two other things fell out of the measurement. Every
re-attach records a resume offset a few hundred bytes PAST the end of the
agent's stream, because `appliedOffset` counts the repaint bytes the agent
injects as if they were stream bytes; the T532 clamp catches it, which is why it
has only ever surfaced as a warning line, but the bytes between the true
position and the head are then skipped (**T739**). And every VT-stripping regex
in `test\win32` is written with `` `e `` for ESC, which PowerShell 5.1 reads as
the letter `e` - so those helpers delete every `e` from the text and leave the
escape sequences in (**T740**).

## 2026-08-11 - typing `ghoztty` in a folder now opens a window in that folder (T506)

On macOS and Linux, `ghostty` typed at a prompt opens where you are standing.
On Windows it opened in your home folder, always, no matter which project you
had cd'd into. The cause was one line: `Config.probableCliEnvironment()`
returned a hardcoded `false` for Windows, under an upstream comment calling it
"not a real supported target". Every Windows launch therefore resolved the
`working-directory` default to `home`, and the divergence was invisible in the
code because it read as a deliberate decision rather than an unimplemented one.

Implementing it properly is more interesting than it sounds, because two PE
subsystems answer the obvious question differently. A **GUI-subsystem** binary -
what a release `ghoztty.exe` is - never inherits its caller's console, so
`GetConsoleWindow()` is null even when a human typed its name. A
**console-subsystem** binary - every Debug build, and `ghoztty.com` always - is
handed a console by Windows no matter who started it, so merely having one says
nothing. `src/os/cli_launch.zig` answers with three signals instead:

- **`GHOZTTY_CLI_LAUNCH=1`**, set by `runComShimGuiRespawn` on the child it
  spawns. PATHEXT resolves a bare `ghoztty` to the `ghoztty.com` twin (T245),
  whose GUI path respawns `ghoztty.exe` DETACHED - no console, and a parent
  already exiting. That is the launch a human actually performs and the one
  nothing can probe, so the twin tells it. The child consumes the variable and
  clears it, so no pane's shell inherits an internal marker.
- **A console shared with somebody else** (`GetConsoleProcessList() > 1`). A
  console-subsystem build launched from a shell inherits that shell's console. A
  console created FOR us - `CREATE_NEW_CONSOLE`, `CREATE_NO_WINDOW`, an Explorer
  double-click - holds exactly one process. That distinction is what keeps every
  GUI launch in this suite non-CLI, which `new-window-cwd.ps1` A5/A6 depend on.
- **No console at all, but a console-owning parent**
  (`AttachConsole(ATTACH_PARENT_PROCESS)`, released immediately). This is the
  release-build leg, and it is not academic: MSYS/git-bash resolves `ghoztty` to
  `ghoztty.exe`, since its transparent-extension magic covers `.exe` and not
  `.com`.

Two shared-core edits ride along, both Windows-guarded so POSIX is byte-for-byte
unchanged. The CLI default resolves to an **explicit cwd path**, not `.inherit`:
`.inherit` reports `value() == null`, and a null working directory on an agent
OPEN does not mean "the app's cwd", it means the AGENT's - `C:\Windows\System32`
for the one the HKCU Run entry starts - which is precisely the defect T144
fixed. And the `$SHELL` lookup stays off on Windows, because `SHELL` there is an
MSYS artifact holding `/usr/bin/bash`, which the win32 spawn cannot execute;
without that guard, a Ghoztty launched from a git-bash prompt would have come up
with every pane trying to run a POSIX path.

New acceptance script `test\win32\cli-launch-cwd.ps1` (ALL PASS) exercises all
four shapes on the box - the twin, the negative control, a shared console, and a
detached spawn from a console-owning parent - plus an arm that types
`echo T506MARK=[%GHOZTTY_CLI_LAUNCH%]` into the pane and reads it back, so the
marker's clearing is measured rather than assumed. That arm was teeth-checked by
making `clearMarker` a no-op and rebuilding: it went red and nothing else moved.
`auto-launch-cwd.ps1`, `new-window-cwd.ps1` and P1-P3 stay ALL PASS; all three
zig lanes pass.

One thing the validation turned up that is not ours: `persistence-flag.ps1` is
red with `undeclared: 4 of 169`, in `agent-attach-refused.ps1` and
`url-scheme.ps1` - files T506 never touched. Filed as **T744**.

- 2026-08-11: T601 - a local .html file now RENDERS in a viewer pane instead of showing its markup, and reloads in place on save. viewer_content gains Mode.html (html/htm) with usesTemplate()/isLivePage() split out from isFile(), a second virtual host (ghoztty-page) whose grant is the file's own directory, and ReloadReason (a save reloads in place and keeps scroll; +reload bypasses caches). ViewerPane pins the grant per navigation, serves the page host strictly under it with Cache-Control: no-store, recognises the page origin ahead of its https=>web test, and falls back to the template's error card for a missing file. Floor: none/win32/agent PASS, P1-P3 ALL PASS, new test\win32\viewer-html.ps1 ALL PASS (40). Filed T749 (a split off a viewer lands in the app's launch folder - a T506 regression, found by viewer-panes.ps1) and T750 (the MIME table has no fonts/wasm/video; must move on both seats).

- 2026-08-11: T603 - Ctrl+W over the machine chooser now dismisses the chooser. The Mac bug it was filed against (upstream `11fe14bc3`: Cmd-W walked out of the panel's responder chain into the MAIN window and closed a pane behind the dialog) does NOT reproduce here, and that was measured rather than argued: built the app with the new `handleKey` case disabled and ran the new script's `-NegativeControl` arm against it, which passed in full - the chord did nothing at all over the chooser, and the window behind kept every pane while the positive control in the same run closed one with the same chord. Win32 cannot reach the Mac state: the chord is a plain WM_KEYDOWN at a chooser control, the owner window is EnableWindow(0) while the dialog is up, and only a Surface WndProc turns a key into a binding. What was missing was the other half of the parity - Mac's Cmd-W dismisses the dialog and ours did nothing - so `MachineChooser.handleKey` now cancels on ctrl+w (and ctrl+shift+w, the same verb), routing to the teardown path Escape and the close button already use. Alt must be up, because AltGr reports as ctrl+alt and an AltGr+W that types a character has to keep reaching the filter EDIT. - 2026-08-11: T533 - dragging a split divider now moves ONLY that divider. The user's report (2026-08-06, right after T495: "resizing the 1st sizer moves the 2nd sizer... I expect only the 2 panels being sized are [affected]") was drag SEMANTICS, not the drag MAPPING T495 fixed: the root ratio is the boundary between the first pane and the whole right SUBTREE, so leaving the nested ratio alone made the second divider slide by half of whatever the first one travelled and quietly shrank the far pane. New pure `src/apprt/win32/split_resize.zig` - sibling to `split_geometry.zig`, which says where the dragged divider goes while this says what the rest of the tree does about it. `plan()` returns the dragged node's ratio plus the compensating ratios that put every other same-axis boundary back on its pre-drag pixel; it recurses (a four-column run behaves like the three-column case at every level), walks THROUGH a perpendicular split rather than around it (a vertical divider is no boundary on the horizontal axis, but both of its children live in the range that changed - so a grid does not shear), and prunes any subtree whose axis range is unchanged, which leaves the other side bit-identical. Two details are the difference between working and nearly working: every tick re-solves from a PRE-DRAG snapshot rather than from the previous tick (ratios are `f16` and `axis` truncates, so "hold it where it is now" drifts over a few hundred motion ticks - and solving from the original also makes a drag exactly reversible), and the held ratio aims at the CENTER of its target pixel, since aiming at the edge lands a pixel low every time anything rounds down. A squeeze that cannot be honored gives way at the same [0.1, 0.9] band a dragged divider obeys, and the walk continues against the geometry that actually resulted. `Window.zig` snapshots the tab's tree into a fixed 128-node buffer at `startDividerDrag` (no allocation on the message loop) and re-validates it each tick; a tree too big, a divider whose region will not resolve, or a tree rebuilt mid-drag all fall back to the pre-T533 single-node resize rather than to a wrong one. 13 unit tests in the none lane, geometry swept at 1.0/1.25/1.5/2.0, including the defect itself as a control. `test\win32\split-divider.ps1` ALL PASS (62): a +-120px drag of the first divider leaves the second reading 1064 -> 1064, with a control arm proving the first one really tracked - teeth-checked by forcing the compensation off and rebuilding, where those arms go red (54px of slide, far pane 147 -> 93). Floor: none/win32/agent PASS, P1-P3 ALL PASS. Mac checked and does NOT compensate either (`SplitView.swift` binds each nested split to its own geometry), so this is a deliberate divergence rather than a parity port; the Mac half is filed as T754.

- 2026-08-11: T539 - a bare file path in a pane banner is a LINK now, so the user's `D:\...\file.mp4` opens Explorer with the file selected instead of doing nothing. T165 had already built the click side (a path-shaped target is a `.file`, a plain click reveals, Copy Path in the menu); what was missing was that nothing ever HANDED it a path - win32 banner markdown had no autolink pass at all, so only `[label](target)` became a link and a pasted path was inert text. `banner_markdown` gains that pass, Mac's `SurfacePaneBanner.autolink` ported rule for rule (scheme-only URL matching, the word-boundary test, trailing punctuation shed with the balanced-bracket exception, nothing inside a code span or an explicit link's label) with the spellings that are native here added: a drive path (`D:\`, `D:/`), a UNC share (`\\server\share\...`), and the backslash form of `~`, `.` and `..`. Two Windows-shaped details carry the change. The pass runs FIRST in the inline loop, ahead of the backslash-escape branch, because a UNC path opens with the escape character itself - `\\server\share` was otherwise eaten one `\` at a time and rendered `\servershare`; a `\` that does not open a UNC path still falls through, so `\*` escapes exactly as before. And resolution is parse-time against a new `PathContext` (`cwd` from `surface.pwd`, `home` from `homedir.home`) because the parser is what decides whether `.\out\a.mp4` is a link at all: with nothing to resolve against it stays plain text rather than becoming a link that goes nowhere, which is Mac's rule for the same field. `joinPath` collapses `.`/`..` itself rather than calling `std.fs.path.resolveWindows`, which falls back to the PROCESS cwd when its base is not absolute - a banner must never point at the app's launch directory. 8 new unit tests in the none lane, plus the one existing expectation this legitimately changes (an escaped `\[x](https://y.io)` now yields three runs, because the URL left sitting in parens is a bare URL and autolinks on its own - Mac splits it the same way). New section 6j in `test\win32\pane-banner.ps1` (ALL PASS, 110): the right-click menu over the bare path is a FILE menu leading with Reveal in File Explorer, Ctrl+click opens a viewer pane whose `url` is the whole path backslashes and all, and the same path minus its drive prefix opens NO menu at the same pixel. That section started as a link-colored-pixel count and was rewritten: ClearType fringes put blue-dominant pixels on the edge of every glyph, so plain text scored 393 "link" px against a real link's 2413 and no threshold separated them - the menu is binary and needs no constant. - 2026-08-11: T723 - if the background agent stops answering and never comes back, the app keeps trying instead of leaving your panes dead. The unknown the task was filed on is now answered by measurement, and the answer was the worst one: the abort was TERMINAL. `Connection.withLink` fires the link observer only on a real state CHANGE, and the only transition left out of `reconnecting` is to `dead`, which `LinkState` reaches solely via `onSessionGone` - a server-sent DETACHED frame that a wedged or killed agent never sends. So no second down edge ever arrived, `beginAgentSettleWatch` was never re-armed, and nothing re-dialed; the panes stayed frozen until the user quit, which is the exact failure in-place recovery exists to remove. An abort now arms a bounded, backed-off retry - policy pure in `agent_recovery.zig` (`retry_delays_ms` 2/4/8/15/30/30s, `retryDelayMs`, `evaluateRetry`), mechanism in `App.armAgentRecoveryRetry`/`tickAgentRecoveryRetry` on a one-shot timer, armed at the single re-dial-failure site so every caller of recovery inherits it. It stands down the moment the old link heals on its own, because the abort left the panes riding that connection (recovery retires one only when the re-dial SUCCEEDS) and rebuilding over a heal would replace working panes. When the schedule is spent the app says so in the pane, as a give-up banner naming the state and the remedy, and a pane already carrying a banner keeps it (T422's rule); the notice is cleared BEFORE the next capture, since the rebuild restores banners FROM the capture and would otherwise re-apply "your shell is frozen" to the pane that just came back. New sections I and J in `test\win32\agent-recovery.ps1` (ALL PASS, 76): I holds the wedge past the re-dial and then KILLS the frozen agent - no healed link to fall back on, so only the retry can answer - and J is the softer resume arm the task named. Teeth-checked by compiling the arming out, where I goes 5 red including the typed-marker liveness oracle while the app-pid and topology arms still pass, which is why neither can be the oracle. One harness lesson worth keeping: the two arms must run kill-first, because a wedge held past `single_instance.heartbeat_stale_after_ms` (45s) lets the app's own spawned challenger take the stale guard and recovery then succeeds on its first try - an arm that inherits an already-frozen agent never reaches the abort under test, which is how the second arm first failed. Floor: none/win32/agent PASS, P1-P3 ALL PASS. Filed T763 (the Mac half - it has a short ladder inside the re-dial plus a background `warmUp`, and whether that covers a longer wedge is unmeasured) and T764 (a pane opened DURING a wedge is handed the stuck shared connection instead of the documented exec fallback, because `sharedConnection`'s fast path only rejects `.dead`).

- 2026-08-11: T268 - the terminal vanishing when you confirm the agent refresh is a JOB-OBJECT KILL, not a hang and not a crash, and that is now measured rather than hypothesised. The trail T229/T421/T426 built finally had something to say: `%LOCALAPPDATA%\ghoztty\ghoztty.log` holds 8 `user confirmed destructive agent refresh` lines and 6 step trails, and NOT ONE of them completes - `agent restart: pid N terminate returned` and `terminated local agent pid` each have 0 occurrences in 425018 lines. The most recent trail (line 421595) reaches T426's job facts, `self_in_job=yes self_job_flags=0x2000 kill_on_close agent_in_job=yes SHARED_JOB=no`, and stops; three lines later the relaunch guard records `app pid 43076 ENDED during the agent refresh` and restarts it as pid 50572, which is the app running on this box right now. So the app dies inside `TerminateProcess(agent)` - and it dies because it is a MEMBER of the agent's own kill-on-close job while the agent OWNS that job's last handle. `pty_child.zig` creates exactly one process-global job with `JOB_OBJECT_LIMIT_KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE` (0x2000, no breakaway bits), assigns every PTY child to it and holds the handle for the agent's whole life; killing the agent closes it, and the job takes every member down with no exception and no chance to log. Measured live from inside a pane rather than argued: a read-only probe from this session reports `in_job=True`, `LimitFlags = 0x2000` - byte-identical to the dying app's own line - over a member list of exactly 8 processes, the agent's three `cmd.exe` pane shells (`ppid` = `ghoztty-agent.exe`) plus their descendants. The app gets in because `upgrade-ghoztty-windows.ps1` relaunches it with a plain `Start-Process` from a pane descendant, and a child of a job member is auto-assigned. `SHARED_JOB=no` is correct and was never an exoneration: a process is not a member of a job it merely owns a handle to, so T426 measured the right thing and asked the wrong question (its own `yes` came from `agent-upgrade.ps1` arm H, the harness's app-owned jail - the opposite direction, which T426 really did remove). The control comes free from the same probe: `IsProcessInJob` answers False for both the live app (relaunched with `escape=breakaway`) and the live agent, so escaping the job is not a theory about what would help, it is the state the surviving process is already in - and it is why this always looked intermittent, why four repro shapes in T229 all passed (every one launched the app from a harness, i.e. outside the agent's job), and why "it worked when I tried it" was never evidence. Consequence worth naming: the confirm dialog's promised rebuild is not failing, it is unreachable - the trail stops before `in-place recovery: re-dialed` every time. No source changed this turn; the deliverables are the write-up in T268.md, T675 re-scoped from "identify who puts the app in a kill-on-close job" to "break out of it" and raised P2 -> P1 with the answer and a repro requirement (the app must be launched FROM a pane), a pointer added to T426 so its "cause established and removed" is read as one direction of two, and new T771 (the probe asks membership when ownership is what kills; the answerable proxy is whether OUR job contains the agent's own children). Floor: none/win32/agent PASS (161s/223s/229s), P1-P3 ALL PASS against a fresh Debug build at HEAD. One self-inflicted lesson re-learned: a `Get-Content -Raw` + rewrite of T268.md mojibaked every non-ASCII character in it (PS 5.1 reads BOM-less UTF-8 as ANSI), repaired by a strict CP1252->UTF-8 reversal and verified with a mojibake/BOM sweep plus a diff showing zero collateral churn.

- 2026-08-11: T269 - the acceptance suite can now run the SHIPPING build beside the terminal the user is sitting in, which it never could. The filed direction turned out to be half done: T167's `GHOZTTY_AGENT_INSTANCE` already forks the guard mutex, the lock/heartbeat files, the agent pipe, the app's state dir, the autostart Run value and the dir `+sessions` reads, and it is honored in RELEASE builds on purpose - unlike `GHOZTTY_AGENT_BUNDLED_VERSION` and `GHOZTTY_AGENT_PROTO_VERSION`, which are debug-only because they destroy rather than isolate. What was missing was any run that exercised it in the release lineage, i.e. against `local` - the guard the user's own installed agent is holding, with their live panes on it. So `test\win32\agent-instance-lineage.ps1` gained `-Release`: the identical arms against the ReleaseFast staging build, isolated on all three axes (`GHOZTTY_AGENT_INSTANCE` for the agent half, `GHOZTTY_PIPE_SUFFIX` for the app's own endpoint, `LOCALAPPDATA` for every file), and measuring the box it is a guest on rather than promising good manners: every agent it did not start is recorded before and required alive after (in release that set IS the user's agent), the user's `GhozttyAgent` autostart value must be byte-for-byte unchanged, and the suffixed value a RELEASE app does write - a debug one does not - is asserted to be ours and then deleted, since a Run entry pointing into `%TEMP%` would try to start a deleted agent at every logon. Two release-only knobs keep the launch from self-healing into the user's world: `GHOZTTY_URL_SCHEME=0` (a release build registers `HKCU\Software\Classes\ghoztty` at its own exe, so it would repoint the user's real `ghoztty://` links at `zig-out-release`) and `GHOZTTY_PATH_SELFHEAL=0`. Result: `-Release` ALL PASS (26), debug unchanged ALL PASS (24), `-Release -TeethCheck` red in exactly the two D2 assertions (2 FAILURE(S), 23 passed), and afterwards the user's agent pid 24620 still alive, the Run key back to `GhozttyAgent` + the watchdog, and `ghoztty://` still pointing at the installed release. PowerShell 5.1 builds a native command line itself, and its builder is not the inverse of the CRT parser every C/C++/Zig program uses to read one back: measured here with a `GetCommandLineW` oracle, it wraps an argument in quotes only when whitespace appears at a position preceded by an EVEN number of `"` characters, and it copies an embedded `"` through unescaped. Both halves corrupt silently at exit 0. The live cost, found by this task: `upgrade-ghoztty-windows.ps1:905/917` and `watchdog-ghoztty-windows.ps1:120` passed `--command=claude --dangerously-skip-permissions --continue "read go.md and go"`, and ghoztty received `--command=claude ... --continue read` plus `go.md`, `and`, `go` as three stray positionals - so every relaunch after an upgrade or a freeze came up with no loop prompt, while the log printed the correct string. `go-loop-watchdog.ps1` had already met this and routed around it with a generated `.cmd` shim, naming the same symptom in a comment, so it was known at one site and unfixed at the other two. The fix is not an escaper, and that is a proof rather than a preference: escaping `"` as `\"` leaves the `"` in place, so it still counts toward PowerShell's parity while the CRT no longer treats it as structural, and for text whose first space is preceded by an ODD number of quotes - `"a quoted phrase" then more`, an ordinary title - PowerShell declines to wrap, the CRT splits at the spaces, and the structural open quote that would fix it flips the parity straight back. A candidate escaper was written and measured first; it passes 17 of 18 payloads with exactly that class failing. So `scripts\lib\NativeArgv.ps1` builds the command line to the CRT's own rules and hands it to CreateProcess through `ProcessStartInfo.Arguments`, which is total and fixes every flag of every verb at once - no `--title-file`/`--banner-file` pair was added, because the defect is in our PowerShell call sites rather than in the product and a CLI flag is a cross-platform obligation bought to work around one shell (D70 records the call). The converted sites are the two relaunches plus the one HELPER in each of `go-loop-exec.ps1` and `go-loop-watchdog.ps1`, so a call added to those scripts later is safe by default; `--keys-file` stays the transport for a prompt. Bonus: reaching CreateProcess directly captures a GUI-subsystem exe's stdout with no `2>&1` merge, so a stderr line can no longer land inside a `+list --json` those scripts parse (T663 for these callers). Acceptance `test\win32\cli-argv-fidelity.ps1`, ALL PASS at 35 assertions: the token quoter as a pure function, then three hazardous payloads and a safe one round-tripped through `+rename --title=` and `+set-banner` against a live debug instance and read back with `+list --json`, with the naive `& $exe "--flag=$text"` transport re-sending every payload as the negative control (it must arrive corrupted) and a safe payload that must survive both ways, so neither an always-red harness nor a set of payloads that were never at risk can produce a pass. Two separate defects sat behind that one symptom, and only one of them is code: the PRESENTATION of a build with no credential, and the fact that no delivered build has one (the second is T795, gated on decision D72 - only the user has the credential). Mac has never had the presentation hole: `MachineChooserView.accountRow` branches on `RelayAccount.isConfigured` and draws a sentence with NO button (MachineChooserView.swift:1148-1155), while win32's account row knew only three states and drew the enabled button unconditionally - so this is a parity gap, not a new design. `chooser_layout.AccountState` gains `unconfigured` as its fourth member, packing the row with no control at all and the sentence taking the whole band (design system: chrome that controls nothing does not appear), asserted at 1.0/1.25/1.5/2.0; `relay_signin.isConfigured` is the shared resolver Mac's `isConfigured` mirrors; the row says `Google sign-in isn't set up in this build` and the footer hint carries the remedy - both ways to supply an id plus `docs/design/relay-oidc-setup.md` - instead of the old `use Sign in with Google above`, which pointed at a button that is no longer drawn. Deliberately narrow: `unconfigured` replaces only the signed-OUT case, so a stored account is still offered Sign Out (which needs no client id) and an in-flight sign-in still describes itself. `onAccountClicked` refuses the flow as well as the widget hiding it, because a synthesized `BM_CLICK` still reaches a hidden button. WHY IT SHIPPED DEAD is the more useful half: every GUI section of `test\win32\relay-account.ps1` sets `GHOSTTY_GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID=cid-e2e` - a legitimate seam for a fake relay, and also a statement that the unset case is untested. The state every real user meets had never once been exercised, so a dead button read as a fully-tested feature. New section 8 launches without one and asserts the whole presentation, including that a click on the hidden button starts no browser flow and logs no failure, and ends with the identical launch WITH an id as its control, so "no button" cannot pass against a chooser whose account row failed to build. That generalises, and is filed as T796. Two neighbours were red as a direct consequence and are repaired rather than weakened: `chooser-controls.ps1` and `ipc-machine-chooser.ps1` both measure the signed-out button, so both now pin a client id for their launches (their subject is the lookup and the geometry, and which state a build lands in must not depend on whether the box has a `google-client-id.txt`) - and `ipc-machine-chooser`'s null-guard around those measurements became an assertion, since it had been silently skipping two of them. `readDevGoogleClientID` also reads a repo-root `google-client-id.txt` now: the id is baked into the Windows binary too, so a Windows seat should not have to put its build config under `macos/`. Validation: `relay-account.ps1` ALL PASS with section 8 (sections 1-7 unchanged), `chooser-controls.ps1` (46), `ipc-machine-chooser.ps1` (74), plus chooser-menu (57), chooser-sessions (17), chooser-sessions-remote (20), chooser-restore-all (31), chooser-restore-all-remote (40), chooser-open-chord (10), chooser-close-chord (14), chooser-link-hover (22), chrome-theme (64) and host-settings (65) - every script that opens a chooser, since hiding a control changes the Tab cycle. Floor: none/win32/agent PASS via `floor-lane.ps1 -Lane all`, P1-P3 ALL PASS (25/20/16).

- 2026-08-12: T748 - a maximized window that comes back after a restart is actually maximized again, instead of a window Windows still calls maximized sitting at a normal window's size with no border. User report, 2026-08-11: after an upgrade every restored window rendered oddly and had no frame. The mechanism was an ordering one. By the time restore applies a recorded frame the window has already been SHOWN - and shown maximized whenever the T85 placement memory says the user's last window was, which for someone who works maximized is every window on every launch - and `SetWindowPos` moves and resizes a maximized window WITHOUT clearing `WS_MAXIMIZE`. So `IsZoomed` stayed true (caption drops its resize border, chrome lays out for a full-screen window) at the recorded restore-down rect, and the `ShowWindow(SW_MAXIMIZE)` behind it could not undo that: asking for a state the window is already in does nothing. Measured directly before the fix: `restored: 800x600 at 32,32 zoomed=True`. The mirror image was equally broken and is the half nobody had reported - a window the manifest records as NOT maximized, restored while the memory says maximized, kept the maximize style at its small rect. `applyRestoreFrame` now applies both halves with `SetWindowPlacement`, the one call that sets `rcNormalPosition` and the show state together, so no intermediate state exists to be caught in; the pre-show case (a window whose first `ShowWindow` has not happened) still moves with `SetWindowPos` and lets the manifest - not the memory - decide `start_maximized`, and a `GetWindowPlacement` failure falls back to an ORDERED two-step that un-maximizes before it moves. Two things fell out of doing it properly. `WINDOWPLACEMENT.rcNormalPosition` is in workspace coordinates (screen, shifted by the primary work area origin) while the manifest, `restore_frame`'s monitor math and `SetWindowPos` are all in screen coordinates, and the capture side had been storing the raw workspace rect for maximized windows - a taskbar-sized drift on any desktop whose taskbar is at the top or the left, invisible on every other one; both ends now go through the new pure `window_placement.zig` (none lane). And `SW_SHOWNOACTIVATE` through `SetWindowPlacement` DOES clear a maximized state - measured on the box, against what `ShowWindow`'s "most recent size and position" wording suggests - so the un-maximized case keeps the pre-existing no-activation promise instead of having to take the foreground. New acceptance `test\win32\session-restore-maximized.ps1` (ALL PASS, 22) runs both directions with the predicate double-checked: a live-maximized window is the positive control for "fills the screen", and the restored window's `rcNormalPosition` is asserted equal to the manifest's frame, which is what distinguishes a real placement from a call that did nothing to an already-maximized window. Teeth-checked against a binary built from the pre-fix `App.zig`: 3 FAILURE(S) there, ALL PASS here. One harness lesson worth keeping: section B patches the manifest on disk, and writing it with `Set-Content -Encoding UTF8` (PowerShell 5.1 emits a BOM) made the JSON unparseable, restore fell back to "no local manifest", and the fresh window it opened instead looked enough like a restored one to score the section green for the wrong reason.
- 2026-08-12: T745 - a banner table that appeared capped at ~50% of a wide pane was drawing exactly the string it was handed. Reported 2026-08-11 with a screenshot: the pane banner's `Prompt` row stopped near the halfway mark of a ~1900px pane, ending in an ellipsis with the whole right half of the row empty. Reproduced end to end on the test desktop with a window capture, and the renderer came back innocent: fed the same two-row table with the FULL text, the value column ran the entire content width and wrapped; fed the text as the user's banner actually receives it, it stopped at the same halfway mark. The ellipsis is not Ghoztty's tail truncation at all - it is the literal `...` that `~/.claude/scripts/ghoztty-banner.sh`'s `prompt-hook` appends after cutting the auto-seeded prompt to 97 characters, before `+set-banner` is ever called. A cap counted in CHARACTERS cannot know how wide a pane is, so it truncates before the width is used, and on a wide pane 97 characters run out around the middle. `banner_layout.columnWidths` was already correct: on overflow the narrow label column keeps its natural width and every unused pixel goes to the wide value column. The hook's cap is now 400 (a bound on what goes in the per-pane state file, past any width a pane can show), leaving where text stops to the renderer, which word-wraps to the pane's content width and only then ellipsizes at 3 lines. What the repo gained is the measurement that was missing: every T123 oracle in `pane-banner.ps1` 6g is a band HEIGHT, and a column granted only half the pane satisfies all of them - the long value simply wraps one line later - so the suite could not have caught the defect it was reported as. New 6g2 measures the text's own right edge against the content column (chevron reservation excluded, ink threshold 200 so the collapse fade and the elevation shadow cannot pass for text at every x): 96.6% of a 1297px content column on the shipped build, and 33% when rebuilt with `T123_NEUTERED = true`, which restores the pre-T123 360px fixed cap and is the reported symptom exactly. Two `columnWidths` tests at 1.0/1.25/1.5/2.0 pin the same property purely - sum of columns plus gaps equals the available width, and the wide column takes more than 90% of it. Filed D73 for the judgement call: a parity task whose fix landed in an unversioned user-config script outside this repo.
- 2026-08-12: T739 - a pane that reconnects to its background session now writes down the position its session actually reached, so the NEXT reconnect replays everything the program printed in between instead of skipping it. `Remote.appliedOffset()` is what the manifest persists as the next attach's resume point, and it counted every byte fed to the parser - including the two things the agent INJECTS on attach that are not the session's stream at all: its `[N bytes of scrollback lost]` marker and its `grid_snapshot` repaint of the visible screen. So every re-attach recorded a point past the agent's own head by exactly the repaint's size (197 bytes, measured), the next attach was clamped back to the head (T532), and whatever real output sat between the two was never replayed. Invisible on a quiet pane, because the repaint covers the same screen; silently lost output on a busy one. The proposal in the task - "a frame anchored at or below where we already are does not advance us" - cannot work, and that is the interesting part: the repaint is anchored at the head S and so is the first LIVE frame after it, identical on the wire, so only the sender can say which is which. The agent therefore frames its injections as `DATA_REPAINT` (0x15, same `DataPayload`), gated on a new `repaint_data` capability for the reason `open_failed`/`attach_failed` are gated - an unknown opcode is a fatal framing error - and the client tracks position by ANCHOR rather than by counting (`Pane.stream_pos`, advanced by the pure `streamPosAfter`, adopted in `drainRing` when a pre-pop read is followed by an empty pop, which proves every byte handed over is parsed). That second half fixes the evicted-scrollback case for free: the position jumps the hole instead of counting bytes across it. Validating it found a second defect that nothing else could have: a new data-lane opcode was SILENTLY SWALLOWED, because both muxes fold one transport back into two lanes with `frame.type == .data`, so `DATA_REPAINT` went to the CONTROL lane where the control reader ignores what it does not recognize - the agent sent a 197-byte snapshot, the client had negotiated it, and nothing arrived, with no crash and no log. The fold is one shared predicate now (`protocol.onDataLane`), used by `client_mux`, the agent's `mux` and the mock that exists to mirror the rule. New `test\win32\session-resume-offset.ps1` (ALL PASS, 68 assertions): three kill/restore cycles where `requested == head` exactly, with `GHOZTTY_RESUME_COUNT_BYTES=1` as teeth (the pre-T739 accounting, from the same tree, overshoots and gets clamped on every cycle after the first) and a suppressed-capability arm for skew. `session-persistence.ps1` section D now runs a SECOND flood cycle, which is the one whose resume point the previous attach wrote. Filed T803 (the Mac seat's measurement) and T804 (the cross-machine case, where nothing repaints behind the injection and the framing is what saves it).

- 2026-08-12: T773 - the "freshly built binary bakes a stale commit stamp" is a MISREAD, and the misread is what got fixed. `+version` answers for two binaries: its own `Version` block, and a `Running Instance` block describing whatever app is running, fetched over IPC (T52) - and that second block owns the only line literally labelled `commit`. The P1's evidence read it, which is also why a Debug build and a ReleaseFast build "agreed" on a 12-hours-old sha: both probes had dialed the same installed release the 05:17 refresh delivered. Measured live at HEAD `66ad87d45`: one document, `- version: ...+66ad87d45` (this binary, == HEAD) above `- commit  : 445780e49` (the running app, pid 50828); `Resolve-GhozttyExeCommit` returns `66ad87d45` and `Test-CommitsMatch` against HEAD is `True`, so every delivery gate was reading the right number throughout and `launch-upgrade.ps1` would not have refused. The agent's stamp was not stale either, for an unrelated reason: `GhosttyAgent.versionString` deliberately stamps the last commit touching the AGENT's compiled sources, not HEAD, so app and agent disagreeing is the design (a HEAD-derived stamp used to make every release look like a newer agent and prompt users to reset live sessions for an identical binary). What was genuinely wrong: the separation between the two blocks is ONE SPACE (`version:` vs `version :`) and no test held it. `test\win32\upgrade-staleness.ps1` gains A31-A35, a payload in that day's shape whose two blocks name DIFFERENT commits - teeth-checked by relaxing the anchor to `version\s*:`, which turns A33 and A34 red and nothing else - plus B11-B13, which make the freeze checkable instead of assumed (the exact `git log` line `GitVersion.detect` bakes must name HEAD; the exe's stamp must be a real commit object reachable from HEAD). The artifact-level form is deliberately not asserted and the script says why: an mtime cannot tell "built from an older tree" from "the tree moved under a good binary", and both seats push here, so it would fabricate failures (T197). `Invoke-GhozttyVersionText` now bounds the running-app query at `GHOZTTY_IPC_TIMEOUT_MS=2000` - reading a FILE's identity had a hard dependency on an unrelated app answering inside the probe's 20s deadline while T755's default is 30s, so a busy app could turn "read this binary's stamp" into "the delivery cannot verify itself". ALL PASS: upgrade-staleness (101), upgrade-no-fork (128), deliver-windows-build, morning-refresh, build-mode-guard, ipc-version. Filed T805 (make `+version` self-disambiguating on both platforms, since the misreading is a real UX defect in the output).

- 2026-08-12: T744 - every launch in the acceptance suite now states what it wants session persistence to do, so the audit that checks it is green and a future red run means a NEW mistake rather than this old one. Five sites were undeclared, not the four the task was filed for: `session-resume-offset.ps1:255` arrived with T739 in the day between filing and repair, which is this defect's own shape - the property regrows at roughly the rate new acceptance scripts land, and nothing runs the sweep between times (evidence noted onto T777, whose premise this is; the aggregate entry point is T732). Each site was fixed by STATING intent, never by widening what the sweep accepts, and the intent differs per site: `agent-attach-refused.ps1:276` and `session-resume-offset.ps1:255` want persistence ON and say so, because one restores the manifest the section above it wrote and the other WRITES the manifest every restore cycle below it reads back - the flag there would delete the fixture, not isolate the test. The three `url-scheme.ps1` activations (359/368/381) are the marker's own named exemption: `runUrlSchemeActivation` answers and exits before the single-instance bind (`src/main_ghostty.zig:86`, T695), so an activation opens no terminal and never reaches the restore path at all. Each of the three needs its own marker because the lookback is six lines per site, which is the rule working rather than a limitation. Measured: `Get-GhozttyLaunchSites` reports `total=186 undeclared=0`; ALL PASS: persistence-flag (20), url-scheme (32), agent-attach-refused (24), session-resume-offset (68), P1 (25), P2 (20), P3 (16); floor lanes none/win32/agent all PASS.
- 2026-08-12: T783 - an acceptance harness that nobody ran now says so, instead of sitting quietly red. `b64c3e8aa` prefixed every `scripts\go-loop-lock.ps1` message with an ISO timestamp; 26 assertions in `test\win32\go-loop-guard.ps1` anchor on the answer's first word (`^ACQUIRED`, `^held`, `^stale-dead`), so the loop's own harness was red for a day against a lock script that was working perfectly - it is not in the P1-P3 floor and nothing tied a `scripts\go-loop-*.ps1` edit to it. `scripts\guard-due.ps1` answers "has anybody run harness X against the code as it now stands?" from a COMMITTED stamp: a coverage table maps a harness to the files it is about (the `go-loop` row covers `scripts\go-loop-*.ps1`, `scripts\loop-session.ps1` and the harness itself), a clean green run stamps the SHA-256 of each, and `check` reports `GUARD CURRENT` or `GUARD DUE` naming every file that changed, appeared or vanished. Four properties it was built for: it is a CHANGE gate, so a file edited and edited back is not due and a stamp never goes stale with time; hashing folds CRLF and strips a BOM, because `.ps1` carries no `text` attribute in `.gitattributes` and a raw hash would report every file as changed on a differently-configured clone; the stamp is committed, so a `git pull` carrying another seat's loop-script edit reads as DUE here, which no local mtime check can see; and only a CLEAN green run stamps - red stays due, and a run with skipped sections prints `stamp NOT updated` rather than certifying code it did not measure. Two wirings, deliberately unequal in force: `go-loop-exec.ps1 claim` (go.md step 0) REPORTS and can never fail, because a claim that exits nonzero over a stale stamp would wedge the loop, which is the disease and not the cure; `parity-tasks.ps1 validate` (step 6, before every commit) FAILS, with a `-NoGuardDue` hatch that prints that it was used. `-TaskDir` given by a caller means a fixture run and is not gated - a distinction that needs `$TaskDirGiven` captured before the default fills the parameter in. Measured end to end on the real repo, in order: `guard-due check` DUE naming `scripts/go-loop-exec.ps1` + `test/win32/go-loop-guard.ps1` -> `go-loop-guard.ps1` ALL PASS + `STAMPED go-loop (7 files)` -> `GUARD CURRENT go-loop (7 files, stamped 2026-08-12 from 8f94d28c8)` -> `validate` ALL PASS (835 tasks). ALL PASS: guard-due (34 assertions, whose sections D and E measure the two forces against each other against a deliberately-DUE fixture repo), go-loop-guard, P1 (25), P2 (20), P3 (16); floor lanes none/win32/agent all PASS. Filed T806 for the rest of the table - every harness outside the floor still has this gap, and adding a row is the whole cost of closing it.

- 2026-08-12: T460 - a crash now yields its stack on the FIRST occurrence, with no re-run. T450's capture re-runs the crashed binary under cdb, which can only ever describe a crash that agrees to happen twice - and the crash it was built for lands on about half of runs, so the occurrence that actually failed the lane was precisely the one it could not see (D6, user: "identify ways to find crash details faster... we want it to be easy to diagnose crashes so that we can capture and fix them faster"). Nothing needed inventing, which is the finding: measured on this box, WER's LocalDumps is already enabled machine-wide, and a zig Debug binary that dies already leaves a minidump in `%LOCALAPPDATA%\CrashDumps` at the moment it dies - unattended, on the first crash, at zero cost to a run that does not crash - and nothing read it. `cdb -z` of that dump yields exactly what the re-run yields: every thread, the faulting frame (`avthread!boom`) sitting BELOW zig's `handleSegfaultWindows` so the handler's own abort does not destroy it, and source lines - in about a second instead of ~10 minutes. So the fix is a reader (`scripts\lib\CrashDump.ps1`), not a new capture mechanism: `floor-lane.ps1` reads the dump first and reaches the re-run only when there is none, and `crash-catch.ps1` gained `-Last`/`-FromDump` (read a crash that already happened) and `-Status` (is this box armed at all). Three measured facts the design turns on. LocalDumps is HKLM-only - an HKCU key with a DumpFolder was ignored outright and the dump still went to the HKLM default - so a full-memory `DumpType=2` needs elevation and is an upgrade, not a precondition; the default mini dump already carries every thread's stack, which is what a stack question needs. The recorded exception is `0x80000003`, zig's handler aborting, NOT the access violation, so the block says so rather than leaving a reader chasing a breakpoint that never existed. And whether a dump is a crash at all is asked of the FILE, not of cdb: cdb reports `80000003 (Break instruction exception)` off the current context for a dump holding no exception - indistinguishable in its output from a real abort - so a T48 freeze-watchdog dump of a healthy process would have read as a crash and manufactured a stack for a bug that never happened; `Test-MinidumpHasException` reads the stream directory for an ExceptionStream instead. A dump older than the run that is asking is never returned, for the same reason: a wrong stack costs more than no stack. Acceptance `test\win32\crash-first-chance.ps1` ALL PASS (49 assertions, 0 skipped), whose lane arm drives a crasher through the new `floor-lane.ps1 -Command` and requires BOTH directions - the dump path when a dump exists, and, under `GHOZTTY_CRASH_NO_WER=1` (a box with no capture, reproduced from this same tree), the re-run fallback, so "the lane did not re-run" is falsifiable rather than merely observed. Also ALL PASS: crash-stacks (the T450 path untouched), crash-diagnostics, P1-P3; floor lanes none/win32/agent all PASS. Added a `crash-first-chance` row to the T783 guard table so this machinery cannot go quietly red - and adding it broke eight arms of guard-due's own fixture-based harness, which is fixed in the MECHANISM rather than in the test: a row covering no file in the target tree is now `GUARD N/A`, not DUE, since there is nothing there that could have changed. That is what T806 needs before it can add rows en masse. Filed T807 (SkipAudit never examines a scorer verdict line that carries no string literal, so a correct `Write-TestVerdict -Skipped` cannot credit the count on its own), T808 (an elevated one-time arm for full-memory dumps) and T809 (nothing yet reads the APP's own first-crash dump when a GUI acceptance script kills it).
- 2026-08-12: T461 - selecting a remote machine in the chooser now dials it ONCE, and everything about that machine rides the same connection. Every roster fetch of a remote row used to dial the relay, run LIST_SESSIONS and free the connection again, so N refetches cost N WebSocket upgrades and N relay authentications - and, the part that blocks the features stacked on top, there was nowhere to hang anything that has to keep LISTENING (T462's per-session CPU meter needs a connection that outlives one RPC, which a dial-read-free probe cannot host by construction). `App.machine_pool` is the remote-side counterpart to `LocalAgent`'s warm connection and the win32 half of Mac's `MachineConnectionPool.swift` (60ccd4f45). The rules are pure and in the `none` lane - `src/apprt/win32/machine_pool.zig`: keying by ENDPOINT (`relay:<base>|<device>` / `tcp:<host>:<port>`, so two rows naming one device share one socket, and a rotated token is the same machine but is still refreshed on every acquire), the lease refcount (dial on first borrow, free on the LAST release, an inert release for a machine nobody holds), a pool-wide monotonic generation so a dial that lands after its machine was released, invalidated or re-dialed is FREED rather than installed, and a 5s cooldown so a refetch storm cannot become a dial storm. The resources are `MachineConnectionPool.zig`: a detached dial posting `WM_APP+28`, link-state and warm-replay notifications on `WM_APP+27` carrying integers only (a link callback runs on the connection's own reader thread, which may not allocate GUI state or re-enter `Connection`), and an atomically refcounted `Entry` - the pool holds one reference, every borrow holds another - which is Mac's ARC retain in win32 dress and is what makes the invalidation path safe with no synchronous delivery: a borrow the "stop using this" notification has not reached yet is holding the transport up by construction. Only a DEAD link invalidates (the FSM enters `reconnecting` on a few missed heartbeats and snaps back on the next authentic packet - `agent_recovery.settle_ms`'s reasoning, minus the settle window, because nothing here rebuilds windows). `SessionRoster`'s worker lost its relay dial and its whole `OwnedRemote` deep-copy; a remote fetch borrows or does nothing, and the `unauthorized` verdict moved to the pool while the roster keeps printing the same `fetch failed ... state=...` sentence, which is what the suite reads. TWO LIFETIME BUGS found on the way, both fixed here: `MachineChooser.close` - the REAL teardown path - never called `roster.deinit()`, so every chooser dismissal leaked the fetched sessions and the parsed layout manifest (only `destroyState`, the early returns in `open`, did); and that same divergence left the pool lease behind, whose callback context is the chooser, so the SECOND chooser's dial notified the first chooser's ghost and the app died at `0xffffffffffffffff` - caught by the new acceptance script on its first run, which is exactly the "crashes far from the cause" the Mac counterpart's comment warns about. Both paths now go through one `releaseOwned`. New acceptance `test\win32\chooser-conn-pool.ps1` ALL PASS (19), whose oracle is the FAKE RELAY's own request log rather than the app's account of itself: five refetches of one machine, zero further connects, paired with the app's load count because one dial only means something if the fetches ran, plus the chooser's close dropping the connection and a second chooser re-dialing as the control that the pool did not simply stop dialing. T328's Kill re-measured over the pooled connection: `chooser-sessions-remote.ps1` ALL PASS (20) and its `-NegativeControl` arm (13). Neighbours green: chooser-roster-refetch (8), chooser-sessions (17), chooser-restore-all-remote (40), persistence-flag (20), plus the five harness sweeps. Floor: none/win32/agent PASS, P1-P3 ALL PASS (25/20/16). `chooser-resume.ps1` is red at its own setup, pre-existing and already filed as T793. Filed T810 (the Activity Monitor and Restore All still dial their own per-machine connections) and T811 - the agent lane's FIRST run of this turn died after 9432/9512 tests with a DebugAllocator panic inside `Connection.destroy` at the end of T739's repaint test, an intermittent this turn's diff cannot reach (win32 apprt only) and which the identical lane passed on the next run; T460's first-chance dump captured the faulting thread, so the task carries a stack instead of a suspicion.

- 2026-08-12: T467 - the audit of every win32 window class for the redraw bug T456 found in one of them. `CS_HREDRAW | CS_VREDRAW` is what makes Windows invalidate the WHOLE client on a resize instead of only the strip the resize uncovered, and it is a property of the class, set once at registration. Twenty-four registration sites: twenty classes in the app, the agent's never-shown tray window, three test-only parents. Four answered yes and lacked it, all the same shape as the banner - owner-painted, laid out against their own bounds, and returning 1 from `WM_ERASEBKGND` so the stale pixels are not even erased. `ActivityMonitor` is the one that mattered: it is the only panel here the USER resizes by dragging its frame, every element of it is measured from the client rect `layout()` reads back, and `WM_SIZE` only re-places the child controls - so a drag left the whole owner-painted table drawn at the width it used to have. `GhozttyViewerNav` (right-anchored buttons, address field spanning the rest) and `GhozttyViewerFeedback` (pill, carousel and send row placed from width) are resized on every bounds sync with `MoveWindow(.., TRUE)`, which paints what is invalid without making more of it invalid. `GhozttyViewerTOC` survived in practice for an accidental reason worth writing down: `place()` calls `SetWindowRgn(.., TRUE)` right after its `MoveWindow` and that redraws - a side effect, not a contract, and the gutter branch passes a null region. Three of the task's own named suspects answered NO, against the filed suspicion: `Scrollbar`, `KeyStateIndicator` and `ReadonlyBadge` never receive `WM_PAINT` at all - they are `WS_EX_LAYERED` windows painted by `UpdateLayeredWindow`, i.e. push-model, where the class style is inert. The scrollbar thumb IS a function of the track height, as filed; it is simply repainted rather than invalidated, and every resize path calls `repaint()`. The rest are no for stated reasons (flat fill; the top-level window invalidating its caption band and tab strip by hand and deliberately, so a resize does not repaint the child-covered pane area; the renderer redrawing the terminal surface whole every frame; fixed-size `WS_POPUP` dialogs with no `WS_THICKFRAME`, no `WM_SIZE` and no self-resize). The audit table is the deliverable and lives in `docs/design/win32-design-system.md` section 5c, where the next window class will be added, not in the task file. Asserted by a shared probe, `src/apprt/win32/class_redraw.zig`: a real window of the class, on-screen at layered alpha 0 (T456's trap - parked off-monitor it has an empty visible region, Windows invalidates nothing, and the assertion passes for the wrong reason), resized along ONE axis at a time so a class carrying a single style bit cannot pass, reading `GetUpdateRect` back. It registers its own positive and negative control classes, identical but for the style bits, so every run re-proves the probe can tell them apart instead of leaving that to an experiment somebody remembers running. - 2026-08-14: T834 - the instrument built to catch the T443 corruption can aim at its target again. `Invoke-DataBreakProbe` read exactly one prologue shape (`push rbp` / `sub rsp,X` / `lea rbp,[rsp+Y]`) and refused `Page.verifyIntegrity`, because this hunt's own diagnostics had grown that frame to `0x1020` bytes - past 4 KB the compiler allocates the frame with a `__chkstk` stack probe and saves two more registers first. The prologue walk is now a cursor rather than fixed indices: `push rbp`, then any run of callee-saved pushes, then EITHER `sub rsp,X` or `mov eax,X; call __chkstk; sub rsp,rax`, then the `lea`. - 2026-08-14: T477 - the test suite only passed because of how we compile it, and behind that were two real defects, one of them in shipping code. The ReleaseSafe test binary died 10 runs out of 10 at `renderer.cell.test.Contents with zero-sized screen`, always the same address, with nothing on stderr; cdb named it in one stop, and the answer was not a panic at all. The instruction at `test.Contents with zero-sized screen+0x23` is a bare `int 3` sitting immediately after the `call setCursor`, i.e. the optimizer deleted the rest of the test as unreachable. It was entitled to: `Contents.bg_cells` was declared `= undefined`, and two functions free it before anything assigns it - `deinit()` on a `Contents` that was never resized, which is exactly what that four-line test does, and the FIRST `resize()`, which frees the previous buffer before installing the new one. That second one is not a test-only path: `generic.zig` builds the renderer's `Contents` with `.{}` and resizes it, so the shipping renderer performs a `free()` on an undefined slice on every startup, and has been relying on Debug's tolerance for it. The fix is one default value - `&.{}`, which is what the sibling `fg_rows` field already used - and freeing an empty slice is a defined no-op, so both callers become well-defined rather than merely lucky. With that gone the suite advanced 62 tests and segfaulted 10/10 somewhere else: `restoreWindowHasAttachableLeaf ... (T398)` had a local helper that built a `Tab` array from a runtime slice and returned a pointer to it, so the window it handed back pointed into a frame that had already returned. Debug left the bytes intact long enough to read; ReleaseSafe reused the frame. Both are the same class - correctness that Debug's allocator and frame reuse were quietly providing - and neither was visible to 26 consecutive green Debug runs. The suite now runs end to end at ReleaseSafe: `pass=10 fail=0 crash=0` over 10 runs of all 4753 tests, floor `ALL LANES PASS`. Swept `src/` for other escaping `&[_]...` locals; every remaining one is a comptime constant. Filed T846, because nothing in the floor builds tests at ReleaseSafe, which is the whole reason two live defects could sit in the tree unseen.
