- 2026-08-14: T478 - the crash catcher no longer reports a dying program as healthy. Reproduced in a sentence: a Zig panic ends in `int3`, cdb OWNS `int3`, and with no `bpe` filter registered the debugger consumed the break as its own, `g` returned, and the script's next command (`q`) quit - leaving a transcript with no crash block, which parsed as a clean run. Measured on a three-line `@panic` binary that dies `0x80000003` every time: `attempt 1 ran clean in 0s / the program ran to completion (exit 0)`. Two changes, and the second is the one that matters. First, `bpe` joins `$FATAL_FILTERS`, so a panic now yields the full capture - `0x80000003 Break instruction exception at panic!abort+0xe`, frames down to `panic!inner [panic.zig @ 3]`, all threads, a minidump. Second, and independent of whatever cdb can or cannot filter: the cdb script now ends `g; .echo GHOZTTY-EXIT-BEGIN; .lastevent; ...; q`, because `.lastevent` is the ONLY place the debuggee's real exit code exists. cdb's own exit code is 0 whenever `q` killed a still-live debuggee, which is precisely the number that made the panicking binary look healthy - the task file's premise that `Invoke-CrashCatch` "already knows the debuggee's exit code" was wrong, and measuring it was the whole fix. So "ran clean" is now a POSITIVE observation - the debuggee was watched exiting 0 - and every other shape (nonzero exit, a break nothing claimed, a transcript truncated by a timeout kill, no transcript at all) is `UNCAUGHT (exit 0x0000001A -> STATUS_...)` with the transcript kept and a new exit code 3 on `crash-catch.ps1`. The decode is exact rather than by low byte, so a plain `exit(5)` is not announced as an access violation the way CrashDiag's table would have to. `test\win32\crash-stacks.ps1` grows the panic capture (with the bare binary's `0x80000003` as a positive control first, so a panic that stopped panicking cannot make the section pass for the wrong reason), the uncaught-exit path, five synthetic transcripts for the ending-classifier, and the one risk this carries: a `bp0` command file and the panic capture in the SAME cdb session, proving DataBreak's planted breakpoints still fire with `bpe` armed. Two guard rows follow from it - `crash-stacks` (nothing tied a `CrashCatch.ps1` edit to the harness that TESTS it, which is how a month-old blind spot went unasked-about) and `CrashCatch.ps1` added to `crash-databreak`'s coverage, since DataBreak plants through `New-CdbScript` - and `crash-databreak.ps1` learned to stamp itself, having had a guard row and no stamp, so its only route to green was somebody remembering to run `guard-due update` by hand. Green: crash-stacks ALL PASS (54), crash-first-chance ALL PASS (49), crash-databreak ALL PASS, guard-due ALL PASS (36), all four floor lanes, P1-P3. - 2026-08-15: T605 - the in-app activity-state machine is now PROVEN on Windows, and the proving found it broken: under Git Bash / MSYS (how agent hooks run here) `kill -0` answers "No such process" for a LIVE native pid, and a hook spawned by a native agent sees PPID=1 - so every subagent liveness marker was recorded with owner pid 1 and reaped the instant the next sweep ran, dropping the pane to idle while background subagents were still in flight. Validation is main's own oracle, not a port: `scripts/test-activity-state.sh` is vendored pristine at `test/win32/lib/upstream/` (blob-identical to origin/main, asserted every run) and executed VERBATIM under Git Bash against the live win32 asset by the new `test/win32/activity-state.ps1` - the only edit is the one SCRIPT= line, asserted to be exactly one line - so "transitions match the Mac oracle case for case" is 16/16 measured cases, not a claim. Section C then proves what the oracle's all-MSYS pids cannot: a marker written by agent-start carries a real owner (never the PPID=1 fallback), holds the pane busy while that owner lives, is reaped the moment it dies, and a live/dead NATIVE owner pid does the same - plus the kill -0 blindness itself as a negative control, so if a future Git Bash learns native pids the fork's reason goes red and it can be reassessed. - 2026-08-16: T705 - the non-destructive agent upgrade now has its design (the pass D59 asked for), and the design's one load-bearing finding reshapes the whole approach: on Windows the ConPTY's control channel (the HPCON from CreatePseudoConsole) cannot cross a process boundary with documented APIs - its signal/reference handles are sealed inside an opaque struct, and the owner's exit tears down conhost, which terminates the shell before the agent's own kill-on-close job terminates it again. So the accepted design (docs/design/agent-nondestructive-handoff.md) transfers nothing at upgrade time: ownership inverts into a per-session HOLDER process (ghoztty-agent.exe --pty-host) that owns the ConPTY, the shell and its own kill-on-close job, talking to the agent over a per-session owner-only pipe with a versioned HELLO and offset-acked replay. An agent restart then carries nothing - the new agent re-adopts the holders - which collapses the upgrade path and the crash path into the already-shipped in-place-recovery re-attach, so sessions survive agent CRASHES too, a robustness win the transfer designs cannot offer. Undocumented escape hatches (peeking HPCON's layout, hand-spawning conhost, writing the resize packet raw) are recorded and rejected by name: they carry the bytes and leave resize/teardown riding reverse-engineered internals, the "carries some of it silently" outcome the task forbids. POSIX's different wall (fds transfer fine over SCM_RIGHTS; waitpid does not) is tabled for the Mac seat. T705 closes as split: T904 (holder mode + protocol) -> T905 (holder-backed spawns, flag-gated) -> T906 (adoption + gap-fill through an agent kill) -> T907 (READY-gated handoff choreography, rollback that can never land on "neither agent", and a third handoff_now policy arm; carries T705's end-to-end validation criteria verbatim), plus T908 (seat: mac). Docs-only turn, no code changed. - 2026-08-16: T904 - the first increment of the non-destructive agent upgrade is real: a session's ConPTY can now live in a per-session holder process (`ghoztty-agent --pty-host`) instead of the agent, so the agent process is no longer welded to every shell's survival. The holder reuses the production spawn path wholesale (`PtySpawner`/`PtyChild`: ConPTY, env overlay, cwd fallback, shell resolution, kill-on-close Job Object - which in the holder process is the holder's OWN job, so a dead holder still leaks nothing) and serves one owner at a time over an owner-only-DACL named pipe (`\\.\pipe\ghoztty-pty-host[-debug]-<user>-<sid>`, bound through the same `PipeListener`/SDDL path as the agent pipe; bind doubles as the double-spawn guard). The protocol (`pty_host_proto.zig`, pure, unit-tested in the agent lane) is a second compatibility boundary with the app-agent contract's rules in miniature: versioned HELLO (build stamp, shell pid, retained replay window, exit state), ATTACH with the owner's ack, offset-tagged OUTPUT with offset-acknowledged bounded replay (ring drops oldest, a reconnect gap-fills and can name exactly how many bytes were lost), INPUT/RESIZE/SIGNAL/EXIT/SHUTDOWN, unknown frames and trailing payload bytes ignored. Not in this increment: the agent-side spawn path (T905, which inherits the smoke's Owner client as its reference), adoption (T906), choreography (T907). Evidence: new `test\win32\pty-host.ps1` ALL PASS (15 assertions) - the `--pty-host-smoke` end-to-end (echo through the holder, RESIZE visible to the shell via `mode con`, owner killed uncleanly leaves the shell alive, reconnect replays the detached-time output with contiguous offsets, `exit 42` arrives as EXIT code 42, holder finishes after delivery, killing the holder takes the shell subtree via its job) plus a live DACL read of a holder pipe (every allow ACE names the current user). All four floor lanes, P1-P3, isolation-meta and agent-sharing-uplink green; guard row `pty-host` added and stamped. Contract note added to docs/claude/sessions.md.
- 2026-08-17: T906 - a session manager that dies and comes back now picks the SAME shells back up instead of rebuilding them. T905 made the shells survive an agent death (their ConPTY, job and process live in a per-session `--pty-host` holder); this increment is the picking up. A starting agent reads `sessions.json`, dials each recorded holder, HELLOs, and re-ATTACHes at the exact output offset that session's on-disk ring snapshot ends at - all of it before the listener serves its first connection, because a viewer that ATTACHed mid-sweep would see a tombstone and offer a RELAUNCH, spawning a second shell beside the running one. `pty_holder_child.adopt()` is an alternate constructor on the existing owner client rather than a second client, so an adopted session presents the identical `session.Child` and nothing above it knows the difference. Reconciliation is offset-exact and the offset is the SNAPSHOT's, not the live ring's: `sessions.json` gains an additive `holder_offset`, captured beside the ring copy under one lock, and the live position is read through a new optional `Child.deliveredOffset()` called from INSIDE `onChildOutput` - the child's reader thread is parked in that very call, so ring content and offset cannot disagree by a frame, which no timer-based sampling could promise. The restart divider is now DEFERRED for a holder-backed record and drawn only by `abandonHolder`: an adopted session never restarted, and telling the user it did reads as lost work. T906 also closes the leak T905's log flagged - a new orphan sweep enumerates the holder pipe namespace and shuts down every holder no live session record claims, which before this could run until the box rebooted, unreachable by every agent and every viewer. That sweep kills, so it is fenced: the pipe name carries the username AND the build-mode segment, the HELLO (not the connect) is the interlock that proves nobody else owns the holder, and a record is un-claimed only when we positively learned the name no longer belongs to the recorded holder - a two-second dial timeout on a busy box keeps its record, or the sweep would end a live session over a hiccup. The skew rule holds: a holder speaking a protocol this agent cannot serve is left RUNNING and reported, never killed. THE BUG THE NEW HARNESS CAUGHT would have shipped silently: the first identity check compared the holder's HELLO `session_id` against the AGENT's session id, but a holder's id is a fresh random value minted before `SessionTable.create` assigns one - so every adoption was refused, every session was quietly relaunched with a new shell, and the abandoned holder was then reaped. Every pane worked; only an end-to-end script comparing the SHELL PID could see it. The shared identity is the recorded pipe NAME (`pipeNamesHolder`, unit-tested). New `test\win32\holder-adopt.ps1` (ALL PASS, 24) is that script: a holder-backed pane with a typed marker, the manager killed, and then the same shell pid, the same holder, the marker still in scrollback, no restart divider, and a live `Test-PaneLive` round trip - plus section D forcing the orphan case (holder alive, `sessions.json` deleted, relaunch) and asserting the reap. `-NegativeControl` inverts exactly the four adoption assertions and nothing else, so the oracle has been seen red. Filed T911: the owner ACKs on delivery and an ACK is the holder's permission to free, so bytes written since the last ring snapshot are not in the replay buffer after a crash - reported out loud rather than silent, and invisible in this harness for an honest reason (the app never restarts, so the grid it reads never went through the agent's ring). New guard row `holder-adopt`. Green: floor lanes lib/none/win32/agent all PASS, holder-adopt ALL PASS (24), pty-holder ALL PASS (22), agent-recovery ALL PASS (76), session-persistence ALL PASS, agent-sharing-uplink ALL PASS (18), isolation-meta ALL PASS (7), P1/P2/P3 ALL PASS (25/20/16). release-artifacts re-ran ALL PASS with only its two Docker packaging checks skipped (Docker down, its designed SKIP path), so this commit uses validate's -NoGuardDue hatch for that one guard until a Docker-up run re-stamps.
- 2026-08-17: T907 - the background session manager now updates itself while you keep working: no dialog, nothing closed. This is the payoff of the T705 split (T904 holders, T905 holder-backed spawning, T906 re-adoption) and it closes the T662 defect - a box with one always-open pane could previously only adopt an agent fix by ending every session or rebooting, so in practice it stayed old for weeks. New `src/remote/agent/handoff.zig`: a supervisor thread in the local pipe daemon watches the binary beside it (its own image path with a trailing `.bak`/`.bak-*` stripped, which IS the newer build's path because every delivery renames the running exe out of the way), probes it with `--version` cached on size+mtime, and on stale-AND-every-live-session-holder-backed spawns it out of our job with the SAME argv plus `--handoff-successor=<private nonce pipe>`. The successor binds that pipe first, sends `READY <pid> <stamp>`, and takes no single-instance guard and binds nothing public until GO - so every failure before GO terminates it and the ORIGINAL agent is untouched, which is what makes 'neither agent' unreachable by construction. On READY the old agent snapshots its rings and persists `sessions.json` (the successor's ATTACH ack offsets) and `exit(0)`s; process death is what releases the holders, so nothing is terminated and the shells never stop. DECIDED BY THE AGENT, NOT THE APP (mechanism call, recorded in the task): it is the only side that knows which sessions are holder-backed, it needs no new wire opcode to act on that, and it must work with no app running at all - the unattended morning refresh deliberately never touches the agent. The app's half is to STAND DOWN, which is the new `agent_upgrade.Action.handoff_now` arm, gated on `capability.agent_handoff` negotiated in BOTH directions so an older peer on either side keeps the pre-T907 policy exactly. Mixed generations drain lazily - a legacy session cannot cross a process boundary at all, so the handoff waits and says so, and `+sessions --agent` now answers `handoff: ready|draining|unsupported` with the count that is holding it back. Two defects the acceptance caught, both in the new code: the debug force seam refused a successor reporting our own stamp, which is exactly the two-copies-of-one-binary shape a test must use, so the whole arm was unreachable; and the shared `Test-PaneLive` oracle sends once and then polls, so its keystrokes landed in a surface the app was about to replace during in-place recovery and could never reappear - the pane was live throughout, which a hand-typed token proved. - 2026-08-17: **A delivered Windows build can sign in, and one that cannot says so** (T795). Relay sign-in needs a public Google OAuth client id stamped in at build time; a build with none can only ever answer `NoClientId`, which since T747 the machine chooser states rather than offering a dead button. What nobody could see is that EVERY published Windows artifact was in that state: `release.yml`'s macOS job has passed `-Dgoogle-client-id` from the `GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID` repository secret since T93, `release-windows.yml` passed nothing, and a CI runner has no git-ignored `google-client-id.txt` to fall back on - so the MSI and portable ZIP from a tag shipped with sign-in unavailable while the DMG built from that same tag worked. Both workflows now bake the same secret, threaded through `dist/windows-installer/build-release-artifacts.sh`, which passes the flag **only when the variable is non-empty**: an explicit `-Dgoogle-client-id=""` satisfies the build option and would short-circuit the repo-root file fallback that is D72's answer for an on-box build. The state is now observable per binary - `ghoztty +version` prints `relay sign-in : configured (<id>)` or `not configured (no google client id baked in)` under Build Config, from `src/cli/version.zig`, so it lands on both seats; the id is printed because it is public (it appears in the browser URL, and macOS ships it readable in its Info.plist), which is what makes a WRONG id detectable rather than only a missing one. The BAKE is reported deliberately, not what `resolveClientId` would resolve, so the line answers "what do these bytes carry" instead of "what would this shell do". `deliver-windows-build.ps1` announces the staged build's state once up front - a build that cannot sign in is a loud WARNING and never a failure, since the id is build configuration a box may legitimately not have - and then compares every delivered `ghoztty.exe`/`.com` against staging; a pre-T795 binary reports nothing, reads as *unreported*, and asserts nothing. Measured on the box, and it is the first end-to-end proof that D72's chosen mechanism bakes at all: a synthetic id in a repo-root `google-client-id.txt` produced `configured (795-onbox-proof.apps.googleusercontent.com)` from the built exe, and the same tree with the file deleted and rebuilt produced `not configured` - which is the state `zig-out` was left in, so no fake id can resurrect T747's dead button. Also added the guard-due row `deliver-verify`: the delivery harness proves the Desktop portable, the share, the loose agent and the ZIP actually received the build, every claim it makes is a read-back, and it had no row at all, so an edit that weakened one turned a delivery back into an assertion with no lane going red. - 2026-08-17: T802 - double-clicking a link in a pane now hands back the whole link instead of the fragment before the first colon. The defect was a product one and it lived in the win32 message pump, not in link detection (which the T757 instrumentation had already shown succeeding): every Windows mouse message carries a client point, and `handleMouseButton` forwarded that point to the core ahead of EVERY button message - the call exists so a press lands on the right cell when no `WM_MOUSEMOVE` preceded it (posted input, a pane appearing under a stationary cursor). With the left button still down the core reads a position update as a DRAG, so the button-up that ENDS a double-click arrived as a zero-distance word-drag and `dragLeftClickDouble` re-derived the plain word over the link the press had just selected; `:` is a word boundary, hence `https`. macOS never had it - `mouseUp` in `SurfaceView_AppKit.swift` sends no position at all - which is why this read as a Windows-only gesture bug. The harness was ruled out by reading it: its one posted move lands before the first press, when no button is down, and nothing is posted between press #2 and its release. Fixed in both layers, because they close different halves: `samePin` in core `Surface.zig` makes a double- OR triple-click drag that resolves to the very cell the click landed on a no-op (re-deriving a word/line from that cell can only reproduce what the click made, or destroy something richer - it was also silently clobbering `ctrl`+triple-click's OUTPUT selection with the plain line, and it is what a trackpad double-tap that wobbles inside the cell hits on any platform), and `cursorMoved` in the win32 apprt stops the redundant event being manufactured at all by forwarding a button message's point only when it is news. Being shared core, the guard reaches macOS: filed T917 for that seat to confirm the gesture and the drag-to-extend behavior there. Green: `terminal-link-paths` ALL PASS (23) with new sections D (a plain double-click selects the whole URL and never the bare `https`), E (the same gesture with a pointer event between press and release - the core guard's own arm) and F (the whole `Q:\Users\David\clip.mp4`), plus a `terminal-link-paths` guard-due row and self-stamp it never had; unit tests both lanes (`samePin` in the core lane, `cursorMoved` in win32); floor lib/none/win32/agent ALL LANES PASS; P1/P2/P3 ALL PASS; `isolation-meta` ALL PASS. `release-artifacts` stays due on a Docker-less box (T914), so `validate -NoGuardDue`. Filed T916 - the acceptance row walk does not actually walk rows: an instrumented build showed the core resolving a y about 39.4x the screen y posted (a constant 100/2.54 across samples), so every probe clamps to the bottom row, which is why section E asserts selection GRANULARITY rather than one exact string until that is understood.
- 2026-08-17: T811 - the intermittent abort at the end of the connection test lane was never a crash in shipped agent code: it was an ordinary test failure whose ERROR PATH detonated. The T739 repaint test tracks a pane whose inbound ring is a STACK `ring.Channel`, and `Connection.destroy` frees any pane still tracked by way of `alloc.destroy(pane.ring)` - correct for the heap rings production always tracks, an invalid free for this one. Before T536's audit the test untracked its pane on the last line of the body, so any early `try` failure after `trackPane` left it tracked and the DebugAllocator panicked `Invalid free`, aborting the process (exit 3) BEFORE the real failure was printed - which is why the 2026-08-12 dump named `Connection.destroy` and the underlying flake stayed invisible. An older agent ignores the field and the client injects after its drain instead - visible-but-racy rather than absent. Because `restore` replays nothing, the defect lives only on the two policies that DO relaunch, so the notice slot here carries the mode reset rather than a sentence. The on-box oracle is new and cost three measured surprises to build: `+send-keys` concatenates adjacent text arguments with NO separator (the first run's probe arrived as `probe.cmdVTPRE1003` and read as "never reset"), `\t`/`\n`/`\r`/`\`/`\e` are escapes in text so a path through `\Temp\t824probe\` grows a TAB, and `[Console]::KeyAvailable` throws the moment stdin is not a console. (1) `OpenClipboard` does not queue - it fails outright while any other process holds it, which something routinely does for a few milliseconds after a copy - and a refused open was a silent no-op. New shared `src/apprt/win32/clipboard_open.zig` retries on a bounded budget (8 attempts, 15ms apart, ~120ms worst case); ViewerPane's two text helpers and `clipboard_image`'s private copy of the same loop both go through it now, which is a user-facing fix as well as a test one - the viewer's link menu Copy (T826) silently did nothing whenever it lost that race. (2) The 10-in-32 flake itself was not the open failing but the BYTES being overwritten: between our browser writing the needle and our poll reading it, a rival test process wrote its own sentinel or put the user's saved clipboard back, so the poll ran out and reported "the copy never landed" over a copy that landed perfectly. No deadline could have fixed that, which is why the obvious-looking retry-with-a-longer-deadline direction was rejected on evidence. The processes take turns instead, on a named mutex (`Local\ghoztty-viewer-clipboard-test`) held across each critical region (sentinel -> press -> read) and across the user-clipboard restore, acquired while STILL PUMPING the message loop since WebView2 delivers every callback through it; WAIT_ABANDONED counts as an acquisition, so a crashed holder cannot wedge the lane. Measured, not asserted: `test-binary-soak.ps1 -Lane win32 -Mode standalone -Runs 32 -Concurrency 32` went from 10 failures in 32 to `pass=32 fail=0 crash=0`, with all 32 logs carrying the real `copy[web]: clipboard=the quick brown fox` line and zero lock-timeout lines - so every run executed the section rather than skipping past it. Negative control: pressing Quote instead of Copy (`selectionDriverJs press_first = true`) puts it red at exactly `expect(copied != null)` after `clipboard=null`, so the lock does not mask a real failure. Floor lanes lib/none/win32/agent ALL PASS (win32 re-run after the last edit), P1/P2/P3 ALL PASS. The code landed in `0d835a1b3`, whose subject is about T857 and not this: a second Claude window sharing this working tree ran an `-A` commit in the gap between this turn's `git add` and its `git commit`, so git committed an index holding both sets of changes, and it was pushed before that was noticed. - 2026-08-17: T851 - starting a second copy of Ghoztty no longer takes the running copy's terminals away from it. The installed release and the Desktop portable copy are same-lineage instances sharing one agent and one session-layout manifest, and launch restore gated every window on "alive OR relaunchable tombstone" with no regard for whether a session was currently ATTACHED. Since the agent rebinds a session to the NEWEST attach, the second launch adopted the first app's window, the first app's pane froze into a picture that ate keystrokes (T652 from the other side), and the steal even suppressed the new app's blank startup window, so nothing anywhere said a running terminal had just been lost. The fix gives AttachProbe a Policy: the two LOCAL rebuilds (launch restore, the chooser's local Restore All) take .skip_live_holders, which withholds every session the roster reports attached and records it in a new `held` set instead of merely dropping it - so "somebody is looking at this" and "these sessions are gone" stop being the same drop. The two REMOTE arms (RemoteReconnect, RestoreAllRelay) keep .attachable deliberately: across a relay that flag is as likely to be our own dropped connection the far agent has not reaped, and a genuine second holder is adjudicated there by attached_elsewhere + the steal retry. Crash recovery - the reason launch restore exists - is protected by a bounded SETTLE rather than by trusting the flag: restoreSessionLayout re-probes every 200ms for up to 2s while a window it would restore reads held, which a dead holder's flag clears out of (the agent's detachAll fires on the broken pipe) and a live holder's never does; the budget-exhausted fallback is the safe one, and a window left alone is CARRIED forward rather than forgotten, with a log line naming it. T411's orphan counter stopped counting other viewers' sessions as unattached at the same time. Validation caught one regression of its own: the new gate pre-empted Restore All's "already open here" skip, so the double-attach guard now runs first and each of the three skips keeps its own explanation. - 2026-08-17: T860 - a Ctrl key you are holding in another app no longer decides where a web page's popup opens. A viewer pane hands an `http(s)` `window.open()` to your default browser; **Ctrl** is the escape hatch that keeps it in Ghoztty instead. Mac reads that modifier off `navigationAction.modifierFlags` - it belongs to the CLICK - but win32 has no modifier on the WebView2 event, so it read `GetAsyncKeyState(VK_CONTROL)`, which answers for the WHOLE DESKTOP. A page opening a window on its own, while the user was in another app entirely with Ctrl down, got hijacked into a Ghoztty window. The hatch now needs a gesture as well as the key (`viewer_popup.ctrlEscape`, `ICoreWebView2NewWindowRequestedEventArgs.IsUserInitiated`), which is what Mac has always done. The real failure is T163 itself - a stray Ctrl adopted the http popup, which overwrote the test sink's single pane slot and orphaned the first pane. Three tasks (T776, T832, T860) could not read that, because two harness defects hid it: `waitFor` returned `void` on timeout, so a 30-second wait that never came true was reported by the next assertion (`expected 1, found 0` on a length), and the sink's single slot turned an unexpected second adoption into a leak. Both fixed: `waitFor` fails with `error.WaitForTimeout`, the sink holds a list, and every adoption logs its location. The evidence is a POSITIVE CONTROL rather than a soak, deliberately: T163 now routes the same `http://127.0.0.1:PORT/elsewhere.html` both ways one run apart - to the browser with no Ctrl, adopted as pane #2 with Ctrl held - which demonstrates the mechanism instead of sampling for its absence, and gives the Ctrl hatch the live coverage it never had (only the pure decision function was tested). The gate's premise is measured too, in the lane log: `gesture flags: page's own window.open()=false, ExecuteScript's=true` - that second value is why gating on `IsUserInitiated` alone did NOT make the test deterministic, and why the test states its Ctrl state through a seam instead of sampling the keyboard. - 2026-08-18: T911 - scrollback printed between two ring snapshots now survives an agent crash. An ACK to a per-session holder is permission to FREE, and the owner ACKed the instant it took bytes off the pipe - so the stretch between the last on-disk ring snapshot and a crash existed in exactly one place, the agent's in-memory ring, and died with it. The holder had already dropped it; the snapshot never had it. It was invisible while the APP stayed up (the app still holds the grid), which is why T906's harness could not see it - but a viewer that restarts too (T907's upgrade handover, a reboot, a second viewer attaching) replays from the agent's ring and reads a hole. The fix makes an ACK mean DURABLE: a new `Child.releaseTo(offset)` vtable entry (`session.zig`), called by `snapshotRings` after a successful write and OUTSIDE the store lock (the `refreshForegroundCommands` collect-then-act shape - no OS I/O under the mutex that serializes child output), with the holder-backed child acking `ackTarget(gate, received, durable) = min(received, durable)`. Never past `received`, because the owner cannot vouch for bytes it has not taken; never past `durable`, because everything after the snapshot exists ONLY in the holder. The 1 MB replay buffer then covers the snapshot interval, and a shell that outruns it drops oldest and reports the gap exactly as before. The gate is ARMED by the store rather than assumed: OPEN, RELAUNCH and startup adoption arm it before the child's reader thread exists (so a session's first seconds are covered, not just everything after the first snapshot), and only when `rings_dir` is set - with persistence off there is no durability to wait for and the child stays byte-identical to its pre-T911 self, retaining nothing for a releaser that would never come. Adoption arms at the offset the snapshot file ends at, which is the same offset T906 resumes from, so nothing is released that disk does not already hold. `GHOZTTY_AGENT_DURABLE_ACK=0` turns the gate off: the escape hatch if per-holder retention ever misbehaves on a box, and - more useful day to day - what makes the new harness's negative control a measurement instead of an inverted assertion. New acceptance `test\win32\holder-durable.ps1` reads the ring snapshot FILE rather than the pane, because the file is what a fresh viewer replays from and the pane is exactly what used to hide the bug: it proves snapshots are live in the run (a warm-up marker followed to disk, which also says a snapshot just fired and the whole interval is available), types a second marker, asserts it is on screen and NOT in any `.ring` file, hard-kills the session manager so nothing flushes on the way out, and then asserts the marker reaches a `.ring` file once the replacement manager adopts the surviving holder. ALL PASS 15 with the gate on; ALL PASS 15 with `-NegativeControl` on the SAME build and box, where the marker is LOST. Floor: lib+none+win32+agent ALL LANES PASS, P1 25 / P2 20 / P3 16 ALL PASS, and pty-host 21, pty-holder 22, holder-adopt 24, isolation-meta 7, stderr-capture 25, agent-sharing-uplink 18, agent-relay-session 18 all re-run green for the guard.
- 2026-08-18: T918 - the relay-account suite stopped reporting six failures that described a state the build could not be in, and started actually measuring the state it was written for. Section 8 is the T747 coverage: a build with no Google client id must draw NO sign-in button, say why in the account row, and refuse to start a flow that can only fail. It decided whether such a build was in front of it by looking for `macos\google-client-id.txt` - the LEGACY spelling, while `Config.zig` reads repo-root `google-client-id.txt` first and its own comment calls that "the spelling to use" for this seat. So a Windows checkout that followed the documented setup baked an id in, the section did not skip, and it failed six assertions for the app behaving exactly as a configured build should. A lying instrument is worse than a red one: the next turn goes hunting a defect that does not exist. Reading both paths would have fixed the lie and left a worse hole behind it - the section would then SKIP on every seat that has sign-in configured, which is every seat that runs the rest of this suite, and unmeasured-on-configured-seats is precisely how T747 shipped. So the section no longer infers the unconfigured state from the checkout; it CONSTRUCTS it. `GHOZTTY_RELAY_NO_CLIENT_ID` (`relay_signin.env_force_unconfigured`, the shape `GHOZTTY_ENROLL_NO_OPEN` already set) makes `resolveClientId` find nothing - env id and bake alike - so the shipped experience is measurable on any seat and the skip branch is gone rather than repaired. Windows forced that mechanism: it cannot hold a present-but-empty environment variable, so "no id" is not expressible through `GHOSTTY_GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID` itself, and a bake cannot be unbaked at runtime by anything. The resolution order moved into a pure `resolveClientIdFrom(explicit, env_id, force_unconfigured, baked)` so every branch is a `none`-lane unit test instead of a thing only a GUI run can reach; the knob suppresses the two AMBIENT sources and not an explicit argument, since an environment variable overruling a function argument is a worse surprise than the knob is worth. Validated on a seat that HAS a client id configured: `relay-account.ps1` ALL PASS with section 8 run rather than skipped, all six assertions green, and the configured relaunch still there as the positive control - now doing double duty as proof the knob, not a broken launch, is what took the button away. Floor all green (lib/none/win32/agent, P1-P3), and the three guards my edits made due (isolation-meta, stderr-capture, docs-routing) re-run green and re-stamped. Filed T972: this harness still has no guard-due row of its own, so relay sign-in code can change under it unnoticed - the T783 gap, on a feature that already shipped broken past a green suite once.

- 2026-08-18: T922 - a pane restored after a reboot now brings back what the lost session left on screen, and what it brings back is RECENT. The paint landed last turn; the arms that scored it were red, and the reason was not the paint. Arm A's two commanded panes came back showing their ping output correctly - it was the plain shell pane that came back holding a screen from before the marker this run printed into it. The manifest that carries those screens is written ONLY on topology mutations (a split, a tab, a rename, a banner), so a pane that has merely been RUNNING for an hour restored the screen it had when a window was last moved: stale by construction, and a stale screen is arguably worse than none, since it is a confident lie about what the session left. So `App` now refreshes it on the panes' own output. A repeating 2s tick sums each pane's lock-free `Remote.appliedOffset` - a cursor that moves iff something painted - and `layout_refresh.decide` turns that into idle / wait-for-quiet / capture: capturing mid-burst is wasted work, so the capture happens on the first tick that finds the panes still, with a 30s ceiling so a pane that never pauses (a build, a `tail -f`) is not the one pane whose screen is never persisted. That ceiling is the local agent's own ring-snapshot cadence, so the two halves of what a reboot brings back are recorded at the same worst-case rhythm. `session_layout.writeIfChanged` compares the serialized body against the last one written, so an idle terminal costs one atomic load per pane and no I/O at all. Two of the red arms were the harness measuring the wrong thing rather than the product: A12 and A17 both took "the first `>` in the dump" to be the fresh shell's prompt, which stopped being true the day the restore started painting the dead shell's prompt above the notice - both now score the first prompt at or after the notice. A third pair (E3/E4) was a real race the paint made likely: `+list` answers with three leaves as soon as the panes exist, while the notice banner arrives later from each pane's IO thread, so arm E read `noticed=0` off a restore whose own manifest, written moments later, recorded the notice banner on exactly the pane E4 expects it on; both arms now wait for every pane to hold SOME banner before scoring which one. The setup no longer sleeps 3 seconds hoping the manifest caught up - it waits on the manifest actually carrying the marker, which is A15's positive control. Green: four floor lanes, session-relaunch-notify ALL PASS (108, re-stamped over 6 covered files), session-layout-preserve (19), printclient-audit, isolation-meta (7), stderr-capture (25), P1-P3 (25/20/16). The refresh policy lives in its own `layout_refresh.zig` with six unit tests precisely so it could join that guard's coverage without dragging `App.zig` in - App.zig is edited by most tasks and would leave a twelve-minute GUI run due every turn; the residual gap (App.zig's wiring of the tick) is written down in `guard-due.ps1` rather than papered over. Filed T978 (seat: mac): the Mac has the same staleness, and says so itself above `syncAllTrackedNow` - "a session that changed only via output (the common case) never triggers the debounced sync" - with a flush at QUIT as the mitigation, which is exactly the path a reboot never takes.

- 2026-08-19: T933 - a floor run now takes as long as its lanes. It took three times longer, and the reason was that the test binaries were spawning THEMSELVES. Inside a test build `std.fs.selfExePath` answers with the zig TEST RUNNER, not the product - so `pty_holder_child.open`, which launches `<our own exe> --pty-host --spec <file>` for every holder-backed session, was launching `ghoztty-agent-test.exe` instead of the agent. Watched live before the fix: pid 8524, command line `...ghoztty-agent-test.exe --pty-host --spec ...`, reparented to explorer.exe by `spawnEscapingJob`'s shell-parent hop - which is to say spawned DETACHED and deliberately out of every job object the lane could tear down. The runner panics on the unrecognized argument and usually dies in about three seconds, so the lane's own log reads `breakaway spawn refused` -> `could not reach holder ... error.HolderExited` -> `holder-backed spawn failed; falling back to an in-process ConPTY child` and everything passes. The copies that do NOT die promptly are the 40 minutes of dead time T829 measured, and a self-spawn whose argv the runner happens to ACCEPT is worse still: no arguments at all re-runs the whole suite (which spawns again, and hosts a tree of `msedgewebview2.exe` while it does), and the build runner's own `--listen=-` leaves a copy blocked on a pipe that will never speak. The fix is structural rather than remembered: `src/os/self_exe.zig` `productExePath{,Alloc}` returns `SelfSpawnFromTestBinary` under `builtin.is_test`, and the four places that launch our own image now ask it - the holder spawn, the relaunch guard (whose child carries NO arguments, the fork-bomb shape), `App.autoLaunchInstance`, and the agent's Run-key command in `adopt.zig`, which under a test build would have registered the test runner to start at every logon. Every one of those callers already had a failure path for a spawn that will not start, so the refusal lands on code that exists; the product is untouched, since `is_test` is false in every shipped binary. The wrapper got the other half T933 asked for. `Get-SelfSpawnedTestPids` names the shape a self-spawn always has - a test binary whose ancestor is also a test binary, plus everything beneath it - and `floor-lane.ps1` drops that CPU from the progress signal, because the stall detector counted it as the lane working and a copy of the suite burning a core is precisely a lane that is not. The leak report now prints the command line each leak was launched with and says `SELF-SPAWN` when it was not the build runner, so the next occurrence explains itself instead of needing a debugger. Measured, both directions: the pre-T933 wrapper on a staged lane whose only CPU is a nested spinner answers `LANE command TIMEOUT in 46s` - it never called a stall - and HEAD answers `LANE command STALL in 25s`. And the headline number, on the same box that filed the task at 17.6 minutes of lanes inside 61 minutes of wall clock: lib 52s + none 299s + win32 367s + agent 358s = 1076s of lanes, `wall=1078s`, with `leaked test binaries: 0` on all four and a WMI command-line watcher over the entire run recording nothing but the two `--listen=-` launches the build runner makes. Green: ALL LANES PASS; floor-lane-leak-sweep ALL PASS (arms 11-14 are this task's); pty-holder 22, agent-adopt 26, isolation-meta 7, stderr-capture 25, printclient-audit and P1/P2/P3 (25/20/16) all ALL PASS. Filed T980 (nothing stops a fifth self-spawn site appearing - a sweep should fail on `selfExePath` feeding a spawn outside `self_exe.zig`, and the sites that spawn a SIBLING from the exe dir only miss by luck in a test build) and T981 (`agent-adopt.ps1` has a guard row but no stamping tail, so its green run had to be stamped by hand - the T883/T898 shape again).
- 2026-08-19: T934 - the viewer's feedback composer stopped being a text control we drive by hand and became the browser engine the page beside it already uses, which is what D43 was answered with and what T635 had shipped the opposite of while the decision sat open. The pill's TEXT RECT is now a second `ICoreWebView2Controller` on the pane's own environment, hosting a `contenteditable="plaintext-only"` page we author (`ViewerFeedbackWeb.zig`, `viewer_feedback_page.zig`, `src/viewer/composer.{css,js}`); the pill, its accent, the carousel and the send row are still painted natively, so nothing about where the composer sits or how it looks moved - the acceptance measures the band at 95 px on both sides of the swap. What the user gets that they did not have: caret and selection, word wrap, undo, the clipboard, drag-drop, IME composition for anyone writing in a language that needs one, and a screen reader that can read the field, all from the engine instead of from us. The real work was the shape change rather than the control. A RichEdit answers `caret()` and `lineCount()` on the caller's stack and a WebView2 cannot, so the direction of truth is inverted: the PAGE owns the live document and pushes a snapshot up on every edit, native keeps the last snapshot as what it lays out and serializes from, and the only write back down is "make the document equal the buffer". Two things turned out to be load-bearing rather than nice. Every seed carries a GENERATION the page echoes, so a snapshot that was in flight when a native write went down is recognisable and dropped instead of resurrecting the text that write replaced - and `ViewerPane.feedbackSetText` re-seeds the page itself, so every writer is covered rather than the ones somebody remembered. And the composer's chords, the pane's, and the whole keybind table are claimed in `AcceleratorKeyPressed` with `put_Handled`, because keys reach Chromium before our message loop and only `put_Handled` stops the browser ALSO acting on one we took; without it a focused composer would be the one place in the app where Ctrl+R reloaded the composer's own page over a half-written report. `webview2_iface.zig` gained the two slots this needed (`NavigateToString` at 6, `PostWebMessageAsJson` at 32), each with its `@offsetOf` assert. Deliberately staged, not finished: quoted blocks are plain text until T935 makes them CSS, image chips stay literal text until T936, a natively-inserted quote or chip is not undoable (T983), and the RichEdit is kept as a runtime FALLBACK - created hidden, shown only when the environment cannot produce a controller, forced by `GHOZTTY_COMPOSER_SURFACE=richedit` - until T937 retires it. That fallback is also what keeps the old suite honest: window messages cannot drive a Chromium window off the input desktop (T233), so `test/win32/viewer-feedback.ps1` pins itself to the RichEdit and keeps proving the EDITING semantics (ALL PASS 71, with a new arm asserting the pin took), the new `test/win32/viewer-composer.ps1` proves the web surface's lifecycle and its round trip (ALL PASS 30: surface=web with zero degrades, the document handed to `NavigateToString`, the page's `ready`, the page echoing the seeded document back as 0 bytes on 1 line, the view sized 657x23 inside the band, closing DESTROYING the controller and its window tree, and a reopen doing all of it again), and the in-process `host floor` test drives a real controller end to end - it now asserts the surface IS the web one, waits for the page's echo, checks the echoed buffer came back byte-identical for five non-ASCII characters plus a blank line and a tail, then quotes at UTF-16 unit 7, sends, and reads the published report off disk. Evidence: floor `-Lane all` ALL PASS (lib/none/win32/agent), `ipc-p1/p2/p3` ALL PASS, `viewer-panes.ps1` ALL PASS (186), the four guards the change made due (printclient-audit, isolation-meta, stderr-capture, docs-routing) ALL PASS and re-stamped, and new none-lane tests for the page document, both message directions, the generation guard and every malformed payload. Filed: T982 (a floor run can die on an empty process-tree sample - `Get-ProcessTree`'s ArrayList unrolls to `$null` and the next parameter refuses it, which aborted a run tonight), T983 (undo), T984 (`viewer-panes`'s guard row does not cover the pane it tests, which is why this change's pane edits never made it due).
- 2026-08-19: T935 - a quoted passage in the feedback composer is a quoted passage again, and it knows its own name. T934 moved the composer's text surface to a WebView2 and the wash, the accent bar and the indent went with the RichEdit formats that carried them, so a quote landed as plain text. It is now a `<div class="q" data-qid="N">` inside the contenteditable, dressed by `src/viewer/composer.css` from custom properties the host pushes - the wash is the pill pulled 14% toward the accent, the bar is 3 DIP at 5 DIP in, the text sits at the design system's 16 DIP step, and all three now come from ONE statement in `ViewerFeedbackBar` that the native fallback's painter reads too. The block deliberately carries no vertical margin or padding, and there is a test that says so: the pill's height is measured as scrollHeight / lineHeight, so air on the block would grow the composer by a line the text does not occupy. The bigger half is identity. `viewer_feedback_doc.zig` derived a quote's identity by matching its passage against line-aligned runs of the text, precisely because RichEdit had no per-run user field to hang an id on - which meant fixing a typo inside a quote silently detached it from the page it came from, and a passage typed twice was ambiguous. A DOM node has that field: the page reports its live blocks in every snapshot (`{id, start, end}` in UTF-16 units), `ViewerPane` keeps them as the truth the report is written from, and the matching survives ONLY as the seeding bridge for a buffer that outlived its page - a reopened composer, a native insertion, a report cleared behind a send. Deleting a block drops its metadata because the node is gone; editing one keeps it. Everything that writes the page goes through one `seedPage`, which builds the span list itself, because a seed that forgot the quotes would flatten every washed block back into plain text and no call site should be able to make that mistake. The page's own repairs are the browser's editing behaviour meeting our invariants: an emptied block is removed (unless the caret is in it), and a block Chromium split in two by an Enter keeps its id on the first half and turns the second into ordinary text. Nothing that reaches the report writer is trusted - a span past the end of the buffer, an empty or inverted run, one that overlaps its neighbour or names a registry entry that does not exist is dropped, and the rest stand. Evidence: floor lanes lib/none/win32/agent ALL PASS, `ipc-p1/p2/p3` ALL PASS, `viewer-composer.ps1` ALL PASS (30), `viewer-feedback.ps1` ALL PASS (71) on the pinned RichEdit fallback, `viewer-panes.ps1` ALL PASS (186), `printclient-audit.ps1` ALL PASS and re-stamped; the proof of the round trip is a REAL browser - the `host floor` test quotes into a composer holding five non-ASCII characters and the page reports the block back as `id=1 span=12..39`, which converts to exactly the quoted passage and names the right registry entry. Filed: T985 (a quote the user edited now files its original wording as the report's metadata beside the edited text, and nothing says which is which - a question that could not arise while editing dropped the quote).
- 2026-08-19: T936 - an image chip in the feedback composer is one object now, and pasting a picture into it is the browser's paste. A chip used to be literally the characters `[Image #3]`, so Backspace beside one bit the `]` off and left `[Image #3` - text that no longer parses, i.e. a picture silently dropped from the report by a single keystroke, which `viewer_feedback_images.chipEndingAt` had to widen a selection by hand to prevent. It is now a `<span class="i" data-img="N" contenteditable="false">` inside the contenteditable, and that one attribute is the whole feature: the engine treats the run as a single character for the caret, for selection and for Backspace, so deleting a chip is ordinary editing and the picture leaves the report with it. The chip's identity is deliberately NOT the node's, unlike a quote's: `[Image #3]` says which picture it is without any help, so `Store.live` still derives the live set from the buffer and the carousel, the report's `images` array and the markdown links are untouched. What the seed carries is only "these runs are chips" (`images: [{n,start,end}]`, built from that same derivation, so an unknown or duplicated chip stays plain text exactly as before). The other half is paste. The RichEdit path intercepted Ctrl+V, asked the clipboard itself whether it held a bitmap, and swallowed the `WM_CHAR` the interception left behind; the page now gets a `paste` event with the picture already decoded, hands the bytes up as base64, and the host does what it always did with them - and a `drop` handler gets the same treatment, so dragging an image file in attaches it, with anything that is not a PNG re-encoded through an OffscreenCanvas instead of refused. - 2026-08-19: T989 - typing into the Activity Monitor's filter box no longer kills the terminal. The panel read its filter EDIT into a 256-unit UTF-16 buffer and converted it into a 128-byte needle with `std.unicode.utf16LeToUtf8`, whose error set covers malformed UTF-16 and NOT an undersized destination - so the `catch 0` that read like an overflow guard never was one, and the `@min` clamp on the next line ran after the write that had already gone past the end. About 130 typed characters, or one pasted path, reached `panic: reached unreachable code` inside `utf8Encode` and took every pane in every window with it; in a release build the same input is a silent buffer overrun. The fix has two halves. New pure module `src/apprt/win32/utf16_text.zig`: `toUtf8Truncating` converts as much as fits and stops on a codepoint boundary, never writes past its destination, and keeps the text before a dangling surrogate half rather than discarding the whole string the way a `catch ""` did (a wide buffer the OS itself truncated can end in exactly that half pair). Nine unit tests, and their presence in the win32 lane was PROVEN rather than assumed - a deliberately broken expectation went red as `apprt.win32.utf16_text.test.*`, then was reverted. The second half is that `needle_buf` is now DERIVED from the wide buffer, `(filter_wide_cap - 1) * 3` - the most UTF-8 that 255 UTF-16 units can be - so the two sizes cannot drift apart again, which is what the bug actually was. Acceptance: section D2 of `test\win32\activity-monitor.ps1` types 140 characters past the old threshold (typed, not set: the crash was per-keystroke), pastes 300 ASCII, pastes 300 three-byte characters - the exact 765-byte worst case - asserts no panic reached the log, and filters again afterwards. ALL PASS at 157 assertions with the fix, and teeth-checked by putting both halves of the bug back: 6 of D2's 8 assertions went red, including "no panic reached the app log". One thing that measurement changed: the liveness check needed a 600ms settle, because a panic writes its stack trace before the process goes and a check taken the instant a state line appears can beat the death it is looking for. Floor lanes lib/none/win32/agent ALL PASS, `ipc-p1/p2/p3` ALL PASS. Filed T990: the machine chooser's filter box is the same 256-units-into-256-bytes read and crashes identically, and a dozen more fixed-buffer readers across the win32 frontend have never been measured against what their callers pass.
- 2026-08-19: T990 - typing or pasting into ANY of the app's text fields can no longer end the process. T989 fixed one filter box; the machine chooser's read a 256-unit wide buffer into a 256-byte destination through `std.unicode.utf16LeToUtf8`, which does not bounds-check what it writes into, so 86 CJK characters panicked and took every pane in every window. Rather than resize that one buffer, all 20 fixed-destination readers in `src/apprt/win32/` were converted onto bounded helpers, chosen by what the text IS: a filter, needle, title or label truncates on a codepoint boundary (`toUtf8Truncating`), while a device name, host name, path, command or URI is all-or-nothing (`toUtf8AllOrNothing`, new) - which is the behavior half of them documented themselves as having ("0 when it does not fit - a truncated path is worse than none") long before anything made it true. Four more reachable crashes fell out of the sweep: the command palette's filter, the terminal search box, "Copy title to clipboard", and the IME commit path. The IME path took neither answer - truncating drops text the user actually typed - so it converts in CHUNKS and continues from where each conversion stopped (`toUtf8Counting`, new, reports the units consumed); the terminal sees the same bytes in more than one callback. New harness `test\win32\machine-chooser.ps1` (19 assertions, + a `machine-chooser` guard row over `utf16_text.zig`) drives the real chooser through typed three-byte characters, 300-character ASCII and CJK pastes, and a filter that still narrows afterwards. Its typing arm deliberately uses three-byte characters: `GetWindowTextW` caps that field at 255 units, so 255 ASCII bytes can never overflow 256, and an arm typing 'a' was measured GREEN against the unfixed build - the teeth-check found that, not a review. Green: floor lanes lib/none/win32/agent ALL PASS, ipc-p1/p2/p3 ALL PASS, and the six harnesses this change made due (isolation-meta, stderr-capture-audit, printclient-audit, pane-banner 130, share-machine 30, chooser-selection 29) green and re-stamped. Teeth: the unfixed `filterText` restored and rebuilt takes the new script to 8 FAILURE(S); `-NegativeControl` takes it to 1. Filed T991 for the same shape in `src/remote/agent/`, which this task did not cover.

Arm A holds the clipboard continuously, which is past the retry budget, and requires the copy to be LOST (the oracle is proven able to see a failure at all); arm B churns 45ms held / 25ms free and requires all eight copies to land - numbers chosen, not guessed, since a 45ms hold can cover at most three of the eight 15ms-spaced attempts while a single attempt lands in a gap about a third of the time; arm C is the source guard that keeps the next call site from reintroducing the shape. Two measurements shaped it and are written into the script so nobody repeats them: a second THREAD of the same process is handed the clipboard rather than refused (so a zig-lane control is impossible - the first attempt at one also deadlocked the lane), and `OpenClipboard(NULL)` excludes NOBODY, so a holder without a real HWND makes every arm pass vacuously. Green: floor lanes lib/none/win32/agent ALL PASS, ipc-p1/p2/p3 ALL PASS, clipboard-retry ALL PASS, clipboard-paste 26 ALL PASS, and the three audits this change made due (stderr-capture 25, isolation-meta 7, printclient-audit) green and re-stamped.
