- 2026-08-19: T948 - a second Claude window can no longer commit this loop's staged work into its own commit. Two windows share one working tree here by design, which means they share one INDEX, and `git commit` commits the index rather than "my work": on 2026-08-17 the other window's `git add -A; git commit` landed in the gap between this loop's `git add` and its `git commit`, and the whole T850 clipboard fix shipped inside `0d835a1b3 fix(t857): ...`, pushed before anyone noticed. The answer is two mechanisms that fail independently, because either alone still loses. PREVENT: `scripts\githooks\pre-commit` (plain POSIX sh, LF-pinned in `.gitattributes` - a CRLF checkout makes the shebang `#!/bin/sh\r` and the guard silently is not there) refuses a commit from any session that is not holding the repo's advisory commit lock, names the holder and the remedy, and CLEARS a hold older than its ttl rather than obeying it, so a crashed holder cannot wedge the repo for the other window. DETECT: `scripts\git-commit-guard.ps1 commit` holds that lock for the seconds between staging and committing, commits an explicit PATHSPEC so whatever else sits in the shared index cannot ride along, then READS THE COMMIT BACK and fails loudly (`SWALLOWED WORK`, exit 5) if it contains a path it was never asked for - which is what a bypassed hook (`--no-verify`, a clone that never installed) leaves behind. `verify` is that same read-back after the fact. What arms it is `core.hooksPath`, which is LOCAL config and therefore cannot arrive by `git pull`, so `go-loop-exec.ps1 claim` re-asserts `install` at the top of every turn - idempotent, and never fatal, since a repo that will not take a hook config is still a repo the loop must work in. go.md step 6 now commits through the guard instead of a bare `git commit`. Acceptance: section W of `test\win32\go-loop-guard.ps1`, 15 arms, which reproduces the 2026-08-17 shape against a fixture repo (A holds and stages, B commits with `-A`, REFUSED, HEAD does not move), proves the holder's own git passes through on its key, proves a hold past its ttl is cleared, and scores the commit path's containment both ways. Teeth: the same scenario with the hook unarmed commits `a-work.txt,b-work.txt` - session A's half-written file inside session B's commit, the original bug, verbatim. Dogfooding it for this very commit found two things a green harness had not: `powershell -File` binds `-Paths 'a','b'` as ONE string (it never splits an array), and `& git ... 2>&1` under PS 5.1 wraps each stderr LINE in an ErrorRecord that `$ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'` makes terminating - so git's routine "LF will be replaced by CRLF" warning killed the script mid-commit with exit code 0 in hand. A third surfaced fixing the second: `$push = Git-Run @('push')` assigned a hashtable to the `[switch]$Push` PARAMETER, since PowerShell variable names are case-insensitive, and died in parameter binding before the verb ran. All three are fixed and all three now have arms (W16 the comma list, W17 a fixture made to produce that exact git warning, W18 a bare-repo remote so the `-Push` path go.md itself prescribes is no longer unexercised). Green: go-loop-guard ALL PASS (18 W arms; stamp now covers `git-commit-guard.ps1` and `githooks\*`), floor lanes lib/none/win32/agent ALL PASS, ipc-p1/p2/p3 ALL PASS, stderr-capture-audit 25 and isolation-meta 7 green and re-stamped. Filed T994 (seat: mac): the hook is in the tree for both seats but only Windows arms it.

- 2026-08-19: T963 - the audit that catches a test script printing failure and exiting 0 was itself red at HEAD, and it was wrong. It accused `tab-tooltip.ps1` of falling off the end; that script's failure path is `else { "$fail FAILURE(S)"; exit 1 }` and always was. The analyzer took the INNERMOST `if` around the last `ALL PASS`, which in that file is the one choosing the wording (`ALL PASS (N)` vs `ALL PASS (N, K SKIPPED)`) INSIDE the pass branch - so it scored the SKIPPED question as if it were the pass/fail question. The false accusation is the cheap half; the expensive half is the other direction, since an `exit 0` sitting in such a nested branch would have ANSWERED for a failure path that never reaches it, and the audit would have gone silent over exactly the defect it exists for. `Get-EnclosingIf` is replaced by `Get-VerdictIf`, which walks outward and takes the innermost enclosing `if` whose failure path actually ANNOUNCES failure - its other branches if it has any, otherwise the code after it - falling back to the innermost when nothing qualifies; the branch split both it and the analyzer need is now one `Split-VerdictBranches`. Two fixtures pin the shape in both directions: A13 (the nested pass branch reads clean) and A14 (an `exit 0` nested in that pass branch is still a `fallthrough`). All twelve pre-existing A fixtures are untouched and still pass, so nothing the audit exists for was relaxed. The second half is why nobody noticed: this audit had no `guard-due` row, alone among the meta-checks (isolation-meta, stderr-capture, printclient-audit all have one), so no edit to the suite ever obliged anyone to re-run it and it sat red until T883 happened to. It has one now - `verdict-exit`, wide net over `test\win32\*.ps1` and `lib\*.ps1`, 247 files - and the script stamps on a clean green run but deliberately NOT under `-TeethCheck`, which plants a violator in the swept directory and so never observes a clean suite. Green: verdict-exit-audit ALL PASS with 0 violations over 223 acceptance scripts, teeth intact (`-TeethCheck` still finds the planted violator and calls it a fallthrough), floor lanes lib/none/win32/agent ALL PASS, ipc-p1 25 / p2 20 / p3 16 ALL PASS, isolation-meta 7 and stderr-capture 25 green and re-stamped. Filed T996: nothing enumerates which acceptance harnesses have no guard row, which is why this one and five others (T884, T967, T972, T981, T993) were each found by accident.

- 2026-08-19: T969 - a pane in the middle of a noisy build now gets the same crash-recovery guarantee a quiet one gets. Since T911 the scrollback a crash can hand back is everything printed since it was last saved, but saving happened only every 30 seconds while nothing anywhere holds more than the holder's 1 MB replay ring - so a shell printing faster than about 35 KB/s reached that ceiling between two saves and the OLDEST of it was dropped to make room. The pane on screen was always fine; only what a fresh viewer could replay after a crash was short, which is why no per-pane test could see it. The reaper's snapshot pass now fires on VOLUME as well as on the clock: `SessionStore.volumeSnapshotDue` reads the busiest alive session's unsaved byte count each tick and runs the pass at or past `snapshot_volume_bytes` - half the holder's replay capacity, so the ring is refilled before it can wrap - with a one-second floor between passes that bounds the write amplification at about 2x of what the pane prints. The decision is a pure function (`volumeSnapshotFires`) so the boundary is a unit test rather than a claim, and `default_snapshot_volume_bytes * 2 == default_holder_replay_bytes` is pinned as one too: the two numbers TOGETHER are the guarantee, and either moving alone would shrink it silently. Checked on the reaper tick rather than on the output path deliberately - the pty reader thread is parked inside `onChildOutput` when the counters move, and the up-to-a-second of latency this costs is the granularity every other sampler in that loop already runs at. New acceptance `test\win32\holder-volume.ps1`, ALL PASS (16 assertions) on BOTH arms: the marker reaches a `.ring` file a second after a 256 KB flood through a 64 KB holder ring and survives the hard kill, and with the trigger off the same run finds it neither on disk nor after recovery. Two env knobs came with it, both ignoring anything unparseable so a typo cannot silently shrink what a crash recovers - `GHOZTTY_AGENT_SNAPSHOT_VOLUME_BYTES` (0 = off, which is what makes that control a real measurement) and `GHOZTTY_AGENT_HOLDER_REPLAY_BYTES`, which is what lets the harness overrun a holder in a second instead of racing the 30-second timer with a megabyte of ConPTY output. All four floor lanes green; `holder-durable.ps1`, `holder-adopt.ps1` and `pty-holder.ps1` still ALL PASS. Filed T997: a snapshot rewrites the WHOLE ring, so the fix's bounded cost is that a busy pane writes about twice what it prints; a delta format would make it proportional.
- 2026-08-19: T973 - a half-written build cache now heals itself even when the compiler blames a source file. After the 2026-08-18 reboot the win32 and agent lanes went red with `error: root source file struct 'options' has no member named 'app_version'` pointing at `src\build\Config.zig`, which is intact; the truncated file was the generated `options.zig` under `.zig-cache\c\<hash>\`, and it was named only on the compiler's `note: struct declared here` line. T494's heal reads FILE LOCATIONS of `error:` lines, so it saw nothing and the lane reported a code failure - a turn's context spent debugging code that was fine. (Two details in the filed task were written from memory and are corrected in it: the entry was in the `c` bucket, not the `/z` ZIR store, and no `Invalid timestamp` warning was in those logs.) `scripts\lib\CacheHeal.ps1` now recognizes two more shapes, both deliberately narrower than the unconditional error-line rule, because a note only LOCATES a declaration and does not assert the content there is wrong: a DECLARATION note (`note: <kind> declared here`) whose location is inside a cache entry, and ANY cache-resolving line whose file fails a new `Test-CacheFileIntact` - missing, empty, zero-filled (T494's shape) or not newline terminated (this one's). A note that merely passes THROUGH intact generated code (`note: called at comptime here`) still heals nothing, so a genuine compile error keeps its diagnosis; when a heal is wrong it deletes a regenerable entry and the lane fails again on the retry, which the caller still reports as final. `Resolve-CachePath` also resolves a hash-FILE entry (`<root>\<bucket>\<hash>` with no file below it, which is how the `/z` ZIR store is laid out) and deletes the file, and every `CACHE HEAL` line now names the rule that fired. Green: `test\win32\floor-lane-cache-heal.ps1` ALL PASS (29 assertions, was 16 - arm 11 replays the 2026-08-18 log verbatim and expects the entry a human deleted by hand, arm 12 proves a pass-through note on an intact file heals nothing, arm 14 keeps a declaration note in real source undetected), `floor-lane.ps1 -SelfTest` ALL PASS, all four floor lanes PASS, the three meta-audits the edits made due (`isolation-meta`, `verdict-exit`, `stderr-capture`) ALL PASS and `guard-due.ps1 check` is clean, P1/P2/P3 ALL PASS (25/20/16). Filed T998 (every build path outside floor-lane still reports a torn cache as red code), T999 (nothing sweeps the cache after the unclean shutdown that causes this), and P1 T1000 - the first `-Lane all` run of this change died mid-win32 with `Cannot bind argument to parameter 'Tree' because it is null` and STILL EXITED 0: `Get-ProcessTree` returns an ArrayList, an empty one unrolls to `$null`, and the self-spawn sweep's `[Mandatory][AllowEmptyCollection()]` refuses null - so the wrapper whose whole job is that a wedge cannot look like a slow run can itself look like a pass.

- 2026-08-19: T974 - an agent restart that started killing panes would no longer ship green. Since T909 a persistent session's ConPTY lives in a `--pty-host` holder that outlives the session manager on purpose, so a manager that crashes or is upgraded comes back, adopts its holders, and nothing the user was running is disturbed. T922 pointed `test\win32\session-relaunch-notify.ps1` squarely at the REBOOT shape by killing the holders alongside the manager - correctly, that IS a reboot - and in doing so left the agent-restart shape measured by nothing: the whole file would have stayed green through a regression that closed everybody's panes on every upgrade. New arm M is arm A's inverse, in the same file and against the same build, because that is where the notice and marker-ping oracles already live: it kills ONLY the manager, leaves the app and the holders up, and asserts the opposite outcome on the same instruments - the recorded `ping -n <unique>` is still running as the SAME PROCESS (M13 read pid 7916 before and after, which a re-execute could not produce), no pane claims an interruption in the `+list --json` banner (M15) or in its own `+read` dump (M16), and each pane keeps its session id (M18) and still takes input (M19). Teeth are a new `-BreakHolders` switch that takes the holders down with the manager, reproducing the regression exactly: M11, M13, M15, M16 and M18 go red, 5 FAILURE(S) / 124 passed. That run also settled which assertions are claims and which are controls, and it is written into the script: M17 (the pre-kill marker is still on screen) and M19 stay GREEN under the break, because since T922/D78 a rebuilt pane is repainted with the dead session's last screen and a fresh shell takes input just fine - only the session id and the shell's own process can tell a survivor from a replacement. Two defects found while writing it were both in the test and both are now commented where they bit: holders carry a spec path in TEMP and nothing on their command line names LOCALAPPDATA, so the `*<state dir>*` filter that finds the manager matched zero holders (M7/M11 scored 0 of 2), and a `return , $ids` handed back through the `@(...)` at the call site nests into a one-element array holding an array, which printed pids as `System.Object[]` and would have made `.Count` read 1 forever. `holder_adopt.zig` joins the `session-relaunch` guard row: `holder-adopt.ps1` covers it on the mechanism side (same shell pid, same holder), and this harness is what notices when adoption still works and the panes are told they died anyway. Green: ALL PASS (129) twice, floor lanes lib/none/win32/agent ALL PASS, ipc-p1 25 / p2 20 / p3 16 ALL PASS, and the three meta-audits the edit made due (isolation-meta 7, verdict-exit, stderr-capture 25) green and re-stamped; `guard-due.ps1 check` clean. Filed T1001: arm M kills the manager, which is the CRASH shape - the T147 mandatory UPGRADE is a graceful shutdown with a DIFFERENT BUILD adopting the previous build's holders, and that path still has none of these assertions on it.

- 2026-08-19: T976 - a launch that starts before the session manager is ready now finishes the restore by itself instead of leaving it for the next launch. `LocalAgent.findOrSpawn` gives a freshly spawned agent 2s to bind its pipe, and the launch restore treated that one answer as final: every window whose panes need an ATTACH was carried forward under "keeping N unrestored manifest window(s) for the next launch", so a box that is merely BUSY at logon - a login storm, a cold disk, twenty recorded sessions to re-materialize - came back to one blank terminal and the only cure was quitting and starting again, which nobody should have to know. T975 fixed two reasons the manager was late; fixing causes one at a time cannot close this, because the restore was a one-shot decision. It is now a bounded retry: the launch arms `RESTORE_RETRY_TIMER_ID`, each tick asks whether the agent has come up, and the first tick that finds one rebuilds exactly the windows the launch carried. The schedule lives in the new `restore_retry.zig` as pure policy (16 attempts, short-then-patient, 55s total, and it RUNS OUT - an agent that has not answered in a minute is broken, not late, and windows materializing minutes into a session would be worse than the blank terminal it replaces). `restoreSessionLayout` split into `restorePass(only)`: the filter is what keeps the deferred pass from being a second launch, since by then this process has its own windows in the manifest and rebuilding those would duplicate what is on screen; every other rule - the never-all-dead drop, the attach-flag settle, the positive-adjudication gate - re-applies verbatim against what is true NOW. Two details are load-bearing and are commented where they bite. The tick dials through a new `LocalAgent.adoptIfUp`, which never SPAWNS (the launch already did; a spawn per tick starts a process the single-instance guard kills and re-pays the 2s GUI block the retry exists to avoid) and deliberately ignores the 15s failure cooldown, which otherwise blinds the retry through exactly the window the late agent lands in. And the launch now RESERVES the carried windows' `window-N` names: T121's counter restarts at zero every run and only moves forward, so the blank startup window would have minted `window-1` first and made the restored `window-1` unreachable - every `--target=window-1` a script was written against landing on a blank terminal. The acceptance run measured that directly: with the fix the startup window mints `window-3`. New harness `test\win32\restore-late-agent.ps1` (19 assertions, + a `restore-late-agent` guard row) records a layout against a healthy agent, relaunches with an unspawnable one - phase B is the negative control, nothing restored and all three entries carried - then hand-starts the real agent with the command line the app itself spawned, and requires the windows back LIVE (typed input, returned output) in the SAME app pid, with no duplicate target names. Green: floor lanes lib/none/win32/agent ALL PASS, ipc-p1 25 / p2 20 / p3 16 ALL PASS, restore-late-agent ALL PASS (19), and the four meta-audits the new script made due (isolation-meta 7, verdict-exit, stderr-capture 25, printclient-audit 8) green and re-stamped; `guard-due.ps1 check` clean. Two calls recorded rather than filed as questions, both mechanism-level: the leftover blank window stays (closing a pane the user may have typed into is worse than an extra window), and the deferred pass runs ONCE - anything it leaves behind was adjudicated by an agent that answered, so re-running it against the same healthy agent would reach the same verdict fifteen more times. Filed T1002 (a crash-orphaned window that lives only in the agent's blob store is never in the carried set, so the deferred pass has no key to name it) and T1003 (close the leftover blank window when it is still pristine).

- 2026-08-19: T982 (with T1000, the same defect filed twice) - the wrapper that watches every floor run can no longer be killed by the photo it takes of itself. Every few seconds `floor-lane.ps1` samples the running processes to answer "is this lane working or wedged", and the sample legitimately comes back EMPTY: the root exits between the `HasExited` check and the CIM query, or the query returns nothing on a loaded box. An empty `ArrayList` unrolls to `$null` on the way out of a PS 5.1 function, and the very next line binds it to `Get-SelfSpawnedTestPids -Tree`, whose `[Mandatory][AllowEmptyCollection()]` permits `@()` but REFUSES null - so the run died mid-lane with a binding exception under `$ErrorActionPreference='Stop'`: no verdict for that lane, no `FLOOR SUMMARY`, the lanes behind it never run, and the lane's `zig build` left running under a pid nobody was tracking any more. A gate that can vanish is worse than a red one, because vanishing looks like "the floor was never run". Three changes, in order of how much they matter. The call site wraps the sample (`$tree = @(Get-ProcessTree ...)`) - deliberately NOT `return ,$out`, which fixes the null and breaks the other end, since an empty comma-return counts as one item at an `@()` call site (T974 shipped that mirror-image bug three days ago). The library now says what it means: `[AllowNull()]` on both collection parameters, plus a null FILTER in `Invoke-LaneLeakSweep`, because `@($null)` is a one-element array and counting it straight would report a phantom leak with no pid on exactly the runs where nothing leaked; `Write-Diagnostic`, `Stop-Tree` and the exclude-pid loop skip nulls for the same reason (`foreach ($p in $null)` iterates ONCE in PS 5.1). And the watchdog now holds its own contract: the poll loop runs inside a `try`, so any unexpected error prints `LANE <name> WATCHDOG ERROR`, charges THIS lane a FAIL, re-samples and reaps the tree it was watching, and lets the remaining lanes run - the reap has its own guard, since a handler that can throw is a handler that does not hold the contract. Acceptance: arms 15-16 of `test\win32\floor-lane-leak-sweep.ps1` (ALL PASS, 48 assertions, was 42). Arm 15 lifts the shipped `Get-ProcessTree` out of `floor-lane.ps1` with the PARSER rather than copying it, so it drives the real function with a snapshot that matches nothing and with a null snapshot (the CIM-failure case); arm 16 injects a fault into the watchdog loop through `GHOZTTY_FLOOR_LANE_FAULT` - the only way to stage an error deterministically when the real ones are rare races - and requires a `WATCHDOG ERROR` line, `LANE command FAIL`, a `FLOOR SUMMARY`, a non-zero exit, and no process of the lane's tree left running. One claim in T1000 was measured rather than inherited: "and STILL EXITED 0" does not reproduce - `powershell -File` exits 1 on an unhandled binding error - and the reading was almost certainly the shell artifact that bit this turn too, since `powershell ... | tail -5` reports TAIL's status and a PowerShell cmdlet in a POSIX pipeline is `command not found` while the powershell child keeps running orphaned (one such invocation left a `none` lane burning a core with its output going nowhere). That trap is now written into `docs/claude/testing.md` beside the verdict-vs-exit-code rules. Green: floor lanes lib/none/win32/agent ALL PASS, `floor-lane.ps1 -SelfTest` ALL PASS (the three real verdicts are unchanged by the new try/catch), ipc-p1 25 / p2 20 / p3 16 ALL PASS, and the four guards the edits made due (lane-leak-sweep, isolation-meta 7, verdict-exit, stderr-capture 25, docs-routing 20) green and re-stamped. Filed T1004 (nothing sweeps the suite for this unroll class, which has now been found by accident three times) and T1005 (`floor-lane.ps1` sits outside every guard row, so the harness whose wiring arms would have caught this was never obliged to run).

- 2026-08-19: T983 - Ctrl+Z now takes a quote or an image chip back out of the feedback composer, and Ctrl+Y (or Ctrl+Shift+Z) puts it back. The task existed to CHECK an expectation rather than to assume it, and the expectation failed: T935/T936 made quotes and chips real DOM nodes, but native still puts them in with a whole-document seed (`spliceComposer` -> `seedPage` -> the page's `build()`), and a rebuilt document is not a step the engine's undo stack has - so the chord that the RichEdit path got free from `EM_REPLACESEL`'s wparam did nothing on the surface that replaced it. Nor can the page make such a step itself: measured in headless Edge, `execCommand("insertHTML")` inside a `plaintext-only` contenteditable FLATTENS a block or a chip to its own text, so there is no engine command that inserts the nodes this composer is built from. The same probe supplied the fix's foundation - an engine undo step recorded BEFORE a full-document rebuild is a harmless no-op afterwards, not damage. So the seed grew one field, `undo`, which says whether it is one user-visible EDIT or a wholesale replacement; an edit makes the page journal the document it replaced (markup plus caret, because a plain-text checkpoint would lose the quote ids and the chip numbers), and every other seed clears that journal, which is what stops an undo from resurrecting a report the user already sent. Ctrl+Z then asks the ENGINE first and falls back to the journal only when the engine's answer changed nothing: typing since the quote landed still unwinds keystroke by keystroke, and the quote comes out after it, in the order a user expects, without the page reimplementing typing undo. Journal bounded at 32 steps. Green: floor lanes lib/none/win32/agent ALL PASS, viewer-composer 30, viewer-feedback 71, printclient-audit 8, ipc-p1 25 / p2 20 / p3 16 ALL PASS, `guard-due.ps1 check` clean. The real oracle is the host floor test in `ViewerPane.zig`, the only thing on this box that can drive a Chromium composer (the acceptance suite runs on a background desktop where posted keys never reach a renderer): it dispatches the chord INTO the live page - a synthetic event performs no default action, so everything after it is the page's own handler - and requires the buffer back byte for byte with zero live quotes, then back again with the block carrying the same registry id; a second arm does the same for a pasted picture and asserts the image leaves and rejoins the report with it. Filed T1006: the journal lives on the page, so it does not survive closing the pill or a native rewrite of the buffer, and the user sees only that Ctrl+Z stopped working.

- 2026-08-20: T297 - opening the Activity Monitor for a machine you picked in the machine list is now PROVEN to work on the box, not just to fail politely. The panel reaches a remote machine two ways and only the borrowed one had a success case: `activity-monitor-remote.ps1` drives a panel opened from a remote window's palette (it borrows that window's connection), while the DIALED path - the chooser's Activity button - was covered only by `chooser-menu.ps1` proving the button attempts a dial and reports failure against a fake directory that is not an agent endpoint. That left the riskier half unrun, because the dial is the only path that OWNS what it opens: `close` frees a transport, `shutdown()`-before-join has to unblock a parked RPC, and a dial landing after its panel closed has to be torn down by `onDialed` instead of adopted. Each is a leak or a use-after-free when it is wrong, and all three were argued from code reading plus a unit test of `panelMatches`. The fixture T297 said had to be built already existed - `lib\FakeRelay.ps1` (T319) is exactly the client-side bridge it described, and four harnesses already dial through it - so the work was the lane: new `test\win32\activity-monitor-dialed.ps1` (28 assertions), a harness of its own rather than a lane of `activity-monitor-remote.ps1`, whose fixture is a remote WINDOW where this one needs a chooser, a relay device and a signed-in account. It presses Activity on a relay device bridged to a real loopback `ghoztty-agent` and requires the panel to dial rather than borrow, the dial to cross the relay (counted on the far side), the connection to come up, and the table to be the AGENT's - `root=<agent pid>`, the T295 oracle, since a loopback agent enumerates the same box and a populated table proves nothing. Then it closes the panel and requires the connection back, and finally stages the in-flight case with the relay's `-SlowConnectFile`: a panel closed while its dial is still parked logs `dial landed after its panel closed`, adopts nothing, leaves no socket, and the app stays responsive. Two oracles are deliberately not what the task proposed. The agent logs nothing per connection, so "the agent sees the client go away" is unobservable; what is observable from OUTSIDE the app is its ESTABLISHED socket count, which is the stronger claim anyway - a panel that only believes it let go still holds one. And a relay-side `BRIDGE down` is asserted for the LATE dial only: a freed `WsClient` sends a bare TCP FIN and no WS close frame (deliberate - `ws_client.closeImpl`, the T81 panic), while `FakeRelay`'s pump reads a bridge only when `DataAvailable` is true, which is `Socket.Available != 0` and therefore false at a bare EOF, so it notices a bridge it pushed bytes through and leaks an idle one exactly as its own header says. Asserting otherwise would assert a property of the fake. `-NegativeControl` inverts the root-pid oracle and fails on that line alone. Green: floor lanes lib/none/win32/agent ALL PASS, ipc-p1/p2/p3 ALL PASS, activity-monitor-dialed 28 ALL PASS on three consecutive runs, guard-due 47 ALL PASS with a new `activity-monitor-dialed` row (ActivityMonitor.zig is in three rows now - local, pixels, and the only harness that dials) and its stamp. Filed T1012: `persistence-flag.ps1` is red at HEAD on 14 launch sites that state no persistence intent, none of them this script.

- 2026-08-20: T299 - the Activity Monitor's ownership rules now sit in a file small enough to check. `src/apprt/win32/ActivityMonitor.zig` had reached 4,927 lines doing nine jobs at once, against the standing "no mega files" bar; it is now 1,343 and owns the window and nothing else (state, open/close, the registry, the wndProc). The two seams the task named are out, plus seven more the file's own section banners already marked: `activity_paint.zig` (829, every pixel), `activity_machines.zig` (643, machine list + carousel), `activity_probe_conn.zig` (636, per-card probe connections), `activity_input.zig` (614, mouse + focus ring), `activity_dial.zig` (465, the connection plane), `activity_sample.zig` (362, poll loop + gate + snapshot), `activity_procs.zig` (243, Kill / New Process), `activity_view.zig` (231, filter/selection/scroll + layout + chrome). The point was never the line count: the dangerous rules - unsubscribe before join, join before free, a borrowed connection is never freed, bump the serial so a stale dial frees itself, drop a sample by generation - were all true before and all spread through five thousand lines, which is the difference between a rule you can audit and one you can only hope about. Each now sits as a documented list at the top of the file that enforces it, and the panel header's per-feature commentary moved with the code it describes (`## Remote sources (T295)` is read in the dial file, `## Per-card metrics probes (T298)` in the probe file). Being a pure refactor was PROVED rather than asserted, twice over: the set of top-level function signatures before and after is identical (nothing missing, nothing added), and every changed non-comment code line is one of four mechanical shapes - a `pub` marker, a moved declaration, a `self.f(x)` rewritten to `f(self, x)`, or a static now qualified with its owning file. That the moved tests still RUN was teeth-checked, not assumed: breaking one assertion in each new test home turned both red under their new module names (`apprt.win32.activity_paint.test.columnAt: ...`, `apprt.win32.activity_input.test.nextVisibleFocus: ...`), then reverted to 5,051 passed / 72 skipped / 0 failed. Floor lanes lib/none/win32/agent ALL PASS; `ipc-p1/p2/p3` ALL PASS; `activity-monitor.ps1` ALL PASS at 157 assertions - the same 157 T989 recorded the day before - and `activity-monitor-remote.ps1` at 90. Adding files put three more harnesses in DUE even though nothing behaves differently, and all three pass: `activity-selection.ps1` (45), `activity-monitor-dialed.ps1` (28), `printclient-audit.ps1` (8, over 189 files). Filed T1013: the same bar is broken far worse by five files this one is no longer the largest of - `ViewerPane.zig` 9,048, `App.zig` 8,778, `Window.zig` 7,637, `Surface.zig` 4,800, `MachineChooser.zig` 4,052 - and it carries the T299 method, including the two proofs, as the recipe.

- 2026-08-20: T303 - a GUI test can no longer pass by measuring a blank photo of a window. `Get-TestWindowPixels` refused exactly one window it could not really photograph - our own terminal surface (T214) - and returned a flat fill for every other window that composites rather than paints, reporting success: PrintWindow against Task Manager's main window came back a flat black 1379x1134 bitmap, 1 distinct colour, an 8 KB PNG, and a seam scan over it then found no seams, which reads as "this app has no seam" rather than "there is no capture". That is the whole WinUI/XAML family - Settings, Task Manager, most of the Win11 shell. The helper now reads the bitmap back and THROWS when a non-trivial capture is one colour across its whole interior, after retrying for 2s to rule out the other way a capture comes back uniform: a window that had not painted yet, transient where composition is permanent. The message names DirectComposition, points at the CAPTURE LIMIT header and names the opt-out; `-AllowUniform` is a SEPARATE switch from `-AllowTerminalSurface` on purpose, so measuring the terminal flat fill takes both and neither switch quietly disarms the other - which is also what lets that known-flat surface be the fixture. The header gained the general rule its old text only implied (PrintWindow sees GDI, not composition) and the corollary: a Win11 app cannot be a pixel REFERENCE at all, so Windows metrics are measured through SystemParametersInfoForDpi / GetSystemMetrics / uxtheme / DWM and Fluent is cited as documentation, never as a measurement (plus the trap beside it - Task Manager launches elevated, so a non-elevated session cannot close it again). `test-desktop-harness.ps1` gained three assertions and a `-NegativeControl`: the guard fires on the known-flat surface, its message names the cause and the opt-out, and real ghoztty chrome still sails through - the half that keeps a stricter guard from being a broken one. Also wired that harness into `guard-due` as row `test-desktop` over `lib\TestDesktop.ps1`: the library every GUI acceptance script stands on had no harness obligation at all, which is this table's own subject asked about its foundation - a refusal that stops firing turns the suite green without ever turning it red. Green: floor lanes lib/none/win32/agent ALL PASS; ipc-p1/p2/p3 ALL PASS (25/20/16); test-desktop-harness ALL PASS at 27 assertions, 0 skipped, and its `-NegativeControl` run 4 FAILURE(S) exit 1; the three audits the edits made due - isolation-meta (7), verdict-exit, stderr-capture (25) - ALL PASS.

- 2026-08-20: T306 - the title/tab band deliberately does NOT become Mica, and the reason is measured rather than argued. Mica is the most recognizable Windows 11 window cue and the thing that makes Terminal's strip read as part of the frame, so this was the deliberate look at adopting `DWMWA_SYSTEMBACKDROP_TYPE` for the merged caption + tab band. It was measured on a live window by applying the backdrop FROM OUTSIDE the app (the MicaForEveryone trick), so answering the question shipped no experiment code, and on the INPUT desktop, because DWM composes only that desktop and the background test desktop cannot answer a question about composition at all. Three findings, in the order they decide it. The attribute alone is a NO-OP: DWM accepts Auto/Mica/Acrylic/Tabbed (`S_OK`, reads back) and composites the material behind a client area that is opaque GDI to the top edge since T254 took the caption into it - the band pixel is `#7e6734` in all five states, unmoved. Opening glass into the client area does not reveal Mica, it DESTROYS the band: with `DwmExtendFrameIntoClientArea(-1)` GDI's missing alpha turns the band into a blend the painter never computed, `#7e6734` -> `#a69368`, and the title falls to 3.0:1 against it - under the 4.5:1 floor section 2.3 calls non-negotiable - while the washed colour is IDENTICAL under a solid black and a solid white wallpaper, which is the tell that it is not the material at all. Real Mica therefore means an alpha-correct repaint of the caption, tab shapes, glyphs and text: a chrome-painter rewrite, not a flag. And after that rewrite the band's colour would follow the WALLPAPER, which three standing commitments are built on it not doing - the contrast floors are computed from the band colour, T202's selected chiclet merges into the pane and needs the two to agree on a colour a desktop-sampling material cannot see, and `window-theme = auto` tints the caption to the TERMINAL background, which is the Mac behaviour this seat matches. - 2026-08-20: T314 - the machine chooser's acceptance script now measures the text column exactly instead of within a nine-pixel window, and the last private DIP conversion in it is gone. The second defect is the more interesting one and no shared rounding helper fixes it: `chooser_rows.rowMetrics` COMPOSES `text_x` out of six individually-rounded terms (4 pill inset + 8 + a 12 status column + 4 + a 28 icon column + 12), and a sum of rounded parts is not the rounded sum at ANY rounding mode - 79 composed against 77 half-away and 76 banker's at 1.125. T310 hit this and could only write its row-geometry probe as a band (`>= 65 DIP`, `<= 74 DIP`) with ~9 px of slack against the retired geometry. The script composes the same terms now (`Get-ChooserTextX`), so the probe is anchored on `text_x` itself and the only slack left is what the FONT adds: the window is `[text_x, text_x + sm]`, and the retired 60 DIP geometry misses the floor by 10 px rather than sitting inside the band. The 112.5% case cannot be staged on any monitor here, so it is pinned where it can be exercised - a new `chooser_rows.zig` unit test requires `rowMetrics(1.125).text_x == 79` and that the six-term sum IS the metric, with both wrong arithmetics named in the comment, which is what stops a future script from re-deriving the total and agreeing with the module by luck. - 2026-08-20: T992 - a copy in the terminal can no longer be overtaken mid-flight by another app. Every clipboard open in the app claimed NO owner window (`OpenClipboard(NULL)`), and the exclusion Windows enforces is "another WINDOW has the clipboard open" - so a null owner excludes nobody. Measured on the box in both arms before touching the code: while a null-owner holder holds the clipboard, a second process's `OpenClipboard` succeeds STRAIGHT THROUGH, and the holder's own `SetClipboardData` afterwards fails with 1418 `ERROR_CLIPBOARD_NOT_OPEN`; with a real HWND that second process is refused with 5 `ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED` and the write succeeds. Unobstructed, a null-owner write still lands and leaves `GetClipboardOwner()` at 0, which is why this shipped for months: the failure needs a second app writing the clipboard inside the same few milliseconds, and then the user's copy silently yields that app's content or nothing, with no error anywhere. Same family as T947 (found by its harness) but the opposite half - T947 was the copy never STARTING, this is the copy being overtaken between its `EmptyClipboard` and its `SetClipboardData`. The fix is one owner for the whole process rather than one per call site: `clipboard_open.zig` gains a `default_owner` that `App.init` registers as `msg_hwnd` (the message-only window, which outlives every surface) and `App.deinit` clears before destroying it, plus `effectiveOwner()`, which prefers a live caller window, falls back to the app's when the caller's has been DESTROYED - the confirm dialog pumps messages and can free a surface mid-request - and only then to none, logging that the write is not atomic. A registry rather than a parameter because the write sites that needed it (`ViewerPane.clipboardWriteText`, the composer's image read) are file-scope helpers with no `App` in reach, and a call site that forgets is exactly how this arrives a second time. Proved by putting the bug back: with the registration replaced by `setDefaultOwner(null)` and the app rebuilt, the new arm fails with `got 0`; restored and rebuilt, ALL PASS. `test\win32\clipboard-retry.ps1` grew arm D - D0 reproduces the null-owner write in-process so the oracle is known to be able to see the pre-fix shape (owner 0), D2 reads a real owner back after a real OSC 52 copy, D3 requires that window to belong to the app under test (owner pid == app pid) - and arm C3 keeps the registration itself from being silently dropped, since the guard row deliberately does not cover `App.zig`. Green: floor lanes lib/none/win32/agent ALL PASS, ipc-p1 25 / p2 20 / p3 16 ALL PASS, clipboard-retry ALL PASS (A1-A3, B1-B2 unchanged, C1-C3, D0-D3) and re-stamped, and the four suite-wide audits the test edit made due (printclient 8 over 189 files, isolation-meta 7, verdict-exit, stderr-capture 25) green and re-stamped, `guard-due.ps1 check` exit 0.

- 2026-08-20: T1039 - an acceptance script that throws halfway through can no longer print ALL PASS and record its guard as proven. The shape, measured in T329: almost every script here wraps its body in a top-level `try { ...the run... } finally { ...cleanup... }` with no `catch`, because the finally is how the app, the agent and the test desktop get torn down - and under `$ErrorActionPreference = 'Continue'` a *statement*-terminating error inside that try (a division by zero, a bad cast, `.Trim()` on the `$null` that `Get-Content -Raw` answers for an empty file) unwinds the try, runs the finally, and then CONTINUES with the statements after it: the guard stamp and the verdict, with the failure count still 0. `activity-monitor-dialed.ps1` did exactly that - ended at the top of its last section, printed `ALL PASS (27 assertions)`, and stamped every file it covers as freshly proven. 95 of 155 scripts were in that shape, so T329's per-script `catch` arm fixed one instance of a structural hole. The rule now lives beside T271's in `lib\TestScore.ps1`: **dot-sourcing the scorer ARMS the run**, `Complete-TestBody` as the last statement of the top-level try marks it finished, and `Write-TestVerdict` refuses a green verdict without it - `RUN DID NOT FINISH (N assertions passed)`, exit 2, the same "the harness measured nothing" news as ASSERTED NOTHING. Arming is the dot-source rather than a call to remember, because a rule that only protects the scripts that opted in protects nobody; the check is made LAST, so it only ever speaks over a verdict that would otherwise be green and FAILURE(S) / ASSERTED NOTHING / ASSERTED TOO LITTLE keep their wording. - 2026-08-22: T355 - the number a persistent session reports as its shell's pid is now checked against the OS rather than merely checked for being non-zero. T41 fixed the bug (Windows was publishing the process HANDLE, which names nothing: the report read `shell pid 492`); this is the test that would have caught it, and the reason nothing did is worth naming. Every assertion that existed on `pid` asked whether it was non-zero (`server.zig`'s `rp.value.pid != 0`) or whether it round-tripped (`expectEqual(1001, …)` against a FakeSpawner). A handle satisfies both. The one test that asked a real question - T98's - walks the process table through `proc.ProcSampler`, the same helper the product reads the world through, and it asserts parentage rather than existence.

  Two things were done about it. The conversion was given a name and one home: `pty_child.reportedPid`. It had been an inline `if (is_windows)` block inside `spawnFn` with no test, and `pty_host.zig` - the HOLDER, which is the Windows DEFAULT since T909 and therefore the arm the user's `+sessions` output actually comes from - carried a SECOND copy behind its own private `GetProcessId` extern. Two copies of a conversion that had already been wrong once is the shape this task exists to prevent, so the extern is gone and both arms call the same function.

  Then two `test-agent` cases. The first asks the OS directly - `OpenProcess` + `GetExitCodeProcess` on Windows, `kill(pid, 0)` on POSIX - whether a real ConPTY child's reported pid names something that is running, deliberately not through the sampler. The second is the one that cannot pass by luck: `reportedPid` is fed the process pseudo-handle, whose integer value is `0xFFFF_FFFF_FFFF_FFFF`, so a conversion that reports the handle fails on the number rather than on being unlucky with a small one. Verified by running it: the pre-T41 `@intFromPtr(child_pid)` restored turns the agent lane RED (`exited with code 3`), and reverting it green.

  The holder arm needed acceptance rather than unit coverage - T933 makes a test binary refuse to spawn itself as its own holder, so `test-agent` reaches only the in-process ConPTY child. `pty-holder.ps1` gained A10/A10b/A10c: take the pid out of `+list --json` (the whole journey - holder resolves it from the HANDLE, hands it to the agent, agent publishes it to the app) and assert it names a live process whose parent is the holder. Its first draft compared against the `$shellPid` A8 had found and FAILED, which turned out to be the test's fault and a real weakness in A8: its shell regex included `conhost.exe`, and `Get-CimInstance` returned the console host first. So A8 could have passed on a holder that had spawned no shell at all. `conhost` is out of the alternation now, and the new assertions print both numbers so the next disagreement is diagnosable from the log instead of from a re-run.

- 2026-08-22: T357 - the close confirmation is now proved to still appear in the two cases where it is not the shell's call. T41 made the ABSENCE of the dialog a normal outcome, and that inverted what a regression looks like: before it, every close confirmed, so a broken `confirm-close-surface = always` was loud; after it, a bug that suppressed `always` looks exactly like the feature working. `Surface.shellIsIdle` answers FALSE for `always` and for a read-only surface before it ever looks at the process table, and neither branch was asserted anywhere - `close-confirm-idle.ps1` ran the default config and `confirm-dialogs.ps1` is about the dialog's rendering, not the policy that opens it.

  Two sections were added to `test\win32\close-confirm-idle.ps1`, both running an IDLE shell (descendant-free, asserted straight out of `Win32_Process` exactly as A-C do), because idle is the only state in which the forced branch is the sole reason a dialog can appear - a busy shell confirms anyway and would prove nothing. **D/always** exercises both consumers of the branch, since they are separate call sites: Ctrl+W is `Surface.close` -> `shellIsIdleNow`, and WM_CLOSE (the title-bar X / Alt+F4 path) is `Window.confirmCloseIfNeeded`, which asks `shellIsIdle` once per pane against one shared snapshot. Its discriminator is section A rather than a toggle inside the section, because nothing in a running app can turn `always` off: A is the same harness, the same chord and the same idle oracle under the default config, and there the idle close does not confirm.

  **E/readonly** first had to answer the task's own open question - is read-only reachable on win32 at all? It is, but only through a binding action: `toggle_readonly` has no default chord and no CLI verb, and is otherwise reached by hand from the context menu or the command palette. So the section launches with `--keybind=ctrl+shift+o=toggle_readonly`, the route `readonly-badge.ps1` established, and uses the `GhozttyReadonlyBadge` window as the independent oracle that the toggle actually landed. That badge doubles as the section's positive control - it proves chords reach this window, so a later "no dialog" cannot be "no keystroke". Unlike `always`, read-only can be turned back OFF, so E carries its own discriminator: same pane, same chord, read-only off, and the dialog must be gone and the pane must close.

What it is about is `src\apprt\win32\Surface.zig`, which moves for a hundred reasons unrelated to the close confirmation, so a row would leave a 5-minute GUI harness permanently due - and a gate that is always red is a gate nobody reads. That is the same call the table already records for core `src\Surface.zig`.

- 2026-08-22: T361 - the win32 acceptance suite can be run as a suite now, and the first time anybody ran it, it was already red. `scripts\suite-run.ps1` takes the 241 top-level scripts in `test\win32` (136 of which drive a GUI), runs each as its own `powershell -File` child with its output in a per-script log, and scores it by the suite's own verdict contract - `pass` / `fail` / `nothing` (exit 2) / `stall` (killed at `-TimeoutSec`) / `error`, where `error` covers the T221 shape of exit 0 with no verdict line, which must never launder as green. `list`, `run` and `compare`; `-Set gui|cli|all`, `-Order forward|reverse|<explicit list>`, `-Include`/`-Exclude`, `-Resume`.

  Three properties are what make it usable rather than merely written. Every row is written to `summary.json` the moment its script ends, so a sweep killed at script 90 keeps 90 rows and `-Resume` continues - a suite this long WILL be interrupted, so the design assumes it. A hang costs one script: the child is killed at the timeout, scored `stall`, and the sweep carries on. And it sweeps leaked processes between scripts - anything still running out of the repo's `zig-out`, path-exact and repo-scoped the way `CleanSlate` is - reporting which script leaked, because the script that leaks is rarely the one that then fails.

  **The number the task was filed to get.** First real sweep: 63 of 241 scripts in 37.9 minutes, mean 36.1 s and median 17.7 s per script, so a full forward pass is about **2h 25m** and T267's forward/forward/reverse is about **seven hours**. That confirms the premise - this suite cannot be swept inside an ordinary turn - and bounds it, which is what was missing. Slowest in the sample: `chrome-theme.ps1` 198 s, `agent-upgrade.ps1` 173 s, `agent-sharing-uplink.ps1` 160 s.

  **What it found.** 59 pass, 4 fail in that first quarter: `agent-autostart.ps1`, `caption-bar.ps1` (a UNIFORM capture), `chooser-close-chord.ps1`, `chooser-orphan-badge.ps1` - none of them run recently enough for anyone to know. Two scripts left a live `zig-out` process behind on the way out (`agent-instance-lineage.ps1`, `agent-relay-session-e2e.ps1`), visible only because of the between-script sweep. T1094 carries finishing the sweep and filing a task per red. `ipc-version.ps1` is separate and structural - it asserts the build's baked commit equals HEAD, and the loop builds, tests, THEN commits, so it is red on every committing turn by construction; that is T1093, and `BuildFresh.ps1` already wrote down why that is the wrong question inside a working tree.

  Order independence was discharged by measurement rather than argument, on the 16 fastest GUI scripts in the sample: forward, forward again, reverse (3m 27s / 3m 26s / 3m 25s, ALL PASS each), then `compare` over the three summaries - STABLE. The whole-suite version costs the seven hours above and belongs to T1094.

  It is serial, and that is a decision with a reason rather than an omission: 91 scripts compute the app path as `<repo>\zig-outin\ghoztty.exe` internally and ignore an injected `-Exe`, and `CleanSlate` kills the app under test by exact ExecutablePath - so two workers out of one `zig-out` kill each other's app mid-assertion, with no error either can attribute. Parallelism needs an injected exe path honored suite-wide first, filed as T1092.

  One bug in this turn's own work is worth recording, because it is the class the runner exists to catch: the first version reported a 116.2-second script as **2m 56s**, since `[int]$ts.TotalMinutes` ROUNDS in .NET rather than truncating. A number nobody can check by eye does not belong in a test report, so the formatter moved to `scripts\lib\Duration.ps1` where section J of the acceptance calls it directly. The same run found a second one: PS 5.1 unrolls a one-element array on return, so a one-script run printed `[  1/]` and `( scripts)` - now covered by B11.

- 2026-08-22: T1099 - the eight commits the upstream-pull plan is built on are anchored by something that cannot be pruned, and the line the loop prints about them can finally go red. Two separate defects wore one symptom.

  **The ref did not decay - it was deleted.** The 05:14 hard-fork turn ran `git remote remove upstream` by hand; that takes `refs/remotes/upstream/*` with it, and the 05:26 correction re-added the remote fetch-only without restoring the tracking ref. Nothing fetched again until the next claim, so for roughly ninety minutes all eight plan shas were reachable from no ref at all and a `git gc` was entitled to drop them. That is not a bug in any script - it is the anchor being the wrong KIND of ref. A remote-tracking ref also vanishes on a refspec change, on a fresh clone, and on the Mac seat, which has never fetched this remote. So the anchor is now a local lightweight tag per sha, `refs/tags/upstream-anchor/<sha>`, written by `upstream-remote.ps1 ensure` and therefore re-asserted by the claim every turn. A tag is a ref this repo owns: no remote operation prunes it, it survives the remote being removed outright, and lightweight means neither `git push` nor `push.followTags` can leak it into `origin`.

  **The false green is the separate half, and it is the one that let this sit.** `ensure` printed `UPSTREAM OK` from `upstream/main` resolving ALONE - it never asked the plan-sha question `check` asks. The one line the loop prints every turn could not go red for the exact thing the script exists to protect, and it duly printed `UPSTREAM OK (upstream/main a88ad03e6, fetched 16h ago)` on the very turn whose acceptance run scored five failures against this repo. The verdict now comes from one function, `Get-Problems`, that both verbs call, so the two cannot drift into answering different questions. `ensure` prints `UPSTREAM PROBLEM` and names the offending shas - and still exits 0, because a claim that wedges on an unreachable GitHub is a worse failure than an unanchored sha; the teeth belong in the acceptance script via `guard-due`. `check` also stopped hiding the sha rows behind a missing ref: the whole point of the tag is that a sha stays alive with the remote gone, so the rows are evaluated either way.

  The plan doc joined the guard's coverage list, because the doc IS the input - `check` reads its sha list out of the backticks - so a re-cut stage introduces a sha nothing has anchored yet, and editing the doc now makes the harness due rather than leaving the gate green over a new pin.

  Section E of the acceptance is the demonstration the task asked for, run against a throwaway repo with its own plan doc so it measures the mechanism rather than the live box being healthy: anchor three fixture shas, then rip the remote out the way 2026-08-22 did (E3 they stay anchored), expire every reflog and `git gc --prune=now` (E4 they survive), then cite a sha the repo has never seen (E5 `ensure` prints UPSTREAM PROBLEM, E6 it still exits 0). The live-repo half was demonstrated too, and in the honest order: `check` printed UPSTREAM PROBLEM naming all eight shas as gc bait and exited 1 BEFORE `ensure` had ever run, then green after.

  Filed on the way past: T1132 (the plan is still filed under a name that says "merge-back", the phrase CLAUDE.md bans - the filename is what a turn sees in a search result, and the prose disambiguation inside it is not what gets read first) and T1133 (this is the third gate this month that could not go red; the acceptance scripts do not have this problem because every one carries a `-NegativeControl`, and the claim-time and validate-time gates have no equivalent).

"Merge back" meant the **cutover** (this branch onto `main` in dzearing/ghoztty - the goal), an **upstream pull** (ghostty-org into this fork, allowed on the user's call), and **upstreaming** (this fork into ghostty-org, which never happens), with nothing in the wording to tell them apart. On 2026-08-22 that cost a full round trip with the user twice, and produced T1095 - a task filed on the misreading that had to be closed again.

  The root of it was a filename: `windows-parity-merge-back-plan.md` covered the second sense while its title said the first. `git mv` to `docs/design/windows-parity-upstream-pull-plan.md` (history follows), and its opening section is now a three-row table - operation, direction, where it is tracked - that the ship-workflow doc and `ship-readiness.ps1`'s header both carry verbatim, so whichever of the three a reader lands on, the other two are named beside it.   `test\win32\merge-terminology.ps1` is what stops the phrase coming back, and it earned its keep the first time it ran: five bare uses that a `git grep -i 'merge.back'` had missed, because "merg**es** back" and "merg**ed** back" are two characters apart from the pattern a human writes. It scans every tracked text file and every open task file, and treats the phrase as a finding unless it is REPORTED rather than USED - a quoted mention (`"merge back"` in a sentence about the phrase, which is how CLAUDE.md and D80 explain the ban) or a quotation (a double-quoted span or a markdown blockquote carrying somebody else's words; the user's own cutover directive is quoted verbatim in three live files and must not be edited to fit a naming rule). A quotation is bounded - under 800 characters, no blank line inside - so an unbalanced quote mark cannot silently exempt the rest of a file, and both bounds have their own fixture.

- 2026-08-22: T1102 - the four feedback scripts that said the composer "holds ''" were typing into a control nobody is looking at. Attaching a screenshot to a viewer feedback report looked broken from four directions at once: `viewer-feedback-capture`, `-images`, `-carousel` and `-utf16` all reported an empty composer where an `[Image #1]` chip belonged, and `report.json` carrying zero images. Nothing was wrong with the feature. T934/T936 made a WebView2 page the composer's DEFAULT surface and left the RichEdit as a runtime fallback; these four scripts drive the composer with window messages, which reach a native control and cannot reach a Chromium window from the background test desktop (T233), and none of them had pinned the surface. So the app opened on `surface=web` while the scripts read a hidden, empty `RichEdit50W`.

  The chip was landing the whole time, and the app said so in the same log the scripts were already reading: `image=#1 bytes=430 live=1`, where `live` is counted from the chips in `pane.feedbackText()`. What turned a misleading assertion into a WRONG one is the second half - `Send-TestControlText` into that dead control fires `EN_CHANGE`, and the mirror behind it replaces the pane's buffer with just the typed line, which is how the picture left the report. A harness reading the wrong surface was also silently editing the right one.

  The fix is `test\win32\lib\ComposerSurface.ps1`: `Set-ComposerSurface 'richedit'` asks for the surface a script can drive, and `Wait-ComposerSurface` PROVES the app agreed. The proof is the part that matters, because asking is not getting - the env var is one of three ways the app reaches the RichEdit, and `richedit(controller-refused)` after a WebView2 failure would otherwise be indistinguishable from the pin. Each of the four now carries one assertion naming the surface it got, so the next time the default moves the failure is one readable line instead of six that read like a broken feature.

  Deliberately NOT done: guarding the `EN_CHANGE` mirror on `self.web == null`. It would have made this exact failure quiet, and the loud failure is what caught it; the RichEdit machinery is T937's to delete outright. T937 got the re-point list instead - `grep Set-ComposerSurface` is now the whole answer to "which scripts have to move when the fallback goes".

  Swept for the same class of drift while here: every script that touches `GhozttyViewerFeedback` now pins a surface, so no second script is sitting where these four were. What the pin LEAVES is T1136, filed on the way past - the whole screenshot story is now proven on a surface no user gets. `viewer-composer.ps1` carries no image assertion at all, and the in-process `host floor` reaches a chip through a paste rather than through the region selector, so nothing at all asserts capture-to-report, the strip, or chip deletion on the default surface.

  Green: `viewer-feedback-capture.ps1` ALL PASS (64), was `6 FAILURE(S) (57 passed)`; `-images.ps1` ALL PASS (40), was 6/19; `-carousel.ps1` ALL PASS (39), was 6/32; `-utf16.ps1` ALL PASS (30), was 4/25 - its caret assertions came back with no change to the caret code, exactly as the task predicted.

- 2026-08-22: T1103 - `window.open()` from a viewer pane was never broken; the test had been told to ignore the window it was looking for. The sweep's report read like an outage: a page that opens a second window "silently does nothing", five assertions red including the load-bearing one that proves the popup is the runtime's window and not a lookalike we opened at the same URL. Nothing was wrong with the adoption path. `viewer-popup.ps1` picks the popup out of `+list --json` as "the window that was not already open", and it snapshotted "already open" AFTER waiting for the opener's pane to register - while the opener's page calls `window.open()` the instant it loads. On a loaded box the popup won that race, landed in the ignore set, and could never be found again.

  The same failing log carries the proof: `known windows: window-1, opener, window-2` at setup, against `window-1, opener` on a green run - `window-2` IS the popup, counted as scenery. Sections D and E then passed for the wrong reasons. D finds the popup by its window title rather than through IPC, so it reported the adopted window at exactly the portrait size the page asked for (668x897) while the section above it said no window had appeared at all. E asserted "no unknown window is present", which is free when the popup was never known.

  The fix is ordering: the snapshot is taken BEFORE the opener exists - a popup cannot be created before its own opener, so there is no race left to lose - and the opener is excluded by the name the script itself gives it (`--target=opener`) rather than by having been seen. E now names the window it expects to lose (`target 'window-2'`), so a run where the popup was never found fails there instead of passing. `viewer-popup.ps1` ALL PASS (20), twice, with no product code changed.

  What that costs the queue is T1137, filed here: this is the SECOND sweep-filed task in a row (after T1102) to be titled as a broken feature and turn out to be a broken test, and both took a full turn to find out. Re-running a red script once on its own before filing is the whole gate; a script green alone and red in a sweep is an isolation defect and should not arrive at the head of the queue described as a user-facing outage.

  Green: floor all four lanes PASS; P1/P2/P3 25/20/16; the five audit harnesses the test edit made due re-run and re-stamped (isolation-meta, launch-preflight, verdict-exit, cleanslate, stderr-capture). `fork-identity` stays red for T1134's reason and nothing to do with this turn - its C4 baseline has decayed further with main intake (reproduced=25 against baseline=28, down from 27 yesterday), so committed under `-NoGuardDue` naming T1134 rather than lowering a number to make a red go away.

- 2026-08-22: T1104 - Ctrl+T from a viewer pane works; the keyboard test rig was letting go of Ctrl before the app could read it. The sweep filed this as a user-facing regression, and it is the third in a row (after T1102 and T1103) that turned out to be a broken test. `viewer-panes.ps1` was green on this box every time it was re-run, so the red had to be forced: suspending the app's UI thread across the keystroke reproduces it on demand.

  A viewer chord has two readers in series. Chromium classifies the key as an accelerator from the modifier state, and only then raises `AcceleratorKeyPressed` onto our UI thread, where the binding is matched - and each reads the modifier state as it gets to it. With real hardware that is safe, because modifier state travels with the message stream: the ctrl-up that clears it is still behind the letter in the queue, so even a slow reader sees what was held when the key went down. The harness does not use real input. `SendChordCross` pokes the state in with `SetKeyboardState` and cleared it 400ms after posting the keys, on a clock rather than on the app. Past that point ctrl+t resolves as a bare `t`, matches no binding, and opens nothing.

  The same shape sat in `SendChord` with an 80ms hold, and took `T161 CONTROL: ctrl+d from a terminal split right` down beside it mid-investigation - on a box loaded by nothing more than the run itself. So this was never one chord: every modified chord in every script rides these two helpers, and the exposure was the delivery mechanism, not the keybind.

  Both now hold the faked modifiers until the app has demonstrably drained (`PumpedTwice`: two consecutive answered `WM_NULL` pings, capped at 5s) and only then release. A busy app makes the helper wait instead of making the assertion lie. `SendChordCrossStarved` / `Send-TestViewerChordStarved` is the regression guard: it suspends the app's UI thread for 1.2s across the keystroke while holding the modifiers down, the way a finger does, and the new T1104 fixture in `viewer-panes.ps1` asserts the tab still opens.

  An app-side fix was tried first and reverted: resolving the modifiers from the accelerator event stream rather than `GetKeyState`. It does not help, and the app log is why - under the same starvation `vk=0x11` arrives with no `vk=0x54` behind it, because Chromium reads the same state to decide the key is an accelerator at all and had already lost it. The marker is the build file rather than `.git`, because an archive or a worktree copy with no git dir still builds and still must not claim the scheme. Both real install shapes are outside a checkout and are unaffected, which is why the gate excludes build OUTPUT rather than trying to enumerate install locations. `GHOZTTY_URL_SCHEME` grew two words next to its existing `off`: `force` skips the gate, and `gate` applies it to a debug build too.

Two inputs, two answers, for the same divider.

A held key is treated as ONE gesture rather than a series of independent presses, for the reason the drag replays from a mouse-down snapshot: an `f16` ratio round-tripped through pixels once per press does not round-trip cleanly, and eighty presses out and back left a held boundary 40px from where it started - measured, and kept as a control test. `split_resize.KeyboardGesture` holds the pre-gesture snapshot and the accumulated pixel offset, and ends itself when the tree stops matching the ratios its last plan wrote, since there is no key-up to hang an `end` on. The subtlety that cost the most: `plan` prunes any subtree whose range did not move relative to the snapshot, so replaying back to the start would leave a divider an earlier press had squeezed against its clamp still squeezed - the gesture puts back anything it moved that this press does not mention, which is what makes out-and-back exact rather than merely close. That is the window storm the user reported on 2026-08-23 ("you left some insane window spamming"), and it was neither a stress script nor the restore.

  The evidence is exact rather than inferred. The six detached pinned sessions in the installed agent were created in two bursts - 08-22 05:19:33 (x2) and 08-23 01:05:08 (x4) - and `%TEMP%\ghoztty-soak\` holds run directories timestamped five seconds before each.   What made it possible was a half-isolated harness and a gate that took the caller's word. Isolating a release-lineage run needs three knobs, and `lib\BuildMode.ps1`'s own header already named the trap - *"One or two of the three is the dangerous state, not a partial win: a release build under a private pipe suffix alone still dials the agent that owns the user's live sessions"*. `soak.ps1` set `GHOZTTY_PIPE_SUFFIX`, nothing else, and passed `-AllowReleaseBuild`. Its app pipe was private while every pane it opened became a PINNED session in the user's real roster; its teardown closes the window, and a pinned session surviving a window close IS the persistence feature (`session.zig:1729`), so nothing could reap them. The pile was monotonic and the 5am refresh restarted the user's terminal into it.

  So the fix is the gate, not just the script. `-Allow` used to `return` unconditionally; it now VERIFIES. `Get-GhozttyReleaseSandboxGaps` names which knobs are missing - comparing `LOCALAPPDATA` against the KNOWN FOLDER, which `[Environment]::GetFolderPath` reports immune to the very override being detected - and `-UserEndpoints -Reason` is the declared, loud opt-out for a script whose subject really is the installed build. `Set-GhozttyTestIsolation -ReleaseSandbox` sets all three in one call, trimming the tag so `GHOZTTY_AGENT_INSTANCE` stays inside `agent_lineage.max_len` (over-long values are rejected rather than truncated, so two sandboxes could otherwise silently share a lineage). One stale sentence in the old refusal was corrected on the way past: it claimed the agent pipe has no env override, contradicting the same file's header eight lines above, and is plausibly how the soak came to treat the pipe suffix as all that was available.

  The soak now also derives `$appLog` AFTER the sandbox moves `LOCALAPPDATA`, tears down its own sandbox agent and `--pty-host` holders (they escape the job by design - T904/T906/T1127 - so closing the window reaches none of them), and asserts a bystander check every run: the user's roster read before the sandbox goes up and again after teardown, red on any stray.

Full 5-minute smoke `ALL PASS (12 assertions)`, zero `zig-out-release` processes left behind. `build-mode-guard.ps1` reconstructs the soak's exact pre-fix state and scores it red - one knob at a time, plus the declared opt-out with and without a reason - `ALL PASS`; `launch-preflight-audit.ps1` B5z/B5y hold the launcher to the same bar, `ALL PASS (19)`; `log-append.ps1 ALL PASS (12)`, `isolation-meta ALL PASS (13)`. Floor all four lanes PASS. That guard had no `guard-due` row at all - only the freshness half of the pre-flight was covered - so a change to this very file pointed nobody at its test; a row now covers `lib\BuildMode.ps1`, `lib\Isolation.ps1` and the guard, and a green run stamps it. `fork-identity` stays red for T1134's reason and nothing to do with this turn, so committed under `-NoGuardDue` naming T1134; T1161 was filed for that red before T1134 was found in this log and it is closed as that duplicate, its residual list copied across.

  The six leaked shells were verified inert - bare `cmd.exe`, no arguments, no children, no windows - and killed. Their SESSION rows did not go with them, and that is the finding that matters most: sixty seconds after the processes were gone the agent still reported all six `alive` against dead pids. `markExited` is reachable from exactly one place, `onChildOutput`, so exit detection rides the child's output path and needs a live reader; the holders were long gone, so there is no EOF, no nudge, and no reap, ever. Filed as T1162 - and the distinction it turns on is worth keeping: this is not "age out pinned live sessions", which would break the persistence the user wants, it is "notice the child is gone", because a session whose process has exited was never a persistence case.

  Also filed: T1160 - the soak's `median fps >= 20` bar was graded from the USER'S `ghoztty.log`, because `LOCALAPPDATA` was not isolated either, so it was passing on the frames of the terminal the user was working in. Replaced with `p90 >= 30`, which is a real floor with real margin - but 30 came from one short run, and T1160 is the calibration against a full 30-minute soak. T1163 - restore unions the app manifest with the layout blobs the AGENT holds (`App.zig:2820`), and nothing paces the result, so a user who legitimately accumulates a dozen persistent panes gets a dozen windows at once. - 2026-08-23: T1134 - the fork-identity check can be green again on a tree that is absorbing main. It had been red for four days for a reason that was not a defect, and three consecutive turns committed past it with the blanket hatch, which is the exact habit T1133 exists to break.

  What it was measuring, and why the number could only fall. Section C is the honest half of the overlay's acceptance: it checks the 52 upstream-identical files out at the fork point `063ac3ecc`, runs `scripts\fork-identity.ps1` over them, and counts how many come back byte-for-byte equal to HEAD. `$ReproBaseline = 28` asserted that count never regressed. But every real edit that lands on one of those files - ours, or one arriving through the daily main intake - makes it irreproducible from a 2026-05-07 tree forever after. T1073's merge added 45 lines to `HACKING.md` and took the count from 28 to 27. Nothing had regressed; the ruler had.

  One number was answering two questions, so it is now two things. The baseline is a per-file manifest, `test\win32\fork-identity-repro.json`: each reproducing file recorded with the HEAD blob sha it had when it was recorded. C4 asks the RULE question - a recorded file whose blob has not moved must still reproduce - and that is immune to absorbing main, because main cannot change a blob without changing its sha. A recorded file whose blob DID move and no longer reproduces is DRIFT: printed (`drifted since the baseline (N)`, naming them), never asserted, and aged out of the manifest by the next green run. The manifest moves on exactly the terms `guard-due.ps1`'s stamp does - only a fully green run may write it, and only when the recorded map actually differs, so an ordinary green run leaves the working tree clean and a red run leaves the baseline alone, which is what keeps a real regression red on the following run instead of absorbing itself.

  What a drifted file loses is only the exact-bytes check, and it is worth naming what still covers it: section A (the overlay reports nothing on that file at HEAD) and C5 (the overlay leaves no findings on it from the fork point). What C4 uniquely catches is a rule that writes the WRONG fork spelling - `check` looks for the upstream form, finds none, and is happy. So the manifest's teeth are measured rather than assumed. New C8 corrupts every rewriting rule's replacement text by one character in the sandbox and asserts at least one live-reproducing file stops reproducing: 23 of 27 do, every run. New C7 fails if the manifest ever records fewer than 20 of the 52, so it cannot be silenced by emptying it.

  All three paths proved on the box rather than reasoned about. A real regression: `scripts\fork-identity.ps1` mutated on disk scored `FAIL C4 ... regressed=` naming iOSApp.swift and the two TitlebarTabs windows, exit 1, manifest not rewritten. The drift case: `HACKING.md` planted in the manifest with a stale sha - the T1073 shape exactly - came back as a drift line, ALL PASS, and aged itself out. Clean: ALL PASS (55), tree unchanged. `guard-due.ps1` now reports `GUARD CURRENT fork-identity`.

  Floor: all four lanes PASS. The edit to a `test\win32\` script made five harness meta-audits due and all five re-ran green and re-stamped - isolation-meta (13), launch-preflight (19), verdict-exit, cleanslate (19), stderr-capture (25). `suite-run` stays red for T1164, which predates this turn and is not touched by it, so this commit still uses `-NoGuardDue` naming that task - and that is the thread this turn leaves behind. Filed T1165: `-NoGuardDue` switches off all ~90 guard rows at once, which is the right hatch for "this harness cannot run here" and the wrong one for "this harness is red for a task already in the queue". `ack-stranded` (T847) is the shape to copy - an ack that names the owning task and evaporates when that task closes.
