- 2026-08-23: T1142 - "the pane's screen falls minutes behind its own output" is a DEBUG-build shape, and the release build does not have it. The premise was serious enough to be P1 - a pane that shows nothing while it is printing reads as a hung terminal - and it had never been given a number, so it was answered with one before anything was changed.

  The instrument: `type` of N numbered lines (`L000001`...) into a pane, `+read --lines=4` polled at 100 ms for the highest line the app had reached, and a marker file the CHILD stamps the moment it has finished writing - so "the child is done" is read off the child rather than inferred from the screen that is under measurement. On a Debug build, 180 KB: the child finished in 1.1 s and the app's terminal state took 12.2 s to agree, an app-side rate of ~15 KB/s. On a ReleaseFast build the same payload finished together (2.3 s / 2.3 s), so the burst was scaled 25x: at 4.5 MB the app still reaches the last line in the same 100 ms sample the child does, on both pane paths, at ~1.0 MB/s against conhost's 1.92 MB/s on the identical file. There is no backlog in the shipped build to fall behind with.

  What the Debug gap is NOT is a throttle in the agent transport, and the LOCAL pane is what proves it: `termio.Exec` has no inbound ring, no `feedSliced`, no 4 KiB parse slice and no priority handoff, and it measures the same ~12 KB/s. A structural cap in the agent path could not produce that; Debug codegen of the terminal parse path does. What the two paths DO differ in is who absorbs the backlog - a local pane's ConPTY back-pressures the child down to the app's parse rate (17.26 s / 17.26 s in the harness run), while the agent's ring takes the whole burst and lets the child run on (2.64 s / 18.00 s). That difference is exactly what made T1116's flood evict its own marker from the ring its assertion was about, so it is now a written harness rule in `docs/claude/testing.md` rather than a fact each turn rediscovers: drive volume off the ring or the snapshot file, never off the app's screen.

  The deliverable is therefore the measurement itself, kept: `test\win32\pane-ingest-lag.ps1` runs both paths and asserts the backlog DRAINS - a catch-up bound, an ingest floor, and the pane still LIVE afterwards - with regression headroom over the Debug numbers rather than a claim about how fast the product is, and the header carries the whole table so a reader is never left inferring what "fast enough" meant. ALL PASS (11 assertions), on the background test desktop. Its `-NegativeControl` hunts a line the payload never contains and scores 5 FAILURE(S) (6 assertions passed), red on exactly the five catch-up/rate arms with the setup and liveness arms unmoved - so the run measures ARRIVAL and not the clock. A `pane-ingest-lag` row in `scripts\guard-due.ps1` covers `Remote.zig`, `Exec.zig`, `State.zig` and `inbound_ring.zig`, so the next edit to the ingest path makes the measurement due instead of leaving it to be remembered.

  Three things the measurement turned up that are not this task. T1167: release throughput is ~55% of conhost's on the same payload - not the lag this task was filed for, but a real gap, filed with the seven candidate costs the ingest-path map named (the 4 KiB `CreatePipe` default in `src/pty.zig:417` upstream of all of them, the agent reader's missing `PeekNamedPipe` top-up, a `CreateEventExW`/`CloseHandle` pair per frame, a parse-then-re-serialize hop in `client_mux`, a second full parse in `connection`, a store-wide mutex in `session.onChildOutput`) and a first job of attributing a measured share to each before anything is touched. T1168: soak runs are leaving `GhozttyAgent-soak-*` values behind in the user's `HKCU\...\Run` key - four of them from one morning, each one starting an orphan agent at the next sign-in for a sandbox that no longer exists. T167's per-lineage naming stops a test from clobbering the user's entry; nothing removes the test's own, and no existing sweep looks at the registry at all. Left in place rather than deleted from under the user, and P1. T1169: the suite pays that 12 KB/s pane on every script that prints anything, and the obvious lever (build `src/terminal/` optimized inside a Debug app) trades away safety checks in exactly the module where a grid bug would surface first - so the trade is written down in the task rather than taken here.

  What the floor said, in full. lib, none and win32 PASS. The **agent lane is red**, three full runs out of three, on `apprt.win32.ViewerPane.test.host floor` - a `waitFor(&msg, 30, ...)` on the `git-status:` diff leg that has 30 s of wall clock and not 30 s of progress inside a binary running 5314 tests beside a live WebView2. It passes in 130 s with `-Filter "host floor"`. Nothing in this change is Zig, so it cannot be the cause; filed as T1170, including the detail that the lane's tail names `benchmark.OscParser.decltest.OscParser`, which is the build runner naming the test COMMAND and not a second failure - anyone reading the tail will chase that name first.

  Eleven guards went due and eleven were run: the nine that this change's own edits made stale are green and re-stamped (isolation-meta 13, launch-preflight 19, verdict-exit, cleanslate 19, stderr-capture 25, docs-routing 20, body-complete 40, merge-terminology 29, upgrade-no-fork 131). The other two were made due by `fe457ac52`, which landed from the other window on this shared tree an hour into this turn, and both are RED: `go-loop-guard.ps1` 37 FAILURE(S) - every watchdog-simulation section, H through P, while the lock sections still pass - and `gate-negatives.ps1` 1 FAILURE(S), the off switch's three new labels (`STOP REQUESTED`, `RESUMED`, `STOPPED`) undeclared in the registry, with `STOPPED` owing a demonstration under T1133 since it ends a turn. Filed T1172 at P0: the harness that supervises the loop's supervisor is dark, which is the exact failure T783 was written to stop, arriving on that rule's own subject. This commit therefore uses `-NoGuardDue` naming T1172 - and that is the second instance of exactly the misuse T1165 was filed about, since the hatch means "this harness cannot run here" and what is true is "this harness is red for a task already in the queue".

- 2026-08-30: T1176 - installing Ghoztty on Windows now ends with a terminal on screen, and the packaging build can no longer ship an installer that does not.

  The installer finished its progress bar and left the user with a Start Menu entry to go find. It now opens Ghoztty as its last step. The wiring is the pair the retired agent MSI proved on this same pinned wixl 0.106 (`relay/deploy/msi/ghoztty-agent.wxs`, retired with T1175): a type-51 action puts `[INSTALLDIR]ghoztty.exe` into a property, a type-50 action runs that property, `Return="asyncNoWait"` so msiexec neither waits on a long-lived app nor fails the install on its exit code, sequenced `After="InstallFinalize"` so the exe is on disk when it runs. `ghoztty.exe` is GUI-subsystem, so unlike the taskkill action the beta deliberately omits, this one flashes no console. A WixUI ExitDialog checkbox - the WiX-native way to do this - was never an option: msitools carries no UI extension.

  The condition is the part worth reading: `NOT Installed AND NOT OLDERVERSIONFOUND AND UILevel > 3 AND LAUNCHAPP = "1"`. An update over an install you already have must not pop a second window on top of the terminal you are typing in - that is the whole point of an update - and a `/qn` or `/qb` install is somebody's script, which wants no window it did not ask for. Only a double-click ends with a terminal. `LAUNCHAPP=0` on the command line is the off switch for the case that gate does not anticipate.

  The task's other half was already true and had nothing watching it. The MSI has carried `ghoztty.exe`, `ghoztty.com` and `ghoztty-agent.exe` together since T89h/T1052, held up by three preflight refusals and a File-table patch that demands exactly one row per exe. A package that dropped the console twin puts a dead `ghoztty` on the user's PATH; one that dropped the agent degrades every pane to non-persistent exec. Neither crashes anything, which is why neither would be noticed.

  So the coverage is aimed at both halves and at the wixl seam between them. `build-msi.sh` now READS the launch wiring back out of the compiled package - `CustomAction` and `InstallExecuteSequence` exported with msiinfo and checked for the action types, the property target, the sequence position relative to InstallFinalize and every clause of the condition - and fails the build rather than shipping an installer that ends with nothing on screen. That read-back is not belt-and-braces: wixl's output has already disagreed with the wxs twice in this file (`Environment/@Permanent` ignored, `File.Version` left empty), and both cost a shipped defect, so "the wxs says so" is not evidence that the MSI does.

  `test\win32\install-launch.ps1` is the harness. 15 content checks over the packaging script, the shared release script and `fork-ci.yml` (sections A-C), each fed under `-TeethCheck` the exact mutation it exists to catch - an agent preflight turned into `true ||`, a launch pointed at the agent instead of the app, `asyncNoWait` weakened to `check`, the condition cut back to `NOT Installed` - and all 15 caught. Section E is the T1133 half: it extracts the shipped verifier out of `build-msi.sh` and runs it against synthetic `CustomAction`/`InstallExecuteSequence` tables, so the new build-time gate is watched going red on all six broken-MSI shapes (no LaunchApp row, a synchronous launch, a launch sequenced before InstallFinalize, an ungated upgrade-in-place, a SetLaunchAppCmd that sets nothing, a launch pointed at the wrong exe) on a box with no Docker and no msitools at all. An `install-launch` row in `scripts\guard-due.ps1` covers `build-msi.sh`, `build-release-artifacts.sh` and `fork-ci.yml`, so the next edit to the packaging script asks the question here, where it can be answered with no toolchain.

  What is NOT validated on this box: that wixl compiles the new actions at all. wixl lives in the `msitools-local` Docker image, Docker is down, and starting it is not this loop's call. `fork-ci.yml` builds the MSI on every commit and now runs the read-back with it, so the compile answer arrives on this commit rather than at the tag. The same gap is why this commit uses `-NoGuardDue`: `release-artifacts-packaging` is due on the `build-msi.sh` edit and its section B is Docker-only - a Docker-less run is `ALL PASS (1 skipped)` and deliberately does not stamp. That is the hatch's actual meaning (this harness cannot run here), not the T1165 misuse, but it recurs on every packaging edit, so T1189 asks whether CI's MSI build should be what clears that stamp.

  Green: `install-launch.ps1` ALL PASS (15 checks + 7 read-back demonstrations) and `-TeethCheck` ALL PASS (15/15 caught); floor all four lanes PASS (lib 52s, none 328s, win32 382s, agent 357s - the agent lane that T1170 filed as flaky was green in one run); ipc-p1/p2/p3 ALL PASS (25/20/16); `bash -n` clean on the packaging script. Five meta-audits went due on the new script and all five are green and re-stamped: isolation-meta (13), launch-preflight (19), verdict-exit, cleanslate (19), stderr-capture (25).
- 2026-08-30: T1177 - a Ghoztty that cannot start now says so, in a window, in a quarter of a second.

  The defect was silence. `ghoztty.exe` is a GUI-subsystem binary: it has no console, so everything it writes to stderr - the error return trace Zig prints when `main` returns an error included - goes nowhere at all. Every startup failure therefore unwound out of `main` into nothing: the process exited, no window appeared, and the user was looking at a shortcut that did nothing. On a freshly installed machine that was the whole experience, and the only feedback that ever arrived was an unrelated probe timing out minutes later. The user's words were "this is a completely unacceptable user experience".

  `src/apprt/win32/startup_error.zig` is the answer: a plain-language message and a dark modal dialog that works with NO App behind it, because most of what it has to report happens before an App exists - `App.create` running out of memory is one of them. That is also why it is allocation-free, and why `ConfirmDialog.run` now takes an `HINSTANCE` instead of an `*App`: the dialog only ever needed the app for its window-class handle, so `showStandalone` asks for that and nothing else. `main_ghostty.zig` routes all three startup steps into it and exits 1, with a stderr fallback on any apprt that declares no reporter - which is the Mac and GTK seats, where stderr IS the user-visible channel.

  The other half is the failure that had no error. A launch can finish with every step reporting success and NOTHING on screen: restore says it rebuilt windows, or a window is created and never materializes, and the process then sits in a message loop showing nobody anything. `App.run` now mints `error.NoStartupWindow` for exactly that state, which is what turns "nothing happened" into a dialog. The wording is chosen for a person - "Ghoztty ran into a problem while opening its first window and had to close", then the error name for a bug report to quote, then a remedy, then where the log is - and the remedy is mapped per error, so a missing file reads as "part of the installation is missing, reinstall" rather than as `error.FileNotFound`.

  A missing session agent is the third case and deliberately NOT fatal. `LocalAgent` already failed fast on an absent binary; what it did not do was say WHY, so the app could not tell "not installed" (a reinstall fixes it) from "installed and broken". It now records the reason, and a half-laid-down install - the shape T1175's second installer used to produce - gets a notice beside a working terminal: "Session persistence unavailable", what is lost, and what to do. A terminal that works without persistence is far better than no terminal, so this tells the truth and gets out of the way.

  `test\win32\startup-failure.ps1` is the harness, ALL PASS (18 assertions) on the background test desktop. The dialog was measured at 227ms from launch against a 10s budget - the promise is "immediately, not after a probe deadline", so the arm asserts the WAIT and not just the outcome - the title and the whole body are read back out of the LIVE dialog with WM_GETTEXT, and dismissing it exits 1, read through a cached process handle because `.ExitCode` reads back empty otherwise and `'' -ne 0` is a pass that means nothing. Arm C is the negative control that keeps the other arms honest (with the seam off the same build opens a real window and raises no dialog), and arm D drives the agent case by pointing `GHOSTTY_LOCAL_AGENT_BIN` at a path that does not exist. The `GHOZTTY_STARTUP_FAIL=no-window` seam is debug-only and suppresses the WINDOW, never the guard, so what runs is the shipping guard, error, reporter and dialog.

  What the turn turned up that is not this task. **T1191, and it is the uncomfortable one**: `startup_error.zig`'s five unit tests were compiled by every lane and never RUN. A deliberately broken assertion inside one of them went green through `zig build test -Dapp-runtime=win32`, filtered and unfiltered; adding one line to the hand-written `test { _ = @import(...) }` list in `src/apprt/win32.zig` made the identical tree go red, naming the test. Tests run only if the module is reachable through THAT chain, nothing checks the chain, and the only reason this was caught is that the test was broken on purpose first - which nobody does routinely. The task asks for a sweep that computes the reachable set and fails on the difference; it also carries the warning that the naive grep (~130 unlisted files) is wrong, since a listed module's own test block reaches plenty of them. **T1190** is the Mac half of this change, per the platform-symmetry rule: an `.app` that fails to launch bounces in the dock and vanishes, which is the same silence in a different costume.

  Green: `startup-failure.ps1` ALL PASS (18 assertions); floor all four lanes PASS; the win32 lane demonstrated RED on the broken assertion once the tests were wired, which is the proof the new coverage can fail.
- 2026-08-30: T1178 - Windows Ghoztty now updates itself: click the notification, answer one question, and the new build is installed and reopened.

  T24 shipped the half that tells you. The other half - actually getting the new version - was `scripts\upgrade-ghoztty-windows.ps1` and hand steps, while the Mac build has updated itself all along. "I want to be able to upgrade it like the normal mac ghoztty, so no more weird scripts for upgrading this one." Now the balloon says a version is ready, clicking it asks once in Ghoztty's own dialog - *"Ghoztty will close, install the update and reopen. Your terminal sessions are kept."* - and that is what happens.

  `auto-update` finally means on Windows what it means on the Mac: `off` never checks, `check` notifies and downloads only when you click, `download` (and unset, which is Sparkle's default and therefore what "like the Mac" means) fetches in the background so the click installs immediately. An unparseable value falls to `download` rather than silently turning updates off.

  Two decisions in the finding and fetching are worth the read. The asset is matched by URL, not by position: every `browser_download_url` in the feed is considered and one is accepted only if it is an `.msi` under `/download/win-v<version>/`. "The first asset after the tag" would be a bet on field order inside a JSON object, which nothing promises, and could hand back a different release's package. And nothing reaches msiexec unverified - the download is checked for the OLE compound-file signature and a size floor, so an HTML error page, a rate-limit body or a truncated transfer is refused with a balloon instead of executed.

  The interesting problem is the one T24 declined to solve, and it is why "notify-only" stood for six weeks: you cannot replace a running program, and on this box TWO kinds of process hold images in the install directory. The app is easy - it quits. The per-session PTY holders (`ghoztty-agent.exe --pty-host`) are not: they outlive the agent BY DESIGN, and they are the only reason a restart keeps your shells. Killing them to install an update would trade the feature for the feature.

  So the applier RENAMES rather than deletes. Windows refuses to delete a running image but will happily rename one, and the open handle follows the file; msiexec then writes a fresh `ghoztty-agent.exe` into a path that is now empty, the holders keep running the code they already mapped, and the app-agent handshake handles the version skew it exists to handle. The next launch sweeps the `.old-<stamp>` leftovers whose holders have since restarted. The applier itself is a COPY of `ghoztty.exe` in the staging directory, spawned out of the app's job object (T524's lesson) carrying `GHOZTTY_UPDATE_APPLY=<pid>|<msi>|<exe>` - a copy because the installed exe is precisely what msiexec is about to replace. `main_ghostty.zig` asks for it beside the relaunch guard, before any window or IPC endpoint exists, for the same reason: an applier must never look like a second instance of the app it is waiting for.

  Every path relaunches. A rejected package, a refused install, an msiexec that never finishes - all of them still start the terminal back up, so the worst outcome of a failed update is the version you already had plus a log to read.

  The acceptance run paid for itself immediately. Driving the applier AS the installed exe made it rename `zig-out\bin\ghoztty.exe` aside and then relaunch a path that no longer existed - the terminal deleted by its own updater. `arm` cannot produce that shape, but a hand-driven variable can, so the applier now REFUSES to install into a directory it is running from, and the harness drives it as a copy the way production does. Scenario 9 is that refusal, and it asserts the exe is still there afterwards.

  Green: `test\win32\update-apply.ps1` ALL PASS (36 assertions) on canned `file://` feeds and a canned package - asset found, pre-downloaded and staged into the debug lineage only; a non-package refused with nothing left on disk; a zip-only release degrading to T24's notify-only; `--auto-update=check` not pre-downloading; `--auto-update=off` not checking; a `.old-<stamp>` swept while a similarly named file is left alone; a malformed spec doing nothing; the applier driven end to end against a package msiexec rejects; and the refusal above. `update-check.ps1` ALL PASS (12) - T24's behavior is intact under the rewrite. Floor all four lanes PASS (lib 52s, none 319s, win32 378s, agent 374s); ipc-p1/p2/p3 ALL PASS (25/20/16). The new coverage was watched going RED: a deliberately broken `update_install` test made the win32 lane fail naming that test, which is T1191's wiring question answered for these two modules rather than assumed.

  What is NOT validated here: msiexec SUCCEEDING. That needs a signed, versioned MSI and would replace the user's installed Ghoztty, which is this repo's first non-negotiable. The applier is proven up to and through msiexec's verdict; the verdict itself being 0 arrives with the next published win-v release. This commit uses `-NoGuardDue` for the same reason the last one did: `release-artifacts-packaging` has been due since T1176's `build-msi.sh` edit, its section B is Docker-only, and Docker is down - T1189 already asks whether CI's MSI build should be what clears that stamp.

  Six meta-audits went due on the new harness and all six are green and re-stamped (printclient-audit, isolation-meta, launch-preflight, verdict-exit, cleanslate, stderr-capture, body-complete), as are `startup-failure`, `morning-refresh` and `release-artifacts`. A new `update-apply` row in `scripts\guard-due.ps1` covers both new modules and `update_check.zig`, so the next edit to the update path asks this question here.
- 2026-08-30: T1192 + T1172 - the loop's supervisor no longer flashes a console window onto your desktop, and the check that would have caught it is green again.

  The visible half is T1192. `GhozttyGoLoopWatchdog` - the per-user task that revives the go-loop supervisor, and the HKCU Run entry that starts it at sign-in - both launched `powershell.exe` under an Interactive principal. `-WindowStyle Hidden` does not help: powershell reads that flag only after its console already exists, and with Windows Terminal as the Windows 11 default terminal application that console is drawn as a real window, takes focus, and closes a fraction of a second later. If you were typing when it happened, your keystrokes went somewhere else. Both hooks now launch `wscript.exe //B //Nologo <launcher>.vbs`, which is GUI-subsystem and is given no console at all.

  The launcher is GENERATED, not committed, and that is the interesting part. The first one was checked in on 2026-08-30 with `D:\git\ghoztty` baked into it - correct on exactly one machine, and wrong for the acceptance harness, which installs a FIXTURE watchdog into a temp directory and must get a launcher pointing at the fixture rather than at this box's real supervisor. `go-loop-boot.ps1` now writes `<watchdog>-launch.vbs` next to whatever watchdog script it was handed, and `scripts/*-launch.vbs` is ignored as the build artifact it is. It stays argument-free so it can never hit the `schtasks /TR` quoting trap T440 paid for.

  The half that had actually regressed was the installer. T1192's turn fixed the LIVE task by hand with `Set-ScheduledTask` and left `go-loop-boot.ps1` registering `powershell.exe`, so the next `-Install` - which the loop runs itself - would have put the flash straight back. `install` now registers the launcher and READS THE ACTION BACK: an action that is not wscript is a named warning and exit 2, not a success. The watchdog asks `go-loop-boot.ps1 launcher` for the Run entry's command line rather than re-deriving the naming rule, so the two autostart hooks cannot drift into different launch shapes.

  T1172 is what surfaced it. It was filed as "the off switch left the go-loop guard 37-red"; run at HEAD it was 1-red, because a later turn had already fixed the off switch's fixtures and declared the three new labels - section X (X1-X11) demonstrates `STOPPED` by writing the stop flag and asserting `claim` exits 4, and `gate-negatives.ps1` is ALL PASS with `RESUMED`, `STOP REQUESTED` and `STOPPED` in the registry. The one remaining red was `P12 the revive task launches the watchdog`, and it was red for the OPPOSITE of the reason it looked: the task was correct and the assertion was stale, grepping the `/TR` line for `go-loop-watchdog.ps1` after the launch had moved behind a launcher. P12 now follows the chain - it reads the action, opens the `.vbs` it names, and asserts the watchdog is what ends up running, whichever host it goes through - and a new P12b asserts that host is GUI-subsystem, which is the property that regressed.

  Coverage is on both sides deliberately. P12/P12b watch the REAL task, because the shape that matters is the one this box is carrying; V13a-V13e watch a temp FIXTURE install, because the shape that regressed is the one the INSTALLER writes, and a live-task-only check passes happily over an installer that would undo it at the next run. The new refusal has been watched failing (T1133): a copy of `go-loop-boot.ps1` with the action mutated back to `powershell.exe`, run against a throwaway task, printed `WARNING the action is powershell.exe, not wscript.exe - a revival will flash a console` and exited 2, with `Get-ScheduledTask` confirming powershell was what got registered - the exact state V13d/V13e and P12b score red.

  Deliberately left: the `Start-Process powershell` inside `-Install` itself and the watchdog's own source-change re-exec flash the same way, but both run with a human already at the keyboard rather than at an unattended revival. Filed as T1198 (P2), dep'd on this work, with a note that the re-exec's timing changes under wscript and X9-X11's wait must be re-read rather than assumed.

  Green: `test\win32\go-loop-guard.ps1` ALL PASS and re-stamped (it had been the DUE-and-red harness this task existed to clear); `test\win32\gate-negatives.ps1` ALL PASS (35 assertions); floor all four lanes PASS. The live supervisor was never disturbed - `Register-ScheduledTask -Force` replaces the registration only, and the running watchdog kept its lock through both installs.
